The top three U.S. electric-aircraft makers are taking different approaches to the same challenge: how to make short-hop flight cleaner, quieter, and commercially useful.

Kyle Clark, a native of Vermont, founded Beta in 2017 to realize his long-held dream of building a hybrid-electric aircraft. (For his bachelor’s thesis at Harvard University, he designed a flight-control system for such an aircraft.) Martine Rothblatt, CEO of the biotech company United Therapeutics and cofounder of SiriusXM satellite radio, invested $48 million in Beta to fund its first prototype, with the eventual goal of using the aircraft to transport organs for transplantation.

The company has kept much of its design and manufacturing in-house, partly because the pieces are closely coupled and partly because suitable aviation components didn’t exist when development began. Vertical integration gives Beta’s engineers control over the interfaces and any failure data. But it also means the company must be competent at several businesses simultaneously: airframes, electric motors, inverters, batteries, software, chargers, and aircraft production.

The production line can build both the fixed-wing CX300 and the vertical-lift A250, which share the same fuselage, wings, pusher motor (for horizontal propulsion), batteries, avionics, and much of the tooling. This results in some one-size-fits-all decisions: The CX300’s twin booms, which connect the wing to the tail surfaces, look superfluous until you see the A250’s four lift propellers mounted on similar structures.

On the CX300, those booms add weight and drag even though they serve no lift function. But the trade-off—a simpler overall design—is part of Beta’s central strategy: Rather than applying for FAA certification for the more novel and complex eVTOL A250, with its multiple lift systems and transitions between hover and wing-borne flight, the company is bringing the runway version forward first. It’s certifying the motor, batteries, fly-by-wire controls, and much of the airframe in the simpler aircraft; it will then reuse evidence and manufacturing experience when it certifies the A250.

The other big reason to start with the CX300 is logistical: The United States has more than 5,000 public-use airports, so the CX300 can operate from infrastructure that already exists. The cargo and medical flights that the aircraft will initially tackle offer tightly defined missions in which lower energy and maintenance costs matter more than cabin amenities. Hence the company’s decision to leave cabin air-conditioning off the CX300, at least for now. “Things that don’t exist on an airplane don’t weigh anything,” Clark says. “They can’t break. You don’t have to service them…. You don’t have to certify them.”

“This strategy, at the beginning, was seen as a failure of their VTOL,” says analyst Sergio Cecutta, a managing partner at SMG Consulting. “But I think a lot of people were very myopic. It was a way for [Beta] to break up the certification in two pieces, and so they have retired a lot of the risk. [A majority] of the [CX300’s] parts are shared with the VTOL, and that means that a lot of the documentation for certification can be easily reused on the VTOL side when that certification starts.”

A decade and a half after electric cars began making significant inroads into the automotive market, electric airplane technology is advancing rapidly. In some ways, an electric car has more complicated power-engineering requirements than an electric aircraft. An electric car’s power demands change constantly, while an electric aircraft operates in a narrower set of power regimes: takeoff, level flight, and descent.

But if your car’s drivetrain fails, you can just pull over to the side of the road. That’s not an option for a pilot 1,000 meters up. The hurdle isn’t that electric motors are inherently fragile; it’s that aviation safety standards are extraordinarily demanding. Catastrophic failure conditions generally must be held to roughly one chance in a billion flight hours or less.

The two versions of Beta’s Alia aircraft—the A250 [shown] and the CX300—share many of the same components, which the company believes will speed up FAA certification.

Because individual electrical components cannot meet that standard on their own, electric aircraft rely on layered redundancy: duplicate power paths, independent inverters, fault isolation, monitoring, and backup capacity. Each layer helps close the safety gap, but each also adds weight and complexity.

To close the reliability gap and satisfy regulators who have little experience with electric aircraft, Beta engineers have built redundancy into the motor itself. When I visit the company’s motor shop, technicians are assembling the H500A pusher motor, which splits up critical components like the inverters and stator sections.

“You could lose an entire half of the system, and it would still function the same,” says Adam Lowe, Beta’s flight operations lead.

The H500A’s broad diameter gives the magnetic forces greater leverage, producing high torque at low rotational speed, a useful trait when turning large propellers. The H500A weighs about 75 kilograms and produces about 640 kilowatts of power. The motor achieves 97.5 percent efficiency, based on internal testing; typical conventional turboprops have an efficiency range of 25 to 35 percent.

Beta had aimed to have its motor certified in the first half of 2026, a deadline that passed without a public announcement. Although the company’s certification strategy is aimed at streamlining the process, getting clearance to fly from the Federal Aviation Administration is probably still its biggest obstacle. For Beta, and any company trying to bring an electric aircraft into service, the FAA must sign off first on the propeller, then the motor, then the aircraft. After that, the manufacturer must pursue a production certificate from the FAA, proving that the company can build the same approved aircraft again and again, with the right tools, records, inspections, quality controls, supplier oversight, training, calibration, and parts tracking.

Beta has found a narrow on-ramp to get the A250 flying before full certification. Under the FAA’s eVTOL Integration Pilot Program, companies and public agencies can run FAA-supervised, real-world trials to test how advanced air-mobility aircraft might operate in the national airspace. For Beta, that included July flights of the CX300 across a Virginia-to-Maryland corridor carrying, among other things, a manufactured transplantable organ in a medical containment system. Beta has also been chosen for six other FAA-backed trials.

For the fixed-wing Alia CX300, customer trials are moving in parallel. In March, Beta’s CX300 successfully completed 23 flights over 10 days on Loganair routes linking six Scottish cities. The airline has since signed a term sheet for five Beta aircraft, with options for five more and service expected to start in 2029.

Beta is pushing so hard for the A250 because the case for electric flight gets even more interesting with vertical-lift aircraft. Helicopters and other VTOLs have a less orderly life than fixed-wing planes do. They must hover, sidestep, turn in place, settle, climb, and hold themselves in the air by main force. But conventional helicopters are built around a rotor speed that varies only a few percent because the engine, transmission, and rotor system are all designed around one narrow operating point.

“One of the dreams of vertical flight has been to vary the rotor rpm,” says Anubhav Datta, an aerospace engineering professor at the University of Maryland, College Park, who studies electric propulsion and vertical flight. Electric motors, he argues, have advanced enough to make that practical. A rotor that can slow down or speed up as conditions change can waste less energy, make less noise, and better match the odd assortment of tasks that vertical flight demands.

Electric propulsion also lets designers break up the work with multiple motors. The weight of an electric motor is tied closely to its torque. If you spread that torque among several motors, each of the motors can shrink, meaning that their combined weight is less than would be needed for one big engine. This is one reason why so many electric aircraft designs appear to have sprouted propellers wherever an engineer found a place to put one.

There is a downside to using multiple smaller motors: If one of the motors quits, the rotor it’s driving has little stored energy compared to the inertia in a conventional helicopter’s one large rotor. This inertia can come in handy if the engine dies, because the rotor will continue to spin and allow the pilot to descend under control, in an emergency technique known as autorotation.

According to Beta Technologies founder and CEO Kyle Clark, his native Vermont—known more for its maple syrup and outdoorsy lifestyle than its technological achievements—is a big part of the secret to Beta’s success at attracting talent. “The recruiting strategy is this: You find anybody who has vacationed in Vermont or went to school here. And you say, ‘You can actually live here and have a high-paying job in a mission-driven business, doing something that you care about with great people.’ ” The company currently employs about 1,500 people, most of them in South Burlington, Vt., and is actively hiring for its engineering, manufacturing, software, flight operations, and commercial teams.

As befits an aviation company, Beta offers flying lessons for all employees—a perk that is intended to give engineers, software developers, pilots, and mechanics a common language. The company also operates a health clinic for employees and their families and is building a day care center. Those programs have an idealistic Vermont flavor that is shaped by Clark and his wife, Katie Clark, who is Beta’s head of brand, creative, culture and spaces. But they also serve a practical purpose: attracting and retaining the best people in a small labor market. —T.C.

Electric-aircraft makers compensate with redundant motors and electrical channels, but most leading designs also have wings to allow gliding. In Beta’s A250, that means that if all else fails, the pilot still has a shot at reaching a suitable landing spot.

That helps explain the convergence in today’s eVTOL designs. Joby Aviation’s S4 uses six propellers that tilt between lift and cruise. Archer Aviation’s Midnight has six tilting propellers and six dedicated lift props. Beta’s A250 keeps its four lift propellers horizontal and uses a separate pusher motor for forward flight.

In Beta’s home state of Vermont, the electricity produced in the state comes almost entirely from renewable sources. Of course, electric aviation’s climate advantage depends not only on how clean the power grid is, but on how efficiently the aircraft uses energy. The turbines in conventional jet engines are marvelous machines, but they throw away a lot of energy as heat. Plus they need to carry the hardware to manage that heat—inlets, ducts, radiators, oil coolers—and the drag that comes with pulling air through all of it.

Kyle Clark [in cockpit], founder and CEO of Beta Technologies, pilots the company’s Alia CX300, an electric plane that Beta expects to receive FAA certification in 2027. Clark began designing a hybrid electric plane while still in college.Beta Technologies

By contrast, an electric design, with no combustion, gearbox, or oil circuits, avoids much of that energy burden. The result is an aircraft that is more than twice as “slippery” in terms of its lift-to-drag ratio. Batteries will never come close to the fuel density of petroleum fuels. But because electric drivetrains are much more efficient than combustion engines, a battery doesn’t necessarily need to match the energy density of petroleum fuel to be useful.

While the motors on an electric aircraft provide the drama at takeoff and landing, the batteries set nearly every boundary: the range, payload, charge time, cooling load, reserve energy, and, ultimately, useful life. For now, the hardest limit on electric aviation is not imagination, software, or even motors. It is the stubborn weight of stored energy.

“One thing you notice about [electric] airplanes is that they are all small,” says Cecutta, the aviation analyst. “They are not small because someone has done a market study and decided that is the optimal size. They are small because you cannot make them big. This limitation is from the batteries.”

In a conventional aircraft, fuel accounts for a significant percentage of the takeoff weight. But that weight gradually disappears during flight. In an electric plane, the battery packs also account for a lot of the weight; in Beta’s CX300, they’re close to half the aircraft’s mass. But a drained battery at landing weighs the same as a fully charged one at takeoff. That means the rest of the aircraft must be light enough to lift a power source that never gets lighter, yet strong enough to endure vibration, turbulence, hard landings, and years of fatigue. The more engineers push to save weight, Datta notes, the more flexible the airframe becomes, making the wings and other structures more prone to bending, twisting, and vibration. In that sense, the battery problem becomes a structural problem, too.

Beta’s CX300 carries five liquid-cooled battery packs of about 45 kilowatt-hours each, giving the aircraft roughly 225 kWh of rated capacity, though not all of that may be usable in flight. Each pack weighs 255 kg and contains 2,772 cylindrical cells. Altogether, about 14,000 cells sit beneath the occupied cabin, each one a tiny storehouse of energy, heat, and potential trouble.

The burden of the battery explains much of what I see elsewhere in Beta’s aircraft: the 15-meter wingspan, the composite structure, and the almost doctrinal effort to leave out every piece of hardware and creature comfort that’s not essential to the mission. The CX300 even does without flaps, which most aircraft use to generate extra lift at low speeds, so it must take off and land unusually fast for an aircraft of its size.

On Beta’s battery line, commercially supplied standard 21-millimeter-diameter, 70-mm-long cells are tested and assembled. Cells become modules, modules become subpacks, and eleven subpacks become a 45-kWh pack. Cooling plates manage heat during normal operation, while passive barriers and electrical isolation are designed to contain the ugly edge cases that Beta’s testing process intentionally triggers.

The modular design of the packs will give Beta’s planes a path to better batteries as the cells and battery chemistry improve. Caputo tells me that the company is already evaluating higher-density cells at its battery testing facility in nearby St. Albans, Vt. More watt-hours per kilogram could eventually mean more range, more payload, or both.

What sets Beta Technologies apart from its competitors is the breadth of its ambitions: It’s not just building electric aircraft. It’s also cultivating a broader ecosystem to nurture the growth of electric aviation.

For instance, Beta intends its motor business to extend beyond its own aircraft. The company has delivered lift motors for Eve Air Mobility’s proof-of-concept aircraft and has a contract to supply up to $1 billion in pusher motors as Eve’s program develops. In addition, Beta is selling flight-control computers and software to Horizon Aircraft. It is also producing propulsion systems for the military, as well as the MV250, a hybrid-electric autonomous aircraft for defense missions.

Beta’s fast-charging stations [left] have been installed at 138 locations. The thermal-management station [right] keeps the battery from overheating during charging. The company uses the open-standard Combined Charging System (CCS) so that other aircraft can use its chargers. Beta Technologies

Further evidence of Beta’s far-ranging plans is visible near the battery line in the South Burlington facility, where workers are readying a few of the company’s 1.5-meter-tall Charge Cubes for shipping. Intended for installation at airports, each cube takes 480-volt AC from the grid and can deliver up to 320 kW at as much as 1,000 volts DC. According to Beta, charging either model of its Alia aircraft takes about 35 minutes, from the minimum charge required under visual flight rules to full state. A separate thermal-management cube circulates water-glycol coolant through the aircraft to keep the batteries from overheating during charging.

The charge cubes use the Combined Charging System (CCS), an open standard increasingly shared across the electric transportation industry. Beta’s strategy resembles Tesla’s decision to treat charging as part of the vehicle business, with one important difference: Beta is courting other aircraft makers, airports, and operators to use its technology. Archer, Atlantic Aviation, Signature Aviation, and government agencies have purchased or installed Beta’s charging equipment. As of October, Beta has 138 fast-charge locations, with additional sites in permitting or construction.

For charging beyond the fixed network, Beta offers a wheeled 40-kW Mini Cube and a 65-kW Mini Cube+ that can ride inside an Alia and plug into more modest electrical service. The Mini Cube can also charge cars, buses, and trucks—any vehicle that uses the CCS standard.

Back above Lake Champlain, the CX300 levels off, and the motor recedes to a faint hum. Then Caputo switches it off, and there’s nothing but the rush of wind around the canopy. The aircraft glides on its long wings while the coasting propeller turns the motor into a generator, feeding about 9 kW back to the battery.

Then we turn to the east and slip into the landing queue behind a National Guard C-130 Hercules, and Caputo powers and slides the throttle forward. The motor springs to life again, pushing the airplane, and perhaps aviation itself, into the future.

This article was updated on 29 October 2026.

Tom Clynes, an IEEE Spectrum contributing editor, is a writer and photojournalist who covers science and the environment.

This sounds like a test plane more than a commercial one, but I guess that makes sense while companies are figuring out how to integrate new technologies into our existing safety regulations.The other thing that stands out to me is how the motors have redundant sub-systems. I can see the value, but it sure seems like a steep price to pay in terms of weight and complexity. Looking forward to seeing how that evolves.

#3250. AMD needs a big quarter to escape Intel’s fate as AI fears grow

AMD's shares are still up more than 120% this year, but investors are punishing any sign of weakness.

AMD reports third-quarter results on Tuesday after its shares fell about 17% in two days alongside Intel. Analysts expect revenue to rise 41%, but investors say AMD needs a big beat and a strong outlook as AI spending fears grow.

AMD needs a strong quarter and a bold forecast when it reports results after the US market closes on Tuesday, investors told Bloomberg.

“A modest report just won’t cut it,” said Neville Javeri, a portfolio manager at Allspring Global Investments, which owns the stock.

The pressure comes from Intel. Its shares had their worst day since at least 1982 on Friday after a weak outlook. AMD fell 10% the same day and another 7.5% on Monday, though it is still up more than 120% this year.

Analysts expect AMD’s third-quarter earnings to jump 92% on a 41% rise in revenue. AMD had guided for about $13B in sales, after a record second quarter.

Part of the hope rests on processors. AI agents lean heavily on CPUs, as AMD’s chief technology officer argued in July, and the success of Meta’s Muse agents has led some analysts to raise their targets. Meta is AMD’s second-largest customer, and AMD’s Helios AI racks are now being tested there.

The risk is the mood around AI. Big spenders such as Alphabet and Meta have been punished for spending that eats into their cash, raising fears of a pullback that would hit chipmakers. In July, TSMC’s shares fell despite record revenue.

“I’m just not super comfortable with the valuation,” said Jim Worden of the Wealth Consulting Group, who has sold his AMD shares.

#3249. Apple Wallet driver’s licenses coming to three new states soon

Apple Wallet driver’s licenses recently launched in Virginia and Oklahoma, but three more states are expected to follow soon, bringing us close to 20 US states on board.

Digital IDs are becoming far more common than they were when Apple first added support in the Wallet app back in 2021. And today, 16 US states plus Puerto Rico support the feature on iPhone.

The latest additions, Virginia and Oklahoma, debuted just in the last couple months.

And it looks like three more states will be coming soon:

This summer evidence was discovered of both Utah and Virginia being added to Apple’s backend for driver’s license support. Virginia has since gone live, so it’s expected that Utah will launch as one of the next supported states.

Kentucky previously announced it will support Apple Wallet driver’s licenses after upgrading its digital ID system this summer. All indications are that the upgrade has been completed, so based on the state’s original plans, we should see licenses in Apple Wallet soon.

North Carolina recently announced the launch of its new digital driver’s license system. As part of the announcement, it confirmed licenses will be supported in Apple Wallet by early 2027.

Additional states might always surprise us and launch in Wallet before Utah, Kentucky, or North Carolina. We’ve seen a clear acceleration of states signing on to offer Wallet driver’s licenses.

But for now at least, the three states above appear the strongest candidates to debut soon.

For more info on states that have pledged Apple Wallet support, see our coverage here.

Would you use an Apple Wallet driver’s license if it launched in your state? Are you using one already? Let us know how it’s going via the comments.

#3247. iOS 27.2 adds two new features I’ve been really loving

iOS 27.2 arrived last week with a variety of new features and changes for iPhone. Here are two new iOS 27.2 features I’ve been loving lately.

I’ve used Apple Podcasts for the last few years after previously sticking with third-party apps. The native Podcasts app won me over with excellent features like transcripts and automatic chapters.

My main hesitation in recommending the Podcasts app, however, has been its confusing Up Next queue. Thankfully, iOS 27.2 delivers a long-awaited fix.

In iOS 27.2, the Home tab in Apple Podcasts splits Up Next into two separate sections: New Episodes and Continue Playing.

These new sections offer, in my view, a much better system than what was there before. I no longer lose track of episodes I’ve previously started, since they’re not getting replaced by new episodes in my queue. Instead, there’s a clear divide between what’s new and what’s in-progress.

Shared Albums have long been one of my favorite features in Apple Photos. I don’t post on social media often, but I do love sharing photos and videos with close family and friends via the Photos app.

iOS 27 brought big upgrades to Shared Albums, the first notable changes in years. And to my surprise, Apple has already introduced even more improvements with iOS 27.2. Per Apple:

Shared Albums in Photos adds the ability to edit captions and comments, to avoid adding duplicate photos, and can display a reminder before albums expire so participants can save important photos and videos

Support for editing captions and comments is long overdue, but a welcome addition. I also love the prompt that helps prevent duplicate photos, because I always find myself needing to double-check if I’ve shared certain photos already—now I don’t have to anymore.

#3246. Systems Thinking Is Vital in the Age of AI

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Machines can automate drudgery but engineers make key decisions

Sufian Aldogom is an IEEE member, a research affiliate at MIT, and a senior leader at Google in Sunnyvale, Calif.

Modern engineering projects increasingly combine human judgment with machine capability. An engineer can define a problem, then ask an artificial intelligence tool to search relevant research and technical standards, generate design options, test them in simulation, and compare the results. The engineer can then bring the results to specialists who understand the parts AI cannot judge on its own, such as whether a design can be built safely, whether it makes sense in a particular setting, or how it might affect its users. The final decision about whether and how to move forward remains a human responsibility.

AI can help engineers do early project steps that once required several people with different technical skills. The engineer’s role is therefore expanding from performing each technical step to deciding how people, machines, and specialists’ knowledge should work together on the project.

Engineering has always been divided into disciplines, and for good reasons. Electrical, mechanical, civil, software, and other engineering fields require deep knowledge that takes years to develop. AI does not replace that need. It simply changes how easily engineers can explore the parts of a problem that sit outside their own specialty.

Consider a software engineer working on a medical device. AI can help the engineer review relevant biomedical research, understand unfamiliar terms, analyze data, and build an early model.

That does not make the engineer a physician or biomedical expert. It allows the engineer to ask better questions before working with the experts.

The same is true in energy, transportation, manufacturing, and many other fields. A problem might begin as a software issue and then quickly involve hardware, safety measures, economics, human behavior, and regulations.

Engineers do not need to master every field; they need to recognize which expertise the problem requires and bring the right people and tools together.

Systems thinking thus becomes especially important. It requires looking at the whole problem: understanding how its parts affect one another, identifying constraints and failure points, and making trade-offs.

AI adds a new element to the process. Engineers must decide not only how the technical parts fit together but also what work to give to AI, what a person must check, when a specialist should make a decision, and when the problem needs to be redefined.

An engineer’s value is not in knowing everything. It is in knowing how to frame the problem, how to ask the right questions, how to test the answers, and when another expert must lead the project.

This aspect is crucial because technical challenges in engineering are seldom static. As new insights emerge, objectives might shift, unseen limitations can surface, and the initial premise might prove flawed. Rather than rigidly following the starting specifications, an effective engineer adapts and refines the scope as a deeper understanding of the system develops.

Thus, engineering extends beyond mastering technical concepts; it is an adaptable, structured approach to navigating evolving challenges.

New evidence can change the goal, reveal a hidden constraint, or show that the original hypothesis was wrong. Effective engineers go beyond merely acting on the initial problem statement. They update it as the system becomes better understood.

In that sense, engineering is not only a body of technical knowledge, it is also a disciplined way of thinking about a project.

AI can produce convincing answers even when its assumptions are weak. It can generate code that works in one test but fails in another. It can summarize research without understanding which evidence is strongest, or optimize a design for the wrong goal. Such limits make human expertise more important, not less.

Machines are useful where speed, scale, search, pattern recognition, and data generation matter. People are essential where context, values, responsibility, and judgment matter. The challenge is to decide where each belongs.

An AI system might generate several designs for a medical sensor, for example, and predict how each will perform. An engineer can test the predictions and reject designs that violate technical requirements. A clinician can determine whether the sensor can be realistically used. Patients and practitioners might reveal problems that neither the engineer nor the developer considered. The final solution emerges from combining the perspectives.

The engineer is still a builder and specialist but increasingly also a coordinator of knowledge.

An engineer’s value is not in knowing everything. It is in knowing how to frame the problem, how to ask the right questions, how to test the answers, and when another expert must lead the project.

The broader form of engineering creates an important role for IEEE. Its societies already bring together expertise in various technologies, engineering education, technical standards, and other fields. That makes IEEE well placed to help engineers work across specialties without weakening the value of specialization.

IEEE could create more communities organized around problems that require expertise from several fields. Examples include trustworthy clinical AI, resilient infrastructure, energy reliability, scientific discovery, and safe autonomous systems. An engineer could begin in a home discipline and then work with specialists from other IEEE communities as a project requires.

IEEE also can help set practical standards for human-machine collaboration. Engineers will need clear guidance on when AI-generated work must be checked, how uncertainty should be documented, when a specialist must make a decision, and who is responsible when a system uses both human judgment and machine output.

Those questions are becoming part of everyday engineering. They should not be left to each company or project manager to answer independently. A professional organization can provide common expectations that follow engineers as they move between jobs, industries, and technical fields.

AI does not make engineering disciplines less important; it makes the connections between them easier to use. Deep expertise gives engineers the foundation to judge what is sound. Systems thinking helps them understand how different parts of a problem fit together. AI can extend engineers’ ability to explore, test, and communicate across fields. Human judgment gives the work direction and responsibility.

An engineer is not defined only by a job title or a fixed set of tasks. An engineer is someone trained to understand complex systems, define and redefine problems, bring together the knowledge and tools needed to solve them, test whether solutions work, and take responsibility for the outcome.

That is what it means to be an “unbound” engineer.

The boundaries between specialties become easier to cross, and machines might take on more of the technical work, but the core of engineering remains human: deciding what problem is worth solving, what evidence is good enough, how the pieces fit together, and what to do when the answer is uncertain.

Sufian Aldogom is an IEEE member, a research affiliate at MIT, and a senior leader at Google in Sunnyvale, Calif.

#3245. Apple Watch’s always-listening AI tools arrive in the iOS 27.3 beta

The update also brings back the redesigned Health app and Apple's first AI features for China before December.

Apple released the first developer betas of iOS 27.3 and watchOS 27.3. They add Audio Intelligence for the latest Apple Watches, a redesigned Health app pulled from iOS 27.2, and Apple Intelligence for China. The full release is due in December.

Apple has released the first developer betas of iOS 27.3 and watchOS 27.3, putting the Apple Watch’s always-listening AI tools into wider testing, Bloomberg reported on Tuesday. The full release is due in December.

The Audio Intelligence features, unveiled in September for the Series 12 and Ultra 4, use the watch’s microphone to follow nearby conversations. Siri Recap turns them into bullet points, while Live Rewind shows a transcript of the last 15 seconds.

The tools work in English only for now. Apple says the audio is processed on the device and not stored, and that the watch plays a sound when Live Rewind is used.

Lawyers in several US states have warned the features could break eavesdropping laws that require everyone in a conversation to agree to being recorded.

The beta also brings back Apple’s redesigned Health app, which it tested in iOS 27.2 but removed in October. It adds a Longevity tab and a Health Age score that estimates a user’s age from their health data, features that rivals such as Whoop and Oura already offer.

iOS 27.3 also carries Apple’s first AI features for China, including writing tools and Genmoji. They leave out Siri AI, which runs on Google models that are not available in China.

Starting with VIVITROL. Net sales in the third quarter were $127.6 million. VIVITROL continued to see strong demand driven by penetration in the alcohol dependence market.

Net sales also benefited from approximately $8 million gross to net favorability, primarily driven by favorable patient mix. For the full year, we continue to expect VIVITROL net sales in the range of $460 million to $480 million. We remain confident in the strength and durability of our Vivitrol business and look forward to continuing our impact with this important medicine. Turning to our psychiatry franchise. Third quarter net sales for ARISTADA product family were $103.9 million. ARISTADA continued to see demand growth driven by expansion in HCP adoption. Net sales also benefited from approximately $7 million of gross to net and inventory favorability. We are encouraged by ARISTADA's continued strong performance within this category.

For the full year, we continue to expect ARISTADA net sales in the range of $365 million to $385 million LYBALVI net sales were $95.9 million in the third quarter. With underlying TRx growth of 18% year over year. Supported by new patient starts and broader prescriber adoption. Net sales also reflected approximately $2 million of inventory benefit. Last quarter, we implemented a strategic expansion of the LYBALVI market access profile that we believe will position LYBALVI for long term growth. Access now stands at approximately 80% of covered lives, as a result, we have already seen positive trends on volume demand in prescription fulfillment. As expected, gross to net adjustments were approximately 42% in the third quarter.

For the full year, we continue to expect LYBALVI net sales in the range of $380 million to $400 million Looking ahead to next year, we expect gross to net adjustments for LYBALVI to be in the 45% range. We expect the benefits of expanded payer access to be reflected first in prescription volume, which we expect will continue to grow nearly 20% year-over-year with an acceleration in net sales growth expected to follow. Beyond 2027, we expect volume growth and net sales growth to track more closely together again. Turning to our sleep franchise. LUMRYZ net sales were $89.9 million in the third quarter.

We reached approximately 4.1 thousand patients on therapy at quarter end, reflecting strong underlying demand, broader prescriber adoption, and increased use among existing prescribers. Net sales also reflected the drawdown of approximately $7 million of inventory build that we highlighted in our second quarter results. Last month, we presented results from the positive phase 3 REVITALIZE study of LUMRYZ in idiopathic hypersomnia at the Sleep Europe meeting. IH is a fast growing segment for the oxybate market. The REVITALIZE data will serve as the foundation for the sNDA submission for IH with the potential launch in March 2028, if approved. IH represents an important potential growth opportunity for LUMRYZ, and we look forward to updating you on our progress.

For the full year, we continue to expect total LUMRYZ net sales of $350 million to $370 million of which Alkermes expects to record $315 million to $335 million reflecting the mid February close of the Avadel transaction. Supporting LUMRYZ, we have an established sleep medicine platform that includes an experienced commercial and medical organization with a deep understanding of the market dynamics and HCP and patient journeys. This platform provides a strong foundation to support the potential launch of elixorexan and our broader ambition to become leaders in sleep medicine across multiple treatment modalities. Across our proprietary portfolio, we expect net sales to be in the range of $400 million to $420 million in the fourth quarter.

We are pleased with what we have accomplished so far this year and remain focused on delivering against our 2026 objectives. As we enter the final quarter, our priorities remain clear. Drive demand for our medicines, expand patient access, and position our brands for continued growth. With that, I will pass the call to Joshua to review the financial results for the quarter.

Blair C. Jackson: As you have heard from Todd and Joshua, our commercial business continues to perform well with a proprietary product portfolio expected to deliver net sales of nearly $1.6 billion in 2026. That foundation allows us to advance an increasingly broad pipeline led by our portfolio of orexin 2 receptor agonists. We are in the early stages of understanding the full therapeutic potential of orexin biology. Over the past several years, we have been generating a substantial body of clinical evidence across central disorders of hypersomnolence. And we are now generating our first clinical datasets from our orexin portfolio in broader areas of neuroscience.

Starting with elixorexin, our most advanced orexin candidate, we reached several important milestones across the development program during the quarter. Our Phase III BRILLIANCE studies in narcolepsy type 1 and type 2 are underway and we are pleased with enrollment progress across the program. We continue to expect top line results from these studies beginning in mid-2027. In idiopathic hypersomnia, we completed enrollment in the VIBRANCE-3 Phase 2 study, which enrolled approximately 130 participants. And will represent the first multi week clinical dataset of an oral orexin 2 receptor agonist in IH. The study is evaluating wakefulness and IH symptom severity with the Epworth sleepiness scale and idiopathic hypersomnia severity scale as primary and secondary endpoints, respectively.

Beyond evaluating the safety, tolerability, and efficacy of elixorexan in patients with IH, we expect the study to provide important insights to inform a potential registration program including dose selection, dosing regimen, and endpoint strategy. The study also includes our first evaluation of split dosing in a hypersomnolence disorder. Which we believe could provide additional flexibility to address the diverse needs of patients. We expect top line results around year-end or in early 2027 and look forward to sharing those data. Hypersomnolence disorders represent a significant market opportunity, And this month, the first orexin 2 receptor agonist is expected to become commercially available for the subset of patients with narcolepsy type 1.

As this new therapeutic category enters the commercial landscape, we believe that if approved, elixorexin's wide therapeutic range dosing optionality, and broad anticipated utility across narcolepsy types 1 and 2 and potentially IH will support a differentiated profile with the potential to provide an important new treatment option to providers and patients. While the commercial opportunity begins to take shape in hypersomnolence disorders, we are advancing our strategy to develop orexin 2 receptor agonist for a range of neuropsychiatric and neurodegenerative disorders.

Last month, we reported the first clinical results for ALKS 7.29 thousand in adults with ADHD This was a 50-subject Phase 1b proof of concept study designed primarily to evaluate safety and tolerability and to generate initial data characterizing the effects of ALKS 7.29 thousand across a range of established clinical scales for ADHD, CNS biomarkers, and objective cognitive performance tests. In the study, ALKS 7.29 thousand was generally well tolerated, with no serious treatment emergent adverse events and no treatment discontinuations among participants who received ALKS 7.29 thousand. Most treatment emergent adverse events were mild and largely consistent with on target effects for orexin 2 receptor agonist.

Across the 2 doses evaluated, ALKS 7.29 thousand demonstrated dose dependent clinically meaningful improvements from baseline on exploratory endpoints evaluating established measures of ADHD symptoms and disease severity. We were pleased to observe improvements across both inattentive and the hyperactivity impulsivity subscales of the adult ADHD investigator symptom rating scale or ACES with effects emerging as early as the first assessment on day 6. ALKS 7.29 thousand also demonstrated clinically meaningful improvements from baseline in overall ADHD disease severity as measured on the CGIS scale. In addition, we observed treatment effects across objective measures related to processing speed, information processing, working memory, and attention.

These findings provide the first clinical evidence of the effects of an orexin 2 receptor agonist in the treatment of adults with ADHD, and further support the dose range selected for the ongoing phase 2 study. That Phase 2 study is already enrolling adults with ADHD, and is designed to evaluate once daily in split dose regimens. Of ALKS 7.29 thousand with change from baseline in AISRS total score compared with placebo at week 4 as the primary endpoint. We expect the ADHD phase 2 data in the second half of 2027. Building our momentum in diseases outside of hypersomnolence, last week we announced the expansion of the ALKS 7.29 thousand development program into major depressive disorder or MDD.

With the initiation of a 150-patient phase 2 study evaluating ALKS 7.29 thousand as an adjunct to antidepressant treatment in adults with MDD who have had a partial response to standard antidepressant therapy. This randomized double blind placebo controlled study is designed to evaluate the safety and tolerability of ALKS 7.29 thousand over 6 weeks while also assessing its effects on depressive symptoms, as measured by change from baseline on the MADRS and CGIS compared to placebo at week 6. The study will enroll adults with and without excessive daytime sleepiness which will allow us to evaluate potential effects of ALKS 7.29 thousand in the overall MDD population as well as in this important subgroup.

Turning to orexin biology and neurodegenerative disorders. We plan to initiate a randomized double blind placebo controlled phase 2 study evaluating ALKS 4.51 thousand in people with fatigue associated with multiple sclerosis or Parkinson's disease. Fatigue is 1 of the most common and consequential symptoms across a broad range of neurological and systemic diseases. Yet effective treatment options remain limited. Fatigue associated with multiple sclerosis or Parkinson's disease are compelling initial areas for development with clearly defined patient populations, significant unmet need, and established clinical scales focused on fatigue.

We believe these disease areas offer attractable development pathway for established clinical proof of concept for orexin 2 receptor agonism in fatigue while also representing meaningful commercial opportunities in these patient populations. Importantly, the study is intended not only to evaluate the potential of ALKS 4.51 thousand in these specific disorders, but also to deepen our understanding of the role of orexin biology in fatigue more broadly. We believe these insights generated could help establish a foundation for evaluating additional disease areas where fatigue remains a significant source of patient burden and unmet need.

Elixorexan and hypersomnolence disorders ALKS 7.29 thousand and broader neuropsychiatric disorders, and ALKS 4.51 thousand and fatigue are components of a broader orexin portfolio development strategy that allows us to evaluate these distinct molecules across a range of patient population and disease settings. As we advance and expand these development programs, we are also continuing to advance additional orexin compounds through preclinical development. We are just beginning to explore the potential clinical utility of orexin compounds and Alkermes is at the leading edge of research for this emerging therapeutic class. Our focus will remain in neuroscience applications.

But with the potential to reach across a broad range of disorders, We believe the opportunity for this class is vast and will be the focus of significant research and development for years to come. Looking ahead, the next year will be a pivotal and data rich period for Alkermes. With 6 important studies expected to read out across our orexin portfolio. We start with anticipated data from the VIBRANCE-3 Phase II study of elixorexin in idiopathic hypersomnia in the coming months. Followed by top line results from all 3 BRILLIANCE Phase 3 studies in narcolepsy beginning in mid-2027.

For ALKS 7.29 thousand we expect phase 2 data in ADHD in the second half of 2027, followed by Phase 2 data in MDD in late 2027. And for ALKS 4.51 thousand phase 2 proof of concept data in fatigue, toward the end of the year. Taken together, these studies have the potential to significantly expand our understanding of where orexin based therapies can make a meaningful difference for patients. Our focus remains on executing with urgency and discipline. Generating the clinical evidence needed to unlock the potential of this novel class and building what we believe can become a leading franchise addressing some of the most significant unmet needs across sleep, neuropsychiatric, and neurological disorders.

We plan to pursue these opportunities while continuing to deliver strong commercial performance and investing thoughtfully to support long term growth and value creation. With that, I will turn the call back to Sandra for the Q&A.

Blair C. Jackson: Thanks for the question, Uy. Yeah. We have looked extensively at other areas outside of hypersomnolence where you could apply orexin agonism. And we did some comprehensive preclinical work really looking at the basic biology behind the orexin agonism and identified a number of different domains where you could apply this, some of them being cognition, fatigue, mood, wakefulness, all these different areas And so as part of that, we did some translational work in many of these areas. And within mood, some of the things we noticed is that we saw a really strong synergistic increase in serotonin in the prefrontal cortex when orexin agonism was given with SSRIs or SNRIs and so synergistically.

And I think that is that is really telling that there is there is a benefit you could have here by having adjunctive therapy with orexin agonism. We also did use the highly translational model as part of that early research which is the chronic social defeat test which is really a way of establishing rodents who have really a depressive phenotype and then providing them with therapy and seeing how they respond to treatment. And what we found is we found similar effects to what you would see with. If those animals were dosed with ketamine, or with fluoxetine. So we feel. To the to the first last part of your question regarding other things, yes, we have a number of other areas that we are looking at within neuroscience, both neurodegenerative and neuropsych and we will talk about those as we get closer to additional activity.

Blair C. Jackson: Yep. Thanks, Joon, for the question. So as we look at the ADHD program, we had 2 programs that are studies that we were running at the same time. We have first and foremost our large phase 2 outpatient study that we are running that is placebo controlled, multiple doses, etcetera. And what we wanted to do in the Phase 1b study was to ensure that we had some information that would inform on, 1, what are some of the types of signals that we would see, and 2, whether we were in the right dosage range overall. In order to do that, what we needed to do is learn a lot about how patients respond to orexin agonism.

Because remember, this is actually first asset of this mechanism that is ever been tested outside of hypersomnia indications. And so we needed to learn what we are doing, and that meant we had to put a lot of different tools within the phase 1 program. And in order to do that, you tried to do that in an outpatient type setting, that would be exhausting for the patient. So it would be very hard for you to operationalize that So that is why we chose an inpatient setting.

What it allows us to do is put those patients in a in a clinic, look at those different outcomes in a more in a more staggered pace that. that is appropriate for the patients. And we do not think that has any change on the overall baseline characteristics. I think overall, when we look at the incoming baseline characteristics, that is consistent with what we see with other ADHD studies. I think where it would. Where inpatient settings tend to have an impact on some of some things is on your safety outcomes. Because that. Sometimes what you tend to see in inpatient settings is those patients talking about their side effects.

And that can sometimes amplify side effects here and there. Again, we saw a very good AE profile from this program. So I think I think all in all, we got exactly what we wanted from this study. I think it validates the approach. And as we have always said, the phase 2 study that is ongoing is going to be the 1 that is gonna determine what is the characteristics or what is the signal size, related to this, to this drug treatment in this population. Great. Thanks so much.

Operator: Our next question comes from Umer Raffat with Evercore ISI. Please go ahead.

Umer Raffat: Good morning, guys. Thanks for taking my question. I wanted to touch up on 7.29 thousand as well, and a couple of points. First, I saw you guys used split dosing when conducting the inpatient ADHD trial. Do you think split dosing could be driving placebo response? And are you intending to continue using split dosing only? Your ongoing outpatient ADHD as well as MDD trial? And then secondly, the fact that you used up to 50 milligram dose of 92, what does that tell us about the potency relative to your narcolepsy Thank you very much.

Blair C. Jackson: Hi, Umer. it is nice to hear from you. I think, on the first question on the split dosing, so as we went into the ADHD study, 1 of the things we wanted to do as we are trying to learn on the signals is we did not want to confound some of the PK differences of single day dosing versus split dosing. We wanna take that out of the equation. So we use split dosing just because it was-- it is a more it just allowed us to standardize. I think as you look at our ongoing Phase 2 study, we are actually using both once daily and split dosing.

And I think that is important because, as you know, in the ADHD population, it is a bit of a lifestyle drug in some in some respects in that it-- patients have different needs. According to what-- whether they are working, whether they are students, what is happening in the evening, what happens in the morning, etcetera. And so I would envision that we will probably introduce other dosing types, maybe PRN and other things in the future after original registration. But we are going to do both. Moving forward, single day dosing as well as split dosing. Through the development program. With regards to the upper dose of 90, it is actually.

You cannot really use that to relate to narcolepsy. This is a fundamentally a different drug. It has different. It has a potency. It has different pharmacological characteristics. And then also keep in mind that the pharmacologic dose level that you need to activate the ADHD circuit may be different than what you need to activate, say, a wakefulness circuit. And so there is a lot of dynamics that are going on there that really do not-- do not really allow you to make that comparison.

Operator: Our next question comes from Ashwani Verma with UBS. Please go ahead.

Ashwani Verma: Hi. This is Leonid on for Ashwani. Thank you for taking our question. For the IH study, is it fair to assume that the baseline ESS scores are similar to what you had in the NT2 study? Also, is it fair to assume that the placebo arm in this IH study could closely resemble how the placebo did in the NT2 study?

Blair C. Jackson: Yeah. I mean, look, we have established very similar entrance criteria as in IH versus NT2. Now who ends up enrolling in the study depends on the study and which patients show up. So we will know that as we as we look at the data moving forward. I think as we as we look at this area overall, I think, you know, we feel pretty good that we are controlling placebo. Obviously, with wakefulness, 1 of the things to keep in mind is you do not tend to see such a big placebo response like you see in neuropsychiatric indications. So you tend to actually.

It really depends more on the treatment arm than it depends on the on the placebo arm. But, again, we will. We do what we can to control that, and we have done that in this in this program by really trying to standardize how we do the tests. Really making sure we have high quality control on our clinical sites.

Ashwani Verma: Got it. Thank you. And if I may have a follow-up I think you alluded to the long-form IH patients earlier. Can you talk about roughly what percentage of your IH patients would be the long-form IH?

Blair C. Jackson: So in our in our study, we have not disclosed what that is. I think as we look at the general population, though, with NIH, typically you see something in the order of around 25%. patients can be can be deemed long sleepers.

Operator: Our next question comes from Ami Fadia with Needham and Company. Please go ahead.

Ami Fadia: Yeah. Good morning. Thanks for taking my question. With regards to the upcoming IH study readout, I am trying to understand what. If we think about the trade off between efficacy of having split dose and maybe potentially implications on safety, Are there any guardrails in terms of those trade offs beyond which you may decide not to pursue a split dosing? And then secondly, is there some process within the study of determining which patients may be best suited for a split dosing, versus not, that could inform your next clinical trial. Thanks.

Blair C. Jackson: Hey, Ami, thanks for the questions. I think I think with the split dosing, you know, the-- there is-- we have a wide therapeutic range with this drug. So we remember when we went into our programs before, we studied in the NT 2 trial up to 18 milligrams. So. And we have an ability to go to go higher if we want to. So split dosing, we do not see sort of a safety question as to what is going to determine whether we move to split dosing. Now obviously, the data will tell us that. When we look at the NT2 data, if we see something unexpected, we will adapt accordingly.

But a priori, we anticipate that being a gating factor. What we are really looking for with split dosing is really a comparison to the once daily dose and in the subset of patients who require additional efficacy in the afternoon, do we see a difference? And if we do see that difference, that is gonna add additional flexibility for physicians to provide that dosage option to the patients. And remember, you know, in our NT2 study, we normalized I would say, about 70 percent of the of the patients on the ESS scale using the once daily dose So we anticipate even in IH that we are gonna see a good response on both dosage forms.

But we wanna have that added flexibility and that added efficacy for patients and that added flexibility that split dosing would provide. The second question was which again? Sorry, what I was trying to ask is there a way to learn from the study? As to a priori, patients may be best suited for a split dosing. Yeah, no, thank you. Thanks for the reminder. Yeah. Yeah. So you know, it is interesting. it is it is a priori what we do not know when patients come into the study is, are. Would you be better on a split dose or an-- or would you be better on a single dose?

And patients obviously in our study are gonna be randomized randomly into that into those categories. We will see if we learn anything from study of whether or not there are any patient characteristics that drive that? I think it would be surprising. I think 1 of the challenges when you get into NT2 and IH populations is there is this-- The science underlying the ideology of the disease is a little unclear. And so, in many ways, it is hard to. You cannot just use a standard biomarker to say a patient's gonna be responsive or nonresponsive or need an afternoon split dose.

So, we will learn in the NT2 study and it may just be that after this study, doctors are gonna have to empirically decide, see how their patients respond to the once daily dose. And then move them on to split dose if it is required. But the data will tell us, and we will adapt from there.

Operator: Got it. Our next question comes from Jessica Fye with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

Analyst: Hi, this is Paul Jeng on for Jessica Fye. Thanks for taking our question. For ALKS 7.29 thousand in MDD, given antidepressants typically fail to address residual fatigue and anhedonia, what magnitude of difference on matters do you consider clinically meaningful for this? Novel mechanism? Thank you.

Blair C. Jackson: Yeah, it is interesting that as you look at the MADRS scores and you look at things that are that are out there, I mean, I think, typically, people see a change versus placebo of somewhere between 2 and 5 as being a meaningful difference on MADRS And in fact, the. What the drug that is out now, Vraylar, which only had a 3-point change, 3.5-point change or so relative to placebo. Has strong uptake because it has unique characteristics. And so it has, a, a different mechanism, and, b, it has a rapid onset. And I think as you look at the MDD space, there is a number of areas where you can provide improvement.

Cognition, anhedonia, fatigue, as you alluded to. And we have seen things like cognition and fatigue benefits in some of our other trials. And so I think you. You know, I think the goal for us is to be able to show a statistical difference between placebo as part of MADRS, under the domains of where we see response, And if we can show something that is different that provides a different a broader profile than you see with the SSRIs, SNRIs, I think there is a there is a lot of opportunity there. I think there is there is a lot of room for improvement for these patients.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question comes from Jason Gerberry Bank of America. Please go ahead.

Jason Gerberry: Hey. This is Chi Meng Fong on for Jason Gerberry. Thanks. I have a follow-up on the expectation for Vibrance-3. What do you expect to see from the data for advancing the program to Phase 3? Is it driven by whether the study meeting the primary endpoint And what do you want to see as differentiated relative to other market offerings such as Do you want to see sort of magnitude of benefit on ESS or IHSS for the IH study?

And just quickly as a follow-up on your earlier commentary around expecting to see a similar response as in the Vibrance 2 study Is that commentary related to QD dosing in ESS scale as we think about the overlapping element between Vibrance-2 and Vibrance-3? Thanks so much.

Blair C. Jackson: Yeah. I mean, there is a lot in your question there. I think as you look at the Vibrance-3 study, you know, as you look at it, obviously, endpoints are ESS and IHSS. And we wanna be able to show a benefit within there. And for us, a phase 2 study, remember, is about is about trying to ensure and understand your signal. it is trying to understand your signal relative to your safety profile. And can you design your phase 3 trial in order to get over the line, show the statistical significance, show a benefit to those patients. Obviously, we wanna hit statistical significance as part of our phase 2 study if we can.

If we were to fall a little bit short, does that mean we would stop the program? No. As long as we feel that we have an appropriate signal that trial design would be able to overcome. That being said, you know, when we look at our early within this patient population, remember we had a once daily dosing. Similar to what we did with the n t 2 population. We saw a similar effect size between NT2 and IH. So our hope is that we see something similar.

We hope that we will provide additional benefit through the split dosing and that we will be able to we will be able to then design our phase 3, meet with the agency, and then and then move that into our phase 3 program. So, you know, with regards to my previous comment, with regards to Vibrance 2 versus Vibrance-3, what I am really just trying to say is that there is a lot of heterogeneity in the patient populations both in NT 2 and IH. there is also a lot of overlap between diagnoses. Patients move between an NT2 diagnosis and an IH type diagnosis, sometimes frequently. So I would expect that there is an overlap of population there.

And that if you have a similar population that the once daily drug would perform would perform similarly with the caveat I mentioned earlier that you have this other patient group in there that we are gonna be learning about that long. The long sleepers. So, again, what I am what I am hoping is that, we have designed the study in a way where we can learn what we need to from this program and move forward quickly into phase 3.

Christian Todd Nichols: Yeah, Luke, this is Todd. I will take that. Yeah, we are spending a lot of time right now talking to payers overall. As you know, there is a lot that goes into pricing, and 1 of the considerations that we will be thinking through is not only just the overall value of with a very broad label and how we plan to differentiate, but also making sure we take into consideration what the reimbursement profile looks like So our expectation is that we will put forward a profile in a pricing dynamic that will allow broad access to both products.

Operator: Our next question comes from Douglas Tsao with H. C. Wainwright. Please go ahead.

Douglas Tsao: Good morning. Thanks for taking the questions. I think for the ongoing study right now, our primary is really on the MADRS. We are really. Yes. Are we are we looking at the individual domains Of course, we do, but we are we are designed to look at the overall response overall. #3240. Consumer Appetite for Personal AI Goes Mainstream

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Nearly 70 percent of respondents say they want an AI assistant in their next device, according to a new report

Qualcomm builds intelligent, connected, computing and AI solutions that transform industries and advance human progress.

A recent report by Qualcomm Technologies, built on a survey of more than 12,000 people across key geographies worldwide, shows that around 70 percent of respondents express strong interest in an AI assistant that can interact naturally through voice and seamlessly manage devices, apps, and everyday tasks.

This article is brought to you by Qualcomm Technologies.

For many consumers, much of the promise and appeal of AI is personal. Consumers are looking past generic tools and want to know how these technologies will help them in their daily lives. These trends coincide with the advent of new classes of wearable devices that, in addition to being able to leverage powerful frontier models, feature built-in intelligence that understand the context of a user. Where are they? What are they seeing and hearing? What are their habits, their preferences, their schedules?

It’s an astonishing pivot, from passive accessories that served mostly to send users smartphone notifications to proactive, intelligent companions. The smartphone is no longer the center of that universe; though it’s still incredibly important, in this personal AI paradigm, the AI is the UI. And it shifts the focus toward you, the user.

These new technologies are exciting. But what do consumers really want?

A Personal AI report, commissioned by Qualcomm Technologies, built on a survey of more than 12,000 people across key geographies worldwide (the U.S., U.K., Germany, India, Brazil, and China) focused on the rise of personal AI in intelligent wearables looks deeply at these developments.

The smartphone is no longer the center of that universe; though it’s still incredibly important, in this personal AI paradigm, the AI is the UI.

Survey respondents are less interested in single devices and are responding more to the idea of connected ecosystems. As people expand their roster of devices, it only makes sense. Instead of relying entirely on a smartphone and a laptop, respondents also have connected technology in their cars, as well as intelligent wearables like smartwatches, smart glasses, hearables, and other wearables like rings, pins, and pendants. They want those devices to work in concert, and the way to do that is to decentralize any single one of them. Instead, the AI agent that knows the user and works across all of those devices becomes the unifying factor.

Consider a typical workday: A user’s watch detects it is time to leave for a meeting and, with permission, their AI agent factors in calendar details, real-time traffic and battery status across their devices. In the car, it suggests the best route and briefs them on their meeting agenda. As they arrive, smart glasses surface a discreet reminder, such as the meeting location or the name of a new contact, while the phone stays in their pocket. No one device has to do everything; each plays the role it is best suited for, coordinated by a personal AI agent that understands the user’s context and acts only at the user’s direction.

With this in mind, simply adding more hardware to the mix isn’t sufficient. Even though respondents will be open to new form factors, they’ll demand more from their ecosystem of devices. They’ll be sensitive to points of friction and needless complexity, and they’ll require each new device to bring something new to the table — “incremental intelligence, convenience, or contextual awareness that their existing devices cannot deliver on their own what the report,” reads the report.

The usage trends are up. The report found that those who own wearables are already using AI frequently (60 percent use it at least weekly), which indicates that it’s becoming less of a fun experiment for early adopters and more of a critical mass habit.

The “always-on” nature of intelligent wearables appears to be winning respondents, too. The report found the following statistics on average continuous wear among users:

But for all the excitement and engagement around intelligent wearables, there’s a gating factor: trust. As use cases for intelligent wearables expands to more personal and persistent experiences, trust is a necessity for Personal AI.

Notably, the report found that respondents expressed more interest in adopting intelligent wearables when Snapdragon was introduced as the enabling platform. This reinforces the value of having an established, trusted technology foundation in the mix.

The report shows that consumer appetite for AI is high, with 60-70 percent of those surveyed expressing interest in advanced AI as they consider a new device. That’s a constant. But remaining purchase drivers differed between device categories.

Audio playback quality is the most influential purchase driver for true wireless earbuds and headphones. For smartwatches, it’s display quality and responsiveness. Respondents are less concerned about technical specifications than aesthetics like materials and finish when it comes to devices like smart rings and pendants. And for smart glasses, it’s all about the type of control, whether it’s voice, gesture, or touch.

Artificial intelligence is entering a new phase, one that is deeply personal, continuously present, and seamlessly embedded into the devices we wear every day. This evolution, which we define as “Personal AI”, represents a shift away from generic, cloud-only intelligence toward AI that understands individuals in context: their habits, preferences, environments, and intent, in real time.

Alongside these purchase drivers is another key finding: Consumer appetite for Personal AI agents has gone mainstream. The report says that 70 percent of respondents “express strong interest in an AI assistant that can interact naturally through voice and seamlessly manage devices, apps, and everyday tasks.” With each individual as the center of their own ecosystem, voice becomes the most critical, natural method for interacting with agents.

Intelligent wearables comprise much of the hardware of this “ecosystem of you.” Consumers are interested in ecosystems instead of single devices, and they’re looking for agentic AI capabilities that understand and act on their behalf.

Yet so much of the industry remains undefined. OEMs and technology makers have an enormous opportunity right now to innovate and iterate on the strong technological foundations that platform makers are building. And the roadmap for what consumers want is clear.

All percentages, consumer behaviors, and attitudes stated in this report are based only on the responses of the individuals who participated in our survey.

Qualcomm Technologies is a global leader in communications and computing technologies, including leading-edge AI, high-performance, low-power computing, and connectivity solutions. Headquartered in San Diego, Calif., the company develops technologies for next-generation mobile networks and smart devices, and designs semiconductors such as mobile processors and AI chips.

The bias is deafening. Qualcomm, a chip manufacturer that is all in on AI, makes a survey and then states they found everyone loves using AI, the very AI that will run on Qualcomm chips. Clearly they don't have a conflict of interest in this. /s

#3239. AI inference startup Fal doubles its value to $16B in a $1.3B round

Demand grew so fast that Fal had to limit customers this summer. Now it is buying more computing power.

Fal, which hosts image, video and audio AI models for developers, raised $1.3B led by Bessemer at a $16B valuation, double its April value. Nvidia and T. Rowe Price also invested. Fal plans to spend the money on more computing power and staff.

Fal, a startup that runs image, video and audio AI models for developers, has raised $1.3B at a $16B valuation, Bloomberg reported. That is double the $8B it was valued at in April.

Existing investor Bessemer Venture Partners led the round, which closed in October. Nvidia, T. Rowe Price, Sound Ventures and HOF Capital also took part.

Fal runs a type of work known as inference, which means running AI models after they have been trained. Demand for it is booming: Fal hit $800M in annualised revenue earlier this year, according to a person familiar with the matter.

“We hit a point in summer where we were not able to serve our customers and had to rate limit them,” said chief executive Burkay Gur.

The San Francisco company will spend the money on more computing power and on growing its 185-person team. It has also started fine-tuning video models with the companies that make them, sometimes in return for licensing fees or a share of revenue.

“The more scale you have, the more likely you are to win at the end of the day,” Gur said.

Investors are betting big on the rest of the field, too. Rival Modal raised $750M at a $15.75B valuation in October. Fireworks raised $1.5B at a $17.5B valuation in July, and Baseten is reportedly set to more than double its value to $30B.
