#3237. Modern Warfare 4 is the shooter you've been waiting for if you skipped the last few Call of Duty games

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

While none of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4’s three modes are perfect, they’re all solid enough to deliver a well-rounded experience anchored by the franchise's incredible gunplay.

DMZ mode is solid and has potential to get better

DMZ mode is a little more PVP than I’d like

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

Platforms: Nintendo Switch 2, PC, PS5, Xbox Series X/S (reviewed)Price: $69 / £69 / AU$109Release Date: October 23, 2026Genre: First-person shooter

The Call of Duty season has arrived, and this year Infinity Ward is back in the driver’s seat. After back-to-back Black Ops games, Activision’s FPS cash cow returns to the Modern Warfare moniker and gameplay style, which I've always preferred (not that I dislike Black Ops; I just prefer MW's cast of characters and gameplay).

Modern Warfare 4 feels like a return to form for the long-running franchise, both in the single-player campaign and in the overall gunplay. The time-to-kill is a little longer than in the last couple of games, letting you use more inventive tactics in firefights. It’s not just about who shot who first. And I’m genuinely torn. It doesn’t feel like what I’m used to from the franchise, but maybe that’s not such a bad thing.

If you never liked COD games, nothing here will change your mind, but if you’re a lapsed fan of the series who wants to see how Captain Price’s story ties up and still enjoy a fun first-person shooter, this might be the one to come back to.

I'm generally not a Call of Duty campaign fan. I usually play a few hours a year and spend the rest of the time longing for multiplayer, so I fizzle out about halfway through. Which is why I was shocked when the Modern Warfare 4 campaign actually hooked me right off the bat and kept me on the edge of my seat the whole way through.

Sure, the story is a little convoluted, especially the Price portion, which has the unenviable task of cleaning up the mess left by the last few Call of Duty: Modern Warfare games. But I think it does a fantastic job of tying up all the loose ends into a coherent story that successfully caps Price’s story (at least until the next time Modern Warfare gets rebooted).

Price’s missions take place five days before the story’s other half (you’re essentially playing two campaigns at once and switching back and forth). His story crescendos with the start of the other plot and a massive Korean invasion.

Price’s story will make you feel like Jason Statham or John Wick, running around shooting and fighting in first-person hand-to-hand combat. The Korean story has a more traditional war-game feel and follows Park Hyun Jun and his squad. They’re entertaining, with a mix of Korean and US soldiers who add lighthearted humor during intense frontline moments.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The two interwoven stories contrast in a way that makes this the best Call of Duty campaign since 2009’s Modern Warfare 2.

Both sides of the campaign can get a little dark and heavy. An early scene puts you in the shoes of an invader on the Korean side, forcing difficult decisions that can make you wonder if you're the hero or villain (or somewhere in the gray middle ground). For example, an early Price fight scene ends in pure and utter brutality.

Then there’s the heavily hyped Stranded mission, a ramped-up version of the DMZ mode with a story and characters you actually care about. While most of the campaign is linear, this mission gives you a level of freedom we don’t often see in COD games. It’s dripping with tension and best of all, it’s fun. It was a dangerous call for Infinity Ward to include one mission that stands out, as it risked making the rest of the campaign feel inferior. However, because the more traditional COD missions are also so well executed and the stakes feel so high, this problem is negated.

I got seriously into Arc Raiders for about a month before some updates made me fall off. It was my first taste of an extraction shooter, and it felt good to return to the genre with DMZ mode. It’s definitely the weakest of the three main modes in Modern Warfare 4, but it’s still fun.

We already know the extraction formula is successful. In my opinion, Call of Duty is the best first-person shooter franchise from a pure gunplay perspective, so it makes sense that smooshing the two together would lead to a solid online mode.

The missions in DMZ are relatively generic and basic, but they’re motivation enough to keep you moving through a session beyond just grabbing the best loot and extracting.

My only issue with DMZ comes from the overall COD culture. Years of competitive multiplayer have created a shoot-first mentality that removes much of the tension that comes from talking to people in other extraction shooters. I love the “hey, are you cool?” interactions I experienced in Arc Raiders (and even in the Dark Zone of The Division), and in the DMZ matches I played for this review, every encounter with other players was instantly hostile.

The thrill of finding loot and getting out at an extraction point is as satisfying as any other game in the genre (perhaps even more so, because getting your loot almost certainly involved fighting another player who attacked as you tried to extract).

And while there wasn’t much in the way of enemy negotiations, I had great experiences with other players in my squad. In almost every match, my random squadmates cared as much about my survival and successful extraction as I did.

I look forward to seeing how Infinity Ward builds on DMZ, both in this Modern Warfare 4 and across future COD titles.

For me, this is the main event of any Call of Duty game. Sure, the campaign is fun for eight hours or so, and other modes like Black Ops’ Zombies and DMZ will hook a certain percentage of the player base; it’s multiplayer that has made this franchise one of the biggest in gaming history.

And while it had a few small flaws at launch (erratic spawns and skill-based matchmaking being all over the place with so many new players), the overall experience is there, and it’s great. The guns are fun to level up and add new attachments (the usual slots are all there), and it even adds new modes that borrow from other FPS games, like Collateral, a round-based plant-and-defuse mode with buy stages like Counter-Strike. It’s a well-executed game mode that feels fresh even if it’s been done before outside of COD.

Frontline is a spawn-campers' dream. Instead of spawning in logical, somewhat “safe” locations, you only spawn in your base. This becomes a problem when you’re on the losing team, because the other squad knows exactly where you’ll pop up next. Sure, you get a couple of seconds of invincibility, but that’s hardly enough to save this mode.

Map selection will always be contentious when a Call of Duty game launches. Some players will call them inventive and fun while others will say they’re more of the same. I'm in the latter camp, as the only map that does anything exciting is Kill Block, with its shifting, evolving nature. Sadly, that’s only available as a 10 vs. 10 map, so traditional 6 vs. 6 players won’t even see it.

However, even if no map in the normal rotation stands out as exceptionally good, none stand out as outright bad. Each map is good enough to have fun shooting enemies across, and that’s really all I’m looking for (though, like most COD launches, spawn points need a tweak, as I’ve had a few times where I died and spawned right in an enemy’s field of view). Hopefully this will be one of the first things IW fixes with the inevitable post-launch patches.

My favorite mode has always been, and always will be, Team Deathmatch. There’s something pure about two teams of six going head-to-head to see who can eliminate the other side more. But I’ve also enjoyed some Domination, another staple of the COD games. Fortunately, Infinity Ward kept these and all the other staples intact for Modern Warfare 4 (Kill Confirmed, Search and Destroy, Hardpoint, etc.). If you’re coming into this game looking for the stuff you already know you love, I can assure you it’s all there and just as good as ever.

I love Modern Warfare 4. I’m confident I’ll keep playing this version of Call of Duty through the rest of 2026 and deep into 2027, until the next game in the annualized series drops (with a break to follow soon for Grand Theft Auto VI).

Infinity Ward has reminded everyone that it is the “A” developer of Call of Duty, and Modern Warfare 4 will be a tough act for Raven, Treyarch and Sledgehammer to follow. All three modes are fun, and the campaign sucked me in and kept me playing, as none have since the original Modern Warfare 2 (which I still stand by as the best COD campaign ever released). I’d go so far as to say this is in the top three COD campaigns of all time.

Add in the multiplayer and the extraction-based DMZ mode, and you have a well-rounded Call of Duty package that will please fans. It probably won’t convince people who already don’t like COD, but lapsed fans and hardcore players will find plenty to keep them coming back again and again.

#3236. Alphabet's Free Cash Flow Just Turned Negative. Should Investors Sell the Stock Now?

Alphabet is spending hundreds of billions of dollars to build its AI infrastructure. But with free cash flow turning negative, should investors be worried about the company's aggressive spending?

Alphabet (GOOG +0.08%)(GOOGL +0.37%) just delivered a mixed third-quarter earnings report. Revenue increased 25% year-over-year to $127.6 billion, while Google Cloud more than doubled its revenue. However, the company also reported negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion, raising concerns about its enormous artificial intelligence investments.

Its shares fell sharply following the announcement. But should investors be worried about the company's financial position, or is this simply the cost of building its next growth engine?

Here are three things investors should understand before making the next move.

Perhaps the biggest concern from the latest earnings report is Alphabet's free cash flow.

The company generated $42.3 billion in operating cash flow during the third quarter. However, it spent $51.4 billion on capital expenditures, resulting in negative free cash flow of approximately $9.1 billion.

This is the second consecutive quarter of negative free cash flow, marking a significant change for a company historically known for generating substantial cash.

The main reason is its aggressive investment in AI infrastructure. Alphabet is building data centers, purchasing servers and networking equipment, and expanding its computing capacity to support growing demand for AI services.

However, there are other factors worth understanding. Alphabet is also building inventory for its custom Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) systems, which it sells to customers. This requires the company to purchase hardware before receiving payment. Additionally, it made a $5.2 billion payment related to a 2018 European Commission fine during the quarter. These factors further affected cash flow.

Importantly, Alphabet generated $179.6 billion in operating cash flow over the trailing 12 months, and trailing 12-month free cash flow remained positive at $19.7 billion thanks to strong cash generation in earlier periods. It also ended the quarter with $265.1 billion in cash and marketable securities, although this includes $90.4 billion of equity investments.

In other words, the company isn't facing an immediate liquidity problem. But investors should pay attention if heavy investments continue to consume more cash, further draining liquidity in the coming quarters.

Despite the disappointing earnings announcement, Alphabet's operating performance remains impressive.

Revenue increased25% to $127.6 billion, while operating income grew 30% to $40.6 billion. Operating margins also improved to 32%.

Google Cloud was particularly strong, with revenue more than doubling to $30.7 billion. Its operating income reached $11.1 billion -- more than tripling year-over-year -- demonstrating that the business is becoming an increasingly important contributor to Alphabet's profits. Its backlog also reached $561 billion, reflecting strong demand for cloud computing and AI services.

Meanwhile, despite concerns about the traditional Google Search business, revenue for this segment increased 12% to $63.4 billion. However, this remains an area worth monitoring as the company evolves its search business due to the rise of generative AI.

Taken together, these numbers suggest that Alphabet's business isn't deteriorating. Its cloud business is expanding rapidly, while its advertising business continues generating substantial revenue.

The bigger challenge is whether AI strengthens its existing businesses rather than undermining their profitability over the longer term -- an area investors should closely monitor.

Alphabet is investing heavily to capture a potentially enormous AI opportunity. If these investments generate attractive returns, today's spending could support years of future growth.

However, investors shouldn't assume that every dollar spent on AI will eventually pay off. There are three things worth monitoring.

First, watch whether Google Cloud can sustain its growth while maintaining healthy profit margins. Its latest results are encouraging, but investors need to see continued profitability.

Second, monitor Search advertising growth. If AI-powered search attracts more users but generates less advertising revenue, it could weaken Alphabet's most important cash-generating business.

Finally, pay attention to free cash flow. Alphabet needs to demonstrate that its enormous infrastructure investments are translating into additional profits and cash generation.

Alphabet remains a powerful technology business with leading positions in search, digital advertising, cloud computing, and artificial intelligence.

Its latest results don't suggest that its core business is falling apart. Revenue and operating income are still growing, while Google Cloud is emerging as another important growth engine.

However, the investment proposition is changing. Investors must now consider whether Alphabet can turn its enormous AI investments into attractive returns while protecting its traditional advertising business.

For existing shareholders, one disappointing quarter isn't necessarily a reason to sell. But it is a good reason to reassess the investment thesis.

#3234. When Electric Cars Were for Women

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Early carmakers decided women wanted cars that were quiet, clean, and easy to start

Allison Marsh is a professor at the University of South Carolina and the codirector of the Ann Johnson Institute for Science, Technology & Society.

When automobiles were still a novelty, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion.

At the turn of the last century, the automobile industry was still new and evolving rapidly. In 1898, there were about 50 carmakers in the United States. A decade later, that number had increased fivefold. In 1901, the companies produced 7,000 vehicles. By 1910, production had reached 181,000.

For several decades, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion, and nobody was sure which technology would come out on top. Steam had the legacy of locomotive technology behind it but came with a risk of fire. Steam-powered vehicles could also become exceedingly hot, depending on the placement of the boiler and the steam piping. Both gasoline and electric cars faced logistical challenges: How far could you travel without refueling or charging? You could always throw an extra can of gasoline in the back of the car, but charging a battery involved more planning. The infrastructure for long-distance travel was not yet in place.

Before the invention of the electric starter in 1911, gasoline-powered engines had to be started with a hand crank; once running, they were loud and emitted noxious fumes. Fully electric vehicles, by contrast, were easy to start; you just turned on the main battery switch, often with a key, and there was no foul exhaust to deal with.

Electric carmakers looking for a way to differentiate their products decided that these attributes made their vehicles perfect for women. (Electric cars were also marketed to doctors so that they could make house calls in the middle of the night without waking the neighbors.) General Electric, which made car chargers based on mercury-arc rectifiers, was so captivated by the idea of women driving electric cars that the company created a series of advertisements featuring stylishly dressed women plugging in their cars and posing with their charging stations.

In ads for its electric car chargers, General Electric featured women using the equipment.miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

A young woman named Fannie Goodnow was an early EV adopter. She owned a 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton, an open two-seater that really did look like a horseless carriage, and she used a GE mercury-arc rectifier to charge it.

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt invented the mercury vapor lamp, which became the basis for the mercury-arc rectifier used in car-charging systems. Bettmann/Getty Images

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt is generally credited with the invention of the mercury-arc rectifier. During the first decade of the 20th century, Hewitt received several U.S. patents for electric lamps and other apparatus for transmitting and using electric currents. U.S. patents 968,896 and 1,163,706, granted to Percy H. Thomas, advanced Hewitt’s designs. Thomas was chief electrician for the Cooper Hewitt Electric Co., which Hewitt had cofounded with George Westinghouse to manufacture and sell his lamps.

The mercury-arc rectifier functioned as a diode. In a car charger like the one Fannie Goodnow used, it converted alternating current from the power grid into direct current needed to charge the car’s battery. A small amount of liquid mercury contained in a glass tube would vaporize and glow as electricity passed through it. Coupled with the carbon anodes, the vapor allowed current to flow in only one direction. This unit took about 12 hours to charge a drained battery.

I couldn’t find any records as to why Fannie Goodnow opted for an electric car. But as a well-to-do woman living in the Boston area, she had more than a half dozen automobile producers to choose from. The one she chose was S.R. Bailey & Co. of Amesbury, Mass.

This early electric car charger used a mercury-arc rectifier to convert AC to DC.Heritage Museums & Gardens

According to Galen Handy, who maintains the Early Electric Vehicles website, Samuel Robinson Bailey started in the carriage and sleigh business as a teenager, winning a best-in-show prize at a carriage exhibition in Portland, Maine, in 1855. Bailey developed a reputation as an inventor and designed processes to streamline the manufacture of his vehicles. He went into business for himself in 1882. Just over a decade later, one of Bailey’s carriages won a gold medal at the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago.

Bailey’s son Edwin attended the exposition, where he likely would have seen a vision of the future: the Morrison electric wagon. This six-passenger, battery-powered vehicle ferried visitors and VIPs around the fairgrounds. It wasn’t long before automobiles began eating into the carriage business. In December 1906, with the carriage industry collapsing, S.R. Bailey & Co. announced it was getting into electric vehicles.

Bailey’s first model, the Victoria Phaeton, used an Edison alkaline battery. Thomas Edison had been working on a lighter, more reliable, and more powerful battery for the auto industry since the 1890s, and announced the achievement with great fanfare in 1903. Unfortunately for Bailey and other carmakers who deployed it, the battery leaked and wouldn’t hold a charge. Edison was forced to go back to the drawing board. By 1910, he had a better battery in production, but by then his friend Henry Ford had introduced the Model T, setting the stage for the internal combustion engine to take over the market.

While Edison toiled to improve his tech, Bailey pivoted to a battery from the Gould Storage Battery Co. of Depew, N.Y. Gould also supplied batteries for railroads, utilities, subways, elevators, and farms. Goodnow’s Victoria Phaeton used a 30-cell lead-acid battery housed in a wooden box that was suspended under the chassis. The standard battery had a range of 64 to 80 kilometers; a larger battery with 50 percent more capacity was available for an upcharge. With the standard battery, the Victoria Phaeton cost US $2,000 (about $73,000 today, or about the list price of an upscale EV like the Audi Q8 or BMW i5).

Fannie Goodnow’s electric car charger now resides at the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. But her 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton has been lost to history. Shown here is a 1911 version of that model.Sarah Thornington/Heritage Museums & Gardens

Goodnow installed a mercury-arc rectifier charging station in the barn adjacent to her parents’ summer home in Hull, Mass. Bill Lillie of Vintage Electric Cars notes that the charging plug was of an unusual design. This is, of course, one of the banes of any early adopter: nonstandardized plugs and cables. The Electric Vehicle Association of America, which formed in 1910, tried to put forward a standard so that electric vehicles could be charged at any charging station. (Modern EV owners can no doubt relate.) But savvy electric car owners knew to carry spare plug adapters and cables when traveling.

When Edison’s improved battery was finally available, Bailey began using it in the Victoria Phaeton and then went on a publicity blitz. In September 1910, the carmaker sponsored a round-trip tour from New York to Boston, with a side trip up New Hampshire’s Mount Washington, totaling about 1,600 km. Sadly, the “This Car Climbed Mt. Washington” bumper sticker hadn’t yet become popular.

Thomas Edison supplied the batteries for an electric car made by S.R. Bailey & Co., which then went on a publicity road trip from New York to Boston. miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

Although Thomas Edison posed for a photo with the new Bailey Victoria Phaeton that featured his new battery, he himself chose a Detroit Electric Victoria for his own use. (Edison was known to be a terrible driver, so someone else likely chauffeured him around.)

Unable to compete against the rising tide of Model Ts, S.R. Bailey sold its factory in 1915, having produced about 500 to 600 electric vehicles.

Although the vehicle Fannie Goodnow chose turned out to be just a blip in automotive history, I like to imagine her driving about town in a beautiful car that embodied all the quirks of early adoption. I hope her friends didn’t make fun of her for investing in electric just before internal combustion took off. I hope she didn’t get stranded without the proper charging cable. I do not know what happened to her or her Victoria Phaeton, but her charging station remained in situ until 2022, when it was donated to the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. Now it stands ready to tell stories of technological change and adoption that continue to resonate today.

Part of a continuing series looking at historical artifacts that embrace the boundless potential of technology.

An abridged version of this article appears in the November 2026 print issue.

References For a detailed history of the development of the mercury-arc rectifier (or valve), see Deepak Tiku’s article in the March/April 2014 issue of IEEE Power & Energy Magazine.Harry Cooke Cushing Jr., a fellow of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote (and updated regularly over a number of years) The Electric Vehicle Hand-Book, which gave general instructions for the care and storage of batteries, including how to charge them with a mercury-arc rectifier. Discussion of the mercury-arc rectifier begins on page 156 of the 10th edition, published in 1922. (The American Institute of Electrical Engineers is one of the predecessor organizations of the IEEE.)

For a detailed history of the development of the mercury-arc rectifier (or valve), see Deepak Tiku’s article in the March/April 2014 issue of IEEE Power & Energy Magazine.

Harry Cooke Cushing Jr., a fellow of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote (and updated regularly over a number of years) The Electric Vehicle Hand-Book, which gave general instructions for the care and storage of batteries, including how to charge them with a mercury-arc rectifier. Discussion of the mercury-arc rectifier begins on page 156 of the 10th edition, published in 1922. (The American Institute of Electrical Engineers is one of the predecessor organizations of the IEEE.)

Allison Marsh is a professor in Women and Gender Studies at the University of South Carolina and codirector of the university’s Ann Johnson Institute for Science, Technology & Society. She combines her interests in engineering, history, and museum objects to write the Past Forward column, which tells the story of technology through historical artifacts. Marsh is currently working on a book on the history of women in electrical engineering.

#3233. UK AI minister says a serious cyber breach is ‘extremely likely’

Kanishka Narayan says government bodies and companies are underprepared as AI tools make hacking faster.

Kanishka Narayan, the UK’s minister for artificial intelligence.

UK AI minister Kanishka Narayan said a serious cyber breach is “extremely likely” in both the public and private sector, and that neither is ready. He pointed to extra funding for the AI Security Institute as the government’s response.

The UK is “extremely likely” to suffer a serious cyber breach soon, AI minister Kanishka Narayan said on Tuesday. Neither the government nor businesses are ready for it, he said, Bloomberg reported.

“I worry about the cybersecurity risks because it’s here now,” Narayan said at the Bloomberg Tech event in London.

“A cyber breach incident is extremely likely in the UK, both in the public sector and private sector,” he added.

His warning came hours after Richard Horne, head of the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre, said British firms were “willfully blind” to threats from Russia, Iran and China. On Monday, a suspected supermarket freezer hack hit stores across Europe, and Horne said a few British firms were affected.

AI is adding to the worry. Hackers are thought to be using AI tools to speed up attacks. This summer, AI models from OpenAI, Anthropic and others broke out of test environments and breached outside websites.

Narayan pointed to the AI Security Institute, which tests leading AI models, as part of the answer. The government gave it an extra £120M in its latest budget. Last month, it won back access to new US models before release, after the White House asked labs to hold them back.

Narayan would not say how long that access would last. “Nothing is a particular guarantee in the world of AI,” he said.

#3231. Guarding the Gates of Knowledge

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

AI can fake a plausible paper at the push of a button. Can detection tools and peer review keep up?

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

A recent scroll through social media got me thinking about trust. About half my feed was filled with AI slop that astute users would call out as being machine-generated, often to the embarrassment of the rube who unknowingly spread it and sometimes to the delight of the poster who shared it deliberately because they found it amusing or useful for sowing confusion.

Remember the good old days of GPT-3 when we could ask the chatbot anything and it would almost instantly and very confidently spit back a plausible but false answer? That’s when the word “hallucination” as applied to AI answers entered the lexicon. Six years and several versions of a few different chatbots later, I still can’t trust the answers I get, even though Claude or Gemini often do useful work for me. That’s the thing about current AI: Trust but verify. And verify you must.

Apply that maxim at scale to maintain the integrity of the scientific record and you get an idea of the challenge facing publishers of peer-reviewed scholarship. In “I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper,” freelance writer and doctor of applied mathematics Benjamin Skuse tells the story of the human gatekeepers trying to beat back the rising tide of AI slop by attempting to get his own AI-generated papers past IEEE’s defenses.

“He basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper.’ And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it.” —Eliza Strickland

As features and AI beat editor Eliza Strickland told me, Skuse was surprised at just how effortless it was to generate a paper that was more or less plausible and more or less science. For one of his experiments, “he basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper,’” she said. “And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it. He just launched it into the maw of the publishing engine.”

Skuse discovered that the combination of IEEE’s human-review processes and research-integrity checker programs are currently keeping pace in what amounts to a cat-and-mouse game against people using free tools. But the more advanced LLMs are no longer making the same dumb mistakes the free versions do. That leaves publishers locked in an arms race between increasingly plausible slop and the systems aimed at detecting it.

Scholarly publishers aren’t the only ones trying to hold the line against slop. So is that global depository of human-generated knowledge, Wikipedia. For this month’s Five Questions, Strickland interviewed Ellia Lebleu, a founding member of WikiProject AI Cleanup, a volunteer effort to detect and delete AI-generated material from the platform. Lebleu’s team is confronting the same problem as commercial publishers, but with fewer people and fewer tools.

“Wikipedia is known as a repository of human-generated information, and they want to hold on to that,” says Strickland. “Who knows how long they’ll be able to do that.”

If we can’t collectively assume that the scientific record is trustworthy or that basic facts about the world are accurate, then our understanding of what is real unspools into uncertainty. Perhaps that delights quantum scientists and the grifters who thrive in an information environment where there is no shared reality. But that uncertainty ultimately undermines trust in the institutions that exist to curate the corpus of human knowledge and to promote the advancement of science and technology for the benefit of humanity.

Or maybe in a world where AI is doing the science and writing the papers, it won’t matter whether or not humans trust the outputs. As Strickland put it, “Doesn’t it just feel crazy that we’ll have AI writing for other AIs at some point? We’ll just get left out of the loop.”

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

#3230. Apple announces Fitness+ Gym Strength program with personalized workout plans

Apple wants to help you get stronger. Apple Fitness+ is expanding to the gym with a new strength training experience. Gym Strength is now available in beta, bringing personalized workout plans, exercise demonstrations, and Apple Watch logging to your lifting routine.

Gym Strength creates progressive, four-week plans based on your strength goals, experience, schedule, and available equipment. After you complete each week of workouts, the following week adapts based on the reps and weight you logged.

The feature is designed for a range of experience levels, from people trying strength training for the first time to experienced lifters looking to make progress. It also aims to help anyone who wants to build a more consistent routine.

When building a plan, you choose your workout days and the body areas you want to focus on. You can select five exercises per workout, which Apple estimates will take about 20–30 minutes, or seven exercises for about 45–60 minutes, depending on your pace.

Each workout recommends exercises, reps, sets, and how much weight to lift.

You move through the workout at your own pace, with short video demonstrations from Apple Fitness+ trainers available for each exercise. The demonstrations can be expanded to show the movement from three different angles.

Apple says Gym Strength includes over 350 exercises across more than 30 types of strength training equipment, including dumbbells, kettlebells, suspension trainers, cable machines, and barbells. Dumbbells are the minimum equipment requirement.

Plans account for the equipment available to you, so the experience can work in a commercial gym or a home gym.

If a machine is occupied or you’re training somewhere with different equipment, you can swap equipment or choose an alternative exercise with a similar movement and body focus. You can also add sets or skip exercises.

#3225. iOS 27.3 and macOS 27.3 add Vertical Tabs, Adaptive Dark Mode, and more to Safari

Apple just released the first betas of iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, and macOS 27.3, with some big changes to Safari. The updates add a new vertical tab layout, Adaptive Dark Mode, and Siri AI Custom Actions.

Safari in iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, and macOS 27.3 is adding a new Vertical Tabs design option. If you choose this design, you’ll see your tabs arranged vertically along the left-hand side of Safari rather than along the top, as in the traditional Safari design.

By default, Vertical Tabs show as icons in order to maximize vertical and horizontal space. If you’d like, you can also resize the tab bar to see website titles.

To try Vertical Tabs in the new iOS 27.3 beta, head to the Settings app, choose Apps, tap Safari, then look for the new Vertical Tabs option. On Mac and iPad, the feature can also be enabled via the “View” menu in the Safari app directly.

Vertical tab layouts have become an increasingly popular web browser feature. Arc from The Browser Company popularized the option. Arc, however, ceased development last year, and The Browser Company announced last month that it will discontinue it altogether in December.

If you regularly visit a website that doesn’t support Dark Mode, Apple’s next round of software updates adds Adaptive Dark Mode. This will automatically apply Dark Mode to websites that don’t support the feature.

If Dark Mode is enabled on your iPhone, iPad, or Mac and you visit a website that doesn’t support it, you’ll see a new “Try” button. If you tap this, Safari will automatically create a Dark Mode version of the website.

You can choose to have Adaptive Dark Mode automatically kick in or use it on a site-by-site basis.

I’ve been using Noir for Dark Mode in Safari, I am very curious to see how it compares against Adaptive Dark Mode.

Finally, Siri AI can now take direct action on tabs in iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, and macOS 27.3. This includes things like using Siri to move, sort, organize, and close your tabs.

In a future update, Siri’s on-screen awareness will also expand to include the entire content of a website, not just what’s visible on the screen at a particular moment.

iOS 27.3, macOS 27.3, and iPadOS 27.3 are rolling out to developers for beta testing today. The update will likely be released to everyone sometime in December. What do you think of these new Safari features? Will you try out the new Vertical Tabs feature? Let us know down in the comments.

#3224. Firefox and Chrome patch 200+ security flaws combined – update both ASAP

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The latest version of Firefox fixes 167 security vulnerabilities, most of which are of high severity, while the newest version of Chrome patches 52 flaws, four of which are critical.

With security vulnerabilities continually plaguing the software we use, it’s time once again to update both Firefox and Chrome browsers to protect yourself from the latest exploits.

Also: Half of all cyberattacks start in your browser: 10 tips for staying safe

This week, Mozilla updated Firefox to version 159, not just for Windows but also for Android, MacOS, and Linux. The latest version includes fixes for 167 security bugs. Among these, 108 are rated of high severity, while the rest are considered moderate or low.

Almost 100 of them are defined as use-after-free (UAF) vulnerabilities, which are memory management flaws that an attacker could exploit to crash the browser or trigger malicious code. Several of the bugs also refer to Firefox’s Sandbox, which means that hackers could break through the browser’s protected Sandbox area to execute malicious code.

Given the nastiness of the security bugs, you’ll want to update Firefox ASAP. For that, open the browser, click the three-line icon at the upper right, move to Help and Report, and select About Firefox. The latest update will then be installed. Restart Firefox to finish the process.

Also: I dumped Firefox, but these 5 features finally won me back

Beyond the security patches, Firefox 159 adds a few handy new features.

With Firefox for the Mac, sharing a page in the browser now displays the built-in MacOS share picker. Here, you can see a preview of the page you want to share along with recent contacts and specific apps such as AirDrop and Messages.

Next up, you’re now able to access Firefox’s passwords tool in the sidebar. This lets you more easily view any website passwords that you’ve saved to the browser. To see this in action, first make sure the sidebar is visible. For that, click the Sidebar button on the Address bar and then click the key icon to display your saved passwords.

And as perhaps the most helpful new feature, Firefox’s AI-powered Smart Window can now watch specific web pages for changes and send you a notification when the page is updated. For this, turn on the option for Smart Window if it’s not already enabled. Click the Firefox icon in the upper right and select Smart Window. Navigate to the website for which you’d like to be notified of any changes. At the chat window, type /watch, fill out the form, and then click the Create Task button.

That takes us to Chrome with version 56.0.8078.73/.74 for Windows and Mac and version 156.0.8078.73 for Linux. Here, the latest update patches 52 security bugs. Out of these, four are rated critical, while 46 are rated high.

The four severe ones point to a memory corruption problem. But like some of the Firefox bugs, they also reference the browser’s Sandbox. In this case, an attacker who exploits any of these vulnerabilities could bypass Chrome’s protected Sandbox area to run malicious code. Also as in Firefox, several of the bugs point to use-after-free (UAF) issues that would allow an attacker to exploit memory management flaws to crash the browser or install malicious code.

Also: Chrome warns you about suspicious websites now

To update Chrome, click the three-dot icon at the top, move to Help, and select About Google Chrome. If prompted, allow the latest update to download and then restart the browser to finish.

Beyond many of the bugs themselves, Firefox and Chrome also share an increasing reliance on AI to find and resolve security flaws. In its advisory, Mozilla cited Amy Burnett, a security research and analyst at OpenAI, for uncovering many of the bugs. In its blog post, Google attributed the discovery of several flaws to Anthropic’s Claude and a few to OpenAI.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, ZDNET’s parent company, filed an April 2025 lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

#3223. watchOS 27.3 beta adds new Siri Recap and Live Rewind features for Apple Watch

Apple has released the first beta of watchOS 27.3 for developers, including two new Audio Intelligence features for Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4: Siri Recap and Live Rewind.

Apple first announced these features at its special event in September, saying they would “arrive in beta later this year.”

As a refresher, Siri Recap creates high-level summaries of conversations that you can review later. When the feature is enabled, Apple Intelligence will automatically generate a title and key points that you can review in the Siri app on iPhone.

Siri Recap ambiently takes notes on your conversations throughout your day and creates high-level Apple Intelligence–generated summaries that you can use later to jog your memory, so you can stay present in the moment. Your summaries auto-delete after 7 days if you choose not to save them.

You can turn on Siri Recap in the Watch app on iPhone. When you enable it, you can set a schedule based on time and/or location, or you can manually turn it on or off. You can also access it via Control Center on Apple Watch.

Live Rewind, meanwhile, helps you recall what was just said in a conversation. You can activate Live Rewind by double-pressing the Digital Crown, and then see a transcript of the previous 15 seconds of a conversation.

Live Rewind recalls what was just said in the last 15 seconds by showing a text snippet on your Apple Watch when you double-press the Digital Crown, so you can catch something you missed or are less familiar with. You can ask Siri about the content of the snippet or simply save it to the Siri app.

Siri Recap’s summary is described as a “brief, high-level summary of conversations,” not a transcript. Apple says it will “exclude sensitive information like financial information or government-assigned identifiers.”

Live Rewind text snippets and Siri Recap summaries are end-to-end encrypted. Apple says the features “do not create or store audio recordings, and raw audio used for processing is completely inaccessible to the operating systems, apps, the user, or Apple.” The company uses the S11 chip’s Secure Exclave to power the features, a “dedicated hardware-isolated compartment that processes audio in complete isolation from the rest of the system, then immediately deletes it.”

Siri Recap and Live Rewind are available in beta with watchOS 27.3, which is available now for developers.

#3222. Your headphones have hidden LE Audio features you’ll want to know about

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Your JBL, Sony, or Bose Bluetooth headphones got a top-to-bottom wireless makeover -- not just Auracast.

The shift from Classic Bluetooth to LE Audio is in full swing, as JBL and Sony release flagship headphones and earbuds with built-in LE Audio. Bose is the latest to upgrade its flagship headphones via an OTA firmware update.

Also: Apple has a Bluetooth problem, and Android is taking advantage

Auracast, the Bluetooth protocol that enables one-to-many audio streams and is the most popular LE Audio feature, but several other LE Audio upgrades don’t get as much attention. These features improve wireless voice call quality, reduce battery drain in true wireless earbuds, and remove ecosystem barriers to low-latency mobile gaming. Here’s why they matter just as much as Auracast.

LE Audio includes the Low Complexity Communication Codec (LC3), which includes the unified Telephony and Media Audio Profile (TMAP) to handle audio streams and voice calls simultaneously. Bluetooth Classic relies on the Advanced Audio Distribution Profile (A2DP) and Hands-Free Profile (HFP), which handle the same functions but require both profiles.

Also: Bluetooth’s latest could solve a common connectivity problem

The profiles in Bluetooth Classic, given that they must alternate, result in extremely poor voice quality during hands-free calls over cellular or video calls on Zoom or Teams. These profiles also account for degraded voice quality when chatting while playing a mobile game.

LE Audio consolidates these two profiles, creating higher-quality, bidirectional audio and preserving voice call quality when using wireless headphones.

Earlier this year, JBL gave its flagship Tour Pro 3 earbuds an OTA firmware update to support LE Audio, and Sony’s WF-1000XM6 earbuds, released in February, have LE Audio support out of the box. There’s one major true wireless earbud improvement wrapped in LE Audio: native multi-stream audio.

Also: Frustrated with multipoint? How it works – and why it sometimes won’t

In Bluetooth Classic, your source device, such as your phone, sends audio to one earbud, which then retransmits it to the other earbud. This complex audio transmission method is why one of your earbuds always has a lower battery than the other. Though premium earbuds usually have an independent stream workaround, many midrange and budget earbuds don’t, and that’s where LE Audio comes in handy.

LE Audio enables independent audio streams built into the Bluetooth stack, so manufacturers don’t need to implement their own methods to avoid asymmetrical battery drain.

Software ecosystems, like Apple’s iOS and Samsung’s Galaxy, dictate which audio features are reserved for devices inside of them and withhold features from devices outside of them. Hardware ecosystems are equally responsible for the fragmentation of audio features across manufacturers, typically through codecs.

Sony’s LDAC codec for high-quality audio is only available on Sony headphones, earbuds, and smartphones with the proper hardware, which is limited in the US market. Snapdragon’s AptX codecs aren’t as widely available on phones either, leaving most people to rely on Bluetooth Classic SBC and AAC codes, even though their headphones support more advanced ones.

Also: Your iPhone may support Bluetooth Channel Sounding – and it’s a big deal

LE Audio eliminates the tedious codec issue, especially in wireless gaming contexts, delivering lower latency, improved voice audio streams, and eliminating asymmetrical audio transmission.

For now, as long as you have a compatible Android phone, you have access to several models of headphones, earbuds, and Bluetooth speakers that support LE Audio. As more manufacturers update their devices to support the Bluetooth audio streaming protocol, this suggests the technology is becoming more reliable.

So, what about your AirPods? I wouldn’t bet on it anytime soon.

No more reverse engineering or cloning of games with Claude

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For the past few weeks, there have been so many instances of AI being used to tinker around with popular video games.

That practice has led to the trend of video game decompilations, which is the process of a developer working backward from a compiled, machine-code game to reconstruct readable, human-understandable source code. Reverse engineering games has also popped up as of late, which is all about a developer analyzing compiled machine code or raw binary files to understand their internal logic, rebuild that source code or port games to new platforms.

Because of those AI uses in connection with video games, Halo: Combat Evolved has been made completely playable within a web browser, Super Mario 64 has been decompiled to also work as a playable title on PC and even game mashups have popped up in the form of Minecraft becoming playable in Elden Ring.

But when it comes to using AI tools to completely recreate those popular types of games, Anthropic is making sure that practice won’t be doable with its Claude Code and Opus 5.5 AI models. Here’s how the AI company is blocking any future attempts at prompting the recreation, reverse-engineering and cloning of identifiable video games.

News of Anthropic’s Claude update blocking the cloning of recognizable video games surfaced after a user on X named @chasmmmmmmmmmmm noticed a new rule added to Claude Code that’s meant to block prompts that request the recreation of existing titles. That rule, which is entitled “tengu_heron_brook,” puts forth the following edict:

“Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user’s own designs and assets. Don’t build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original.”

In response to that X user’s Tweet, Addy Osmani, an engineering leader at Anthropic, gave this statement on the matter:

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

“We added two sentences to Claude Code's prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else's specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy. Original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets are meant to keep working. We'll continue to iterate to ensure we're striking the right balance. In the meantime, if Claude turns down something that's yours, send it my way.”

We added two sentences to Claude Code's prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else's specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy. Original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets are meant to keep working. We'll continue to iterate to ensure we're striking the right balance. In the meantime, if Claude turns down something that's yours, send it my way.October 30, 2026

It’s interesting to see Anthropic fight back against people using its AI tools to alter certain video game titles in a major way or remake them altogether.

Looking at the list of games that have had Claude involved in their reverse engineering practices points to just how many retro classics have been altered in a surprising way. Witnessing Skate 3 skateboarding physics crossing over with Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2 multiplayer maps and seeing Escape from Tarkov's gunplay, loot systems and extraction mechanics make their way into the fantasy realm of The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim has come courtesy of AI coding assistants like Claude Opus 5.5.

It’s been interesting to see the flood of reverse engineering video game projects that have begun popping up all over the net. There’s even a GitHub project page dedicated to games that have already been reverse-engineered, decompiled and rebuilt thanks to the implementation of numerous AI models and agentic tools.

The manner in which AI tools have been used to tinker with popular video games has been crazy to see. I never imagined that I’d get to see Marvel’s Spider-Man from the PlayStation series of games be able to swing around Batman’s rain-soaked Gotham City from Arkham Knight. But that has become possible due to the use of AI tools.

Claude’s new AI model update is blocking attempts to completely copy someone else’s video game IP, which also falls in line with Anthropic making sure Claude isn’t used to reverse-engineer smart TVs as well. It seems like Anthropic is moving against any more attempts to have its AI models be used to get caught up in the copyright infringement of existing video game titles.

He is also an experienced tech writer who has covered video games, mobile devices, headsets, and now artificial intelligence for over a decade. Since 2011, his work has appeared in publications including The Christian Post, Complex, TechRadar, Heavy, and ONE37pm, with a focus on clear, practical analysis.

Today, Elton focuses on making AI more accessible by breaking down complex topics into useful, easy-to-understand insights for a wide range of readers.

#3219. Xometry (XMTR) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

First GAAP profit arrives alongside a raised full-year outlook.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Xometry, Inc. (XMTR +16.55%) surpassed a $1 billion revenue run rate during the third quarter, reporting its first period of GAAP profitability and a record marketplace gross margin of 36.0%. Management attributed the performance to the execution of a product-led growth strategy and the expanding role of its AI-native marketplace as digital infrastructure for custom manufacturing. Revenue increased 40% year over year, led by a 43% expansion in marketplace revenue and record net additions of active buyers. The company raised its full-year 2026 revenue and adjusted EBITDA guidance, citing robust demand and operating leverage across its U.S. and international segments.

Operator: Good day, and thank you for standing by. Welcome to Xometry's third quarter 2026 conference call. At this time, all participants are in a listen-only mode. After the speaker's presentation, there will be a question-and-answer session. As a reminder, to ask a question, please press star one on your telephone and wait for your name to be called. To withdraw your question, please press star one again. Please be advised that today's conference call is being recorded. I would now like to hand the conference over to your first speaker today, Shawn Milne.

Joining me are Sanjeev Singh Sahni, our Chief Executive Officer, and James Miln, our Chief Financial Officer. During today's call, we will review our financial results for the third quarter 2026 and discuss our guidance for the fourth quarter and full year 2026. During today's call, we will make forward-looking statements, including statements related to the expected performance of our business, future financial results, strategy, long-term growth, and overall future prospects. Such statements may be identified by terms such as believe, expect, intend, and may. These statements are subject to risks and uncertainties, which could cause them to differ materially from actual results.

We caution you to not place undue reliance on forward-looking statements and undertake no duty or obligation to update any forward-looking statements as a result of new information, future events, or changes in our expectations. We'd also like to point out that on today's call, we will report GAAP and non-GAAP results. We use these non-GAAP financial measures internally for financial and operating decision-making purposes and as a means to evaluate period-to-period comparisons.

Non-GAAP financial measures are presented in addition to, and not as a substitute or superior to, measures of financial performance prepared in accordance with U.S. GAAP. To see the reconciliation of these non-GAAP measures, please refer to our earnings press release distributed today and our investor presentation, both of which are available on the Investors section of our website at investors.xometry.com. A replay of today's call will also be posted on our website. With that, I'd like to turn the call over to Sanjeev.

Sanjeev Singh Sahni: Thanks, Shawn. Good morning, and thank you for joining our Q3 earnings call. Our continued robust growth and stellar Q3 results demonstrate the expanding strength of our AI-native marketplace. Q3 was a record quarter for Xometry across many fronts, including revenue, gross profit, marketplace gross margin, and adjusted EBITDA. Q3 also marked several major milestones: a $1 billion plus revenue run rate, our highest-ever marketplace gross margin, and our first quarter of GAAP profitability. Q3 revenue increased 40% year-over-year to a record $252 million, our second consecutive quarter of at least 40% growth. Marketplace revenue increased 43%, driven by broad-based strength across many verticals and increasing buyer adoption.

We drove strong structural enterprise growth as we expanded wallet share with large existing accounts. Our proprietary AI models are effectively optimizing conversion, buyer growth, and market share gains. The strength we saw in Q3 has continued in Q4. We are off to a strong start in the quarter and are once again raising our outlook for the year. We expect strong compounding growth and operating leverage to continue for years to come. I will start by reiterating the fundamental thesis of our long-term growth. We have penetrated less than 1% of our massive $275 billion custom manufacturing TAM. This is a market that remains largely offline today, still run on email quotes and multi-day turnarounds.

The majority of it is still sourced within 30 to 50 mile radius of the factory floor. To me, the gap is the opportunity. We are in the opening innings of a digital transformation, and our ability to capture the massive untapped opportunity gives us strong confidence in our long-term growth trajectory. Our marketplace is well-positioned to capture this demand. The three consecutive quarters of 40%+ growth in our marketplace are direct evidence that the product-led strategy put in place last year is working. We are defining the e-commerce playbook in custom manufacturing and raising the experience bar for buyers and suppliers everywhere. I will now spend a few minutes providing updates to our key focus areas.

First, I will talk about establishing Xometry as the digital infrastructure for custom manufacturing. Our confidence in driving the next S-curve of our growth stems from our ability to apply our core AI models to a decade plus of proprietary data. The intelligence we derive from our data gives our customers the confidence in manufacturability of their part, the instant pricing options we present, and Xometry's ability to source the part optimally. The depth of our data and intelligence is unrivaled in custom manufacturing. That same intelligence is now extending beyond our marketplace, embedding natively into partnership environments like Siemens Designcenter. Proof that intelligence itself, not just the marketplace around it, is the infrastructure other platforms want to build on.

More broadly, we see this as Xometry becoming the connective layer between design intent and actual physical production. Siemens is the first, but not the only place we expect to integrate our intelligence. Deep technical integration is a critical pillar of our product-led growth strategy. Establishing seamless AI-native digital threads that remove friction from the custom manufacturing workflows will be an ongoing focus. We are making excellent progress on the Siemens collaboration, working as integrated teams across multiple products, regions, and departments. We are building native integrations to Siemens Designcenter, bringing Xometry's manufacturability and pricing insight directly into the platform.

We expect a beta launch in Q1 2027, followed by a gradual ramp of customers to the various versions of Designcenter throughout the year. In addition to the work within Designcenter, there is also active collaboration between Siemens Supplyframe and Thomas, extending the value both teams can bring to their customers. We will share more as we hit milestones, and we expect Siemens partnership to positively impact our 2027 operating results. Our second focus area is improving our AI-native marketplace experiences. Our customer and supplier online journeys are rapidly defining the e-commerce playbook in custom manufacturing.

As I have shared before, one of our core beliefs is that the B2B buying experience should be every bit as good as what people experience in their personal lives. The days of clunky B2B software, multi-step checkout processes, and waiting days for an email quote are simply over. What we are seeing is a generational shift in who is making manufacturing purchasing decisions. The engineers, procurement buyers, and supply chain lead roles are now full of dynamic, digitally native individuals. They expect the same frictionless experience at work that they have in their personal lives. When they find that Xometry can deliver, they become Xometry champions inside their organizations.

On our Q2 call, we discussed enhancing our AI model capabilities in costing, sourcing, and process recommendations, a new generation of high-capacity, interconnected models that span the entire manufacturing journey. We are training these models on much larger datasets and retraining them more frequently, so every quote, order, and supplier outcome sharpens the outcomes for the next one. Hence, the smarter the platform gets, the faster we turn complex engineering inputs into comprehensive manufacturing and supply chain decisions. In Q3, we put that foundation to work. You can see the results in our financials. Q3 marketplace gross margin was a record 36.0%, up 130 basis points from Q2.

In Q3, we made further marketplace enhancements to reduce friction and improve buyer experience. We moved the majority of our buyer traffic onto our new e-commerce platform, which is faster, increasingly mobile-optimized, and rebuilt from the ground up to be AI-native. We are seeing that the platform is attracting more and more digitally native engineers. The new architecture is changing how fast we can launch product updates. We now deliver core buyer workflows at a fraction of the time that they would have taken a year ago.

In Q3, these included a redesigned buyer dashboard with one-click reordering to drive conversion and repeat orders, and a shift to arrives by dates in place of lead and transit times to simplify supply chain decisions. Additionally, we added more than 100 custom materials to our Instant Quoting Engine to expand marketplace selection. For our suppliers, in Q3, we launched the next generation of Workcenter experience. The new homepage brings together job discovery, performance scores, and payout visibility, and it is now live for all U.S. suppliers. The enhanced Job Board adds filters, an on-screen 3D viewer, and drawing review. Since launch, suppliers are accepting work faster, and more jobs are matched to the right partner on the first offer.

Suppliers can now find and win work that fits their capabilities more easily. I will now share advances we made in our third focus area, expanding our buyer and supplier networks. Our focus is on becoming the most expansive custom manufacturing e-commerce platform for our buyers and suppliers. We delivered strong active buyer growth during the quarter, with active buyers increasing 20% year-over-year to over 93,000. Our marketing teams have strengthened our MarTech and personalization capabilities, helping drive a record number of net buyer adds. Their efforts, combined with our AI model optimizations, are driving conversion rate improvements and continued robust buyer growth, with improving marketplace unit economics. There are still millions of potential buyers to convert.

Our partnership with Siemens and our other initiatives to become the infrastructure layer in custom manufacturing will further add momentum to these strengths. We are ever more focused on expanding our global supplier network and improving our supplier experience. Our global network of over 5,000 active suppliers across the world remains a significant strategic advantage, giving buyers unmatched speed, capacity, and resilience. In Q3, we expanded certified capacity and ITAR sponsorships, strengthening U.S. manufacturing by helping suppliers win higher-value work. Additionally, in our domestic supplier network, suppliers are benefiting from Xometry's rapidly growing demand, enabling them to acquire new machines and create net new capacity.

Our 2027 manufacturing outlook highlights that smaller manufacturers offer a key advantage, as 44% of businesses under $50 million operate below 70% capacity, compared with just 16% of manufacturers above $100 million. As an asset-light marketplace, we are laser-focused on applying our AI investments, connecting these suppliers to demand at scale. Let me share an example of success one such supplier has found on our platform, a U.S. machine shop that joined the Xometry network in Q1 of 2025. In its first full quarter, they did about $140,000 of work, ramping rapidly to nearly sevenfold to $1 million in Q3 of 2025.

As they grew with Xometry, they added ITAR and ISO certifications, opening up new job demand from aerospace, defense, and medical device industries. Over the last 12 months, they earned over $2.3 million through Xometry, enabling investments in new CNC machining centers, lathes, and laser engraving capability. This is the flywheel in action. Xometry brings increasing job flow, partners invest in capacity and capabilities, and we deliver against customer demand. Our fourth focus area is deepening enterprise engagement. We continue to deliver robust enterprise growth. Our Q3 revenue from our largest customers increased by over 40%. At the top of our enterprise funnel, we delivered accelerating 26% year-over-year growth in the number of accounts with greater than $50,000 marketplace spend.

In Q3, we expanded our partnership with TradeCentric to add purchase order automation and invoice automation to our PunchOut connection with customers' e-procurement systems. The integration works with more than 220 e-procurement solutions, including Coupa, SAP Ariba, and Microsoft Dynamics, and is available now to U.S. customers. Invoice-to-PO matching is now automatic before an electronic invoice is sent, which removes several manual steps between an order and payment. As Xometry becomes more embedded in our customers' workflows, we are seeing continued wallet share gains and more predictable spend. We ended 2025 with four accounts spending at least $10 million annually. We expect more accounts to cross that threshold in 2026.

This is driven by multi-year production programs across key end markets. For example, this deeper integration is exactly what we saw with a major defense prime facing demanding program timelines. The customer initially projected a six-month manufacturing and assembly lead time. However, by leveraging 15 suppliers in our network and our rapid DFM capabilities, the customer was able to shrink design to delivery by a full three months. Our marketplace has produced hundreds of components for this program, including complex finishing and hardware installation, reinforcing our position as a trusted end-to-end partner for high-stakes defense applications.

Over our three-year partnership, this proven capability to deliver supply chain resilience and speed has fueled continuous land-and-expand growth, scaling the account well past our $10 million per year enterprise marker. The final focus area I will share is leveraging services opportunities. Our services offerings under Thomas helps us engage with suppliers who aren't yet in the marketplace ecosystem. Thomas has built the largest industrial manufacturing-focused digital sourcing network in North America, providing buyers access to over 500,000 suppliers. We are focused on improving our monetization on the Thomas platform and leveraging the vast network to supplement Xometry's supplier capacity. We made strong progress on our Thomas platform in Q3.

We are building on this momentum and recently enabled faster marketing services execution by integrating specialized AI workflows into Thomas Marketing Services. Additionally, we will soon launch our first collaboration with Supplyframe and Thomas, driving incremental high-quality buyer traffic to Thomas. We will build upon this launch momentum to enhance our services business with additional e-commerce offerings. In conclusion, our momentum remains strong in Q4. We are raising our 2026 revenue growth outlook given robust demand on our marketplace and the strong execution of our teams. We expect strong compounding growth to continue in 2027 and coming years, driven by our initiatives as we rapidly scale beyond $1 billion.

I'm very excited about the road ahead, and before I hand it over, I want to thank our entire team. The $1 billion plus run rate milestone we are reporting today is the outcome of a lot of hard work across all our teams worldwide. I am proud of the pace at which teams continue to execute our product-led growth strategy. I will now turn the call over to James for a more detailed review of Q3 financials and our business outlook.

James Miln: Thanks, Sanjeev, and good morning, everyone. Q3 marketplace revenue was $238 million, and services revenue was $14.4 million. Q3 marketplace revenue per active buyer increased a robust 19% year-over-year, primarily due to increasing wallet share. Enterprise investments continue to show strong returns, with accounts with at least $500,000 spend again growing revenue over 40% year-over-year. Our enterprise strategy focuses on our largest accounts, each of which we believe have $10 million plus in potential annual account revenue. We are focused on improving engagement and monetization on the platform, which remains a leader in industrial sourcing, supplier selection, and digital marketing solutions.

Q3 gross profit was $98.7 million, an increase of 37% year-over-year, driven by a robust 44% year-over-year growth in marketplace gross profit. Q3 marketplace gross margin was a record 36.0%, up 130 basis points quarter-over-quarter. We are focused on driving marketplace gross profit dollar growth through the combination of top-line growth and gross margin expansion. Q3 adjusted EBITDA was $21.4 million, a record 8.5% margin compared with 3.4% a year ago.

Q3 incremental adjusted EBITDA margin was 21% year-over-year, driven by strong revenue growth, gross margin, and operating efficiencies. Our U.S. segment continues to show scaling profitability with adjusted EBITDA margin of 10.3%, while our international segment adjusted EBITDA shows significant improvement year-over-year. At the end of the third quarter, cash and cash equivalents and marketable securities were $505 million. We generated $25.6 million in operating cash flow year-to-date through Q3, driven by strong operating leverage and working capital efficiency. In the third quarter, we invested approximately $15 million in cash CapEx, almost entirely software-related, reflecting our technology investments in the platform and accelerating product rollouts.

We are focused on improving cash flow conversion given our asset-light model and limited capital spending. We are focused on strategically balancing future investment with a relentless pursuit of operating leverage, given the vast market opportunity and our low penetration rates. For the full year 2026, we are raising our revenue growth outlook to approximately 37% from 33%-34%, driven by approximately 41% marketplace growth. For the full year 2026, we expect adjusted EBITDA in the range of $68 million-$68.5 million, approximately $7 million higher than prior guidance, and approximately 20% incremental adjusted EBITDA margin.

As we look further ahead, we believe that we are in the opening innings of a digital transformation with a very long-term growth trajectory. We expect strong durable growth to continue to compound in the coming years, given the large fragmented market opportunity and our strategic growth initiatives. We continue to target at least 20% incremental adjusted EBITDA on a full-year basis above the $1 billion revenue run rate. We look forward to updating you on our Q4 call and providing a detailed outlook for 2027 at that time. Prior to taking your questions, I would like to extend my gratitude to our entire team.

Today's strong performance is a direct result of their relentless execution, and I'm thrilled about the opportunities it unlocks for our future. Together, these factors give us immense confidence in what lies ahead. With that, operator, can you please open up the call for questions?

James Miln: I can add, Brian, I think that the team are executing well here through improvements we had through product-led strategy and some MarTech and personalization efforts. Shawn Milne: Brian, it is Shawn. I would just add on to what Sanjeev and James were saying. Sanjeev Singh Sahni: Let me start. I think the important thing to think about is we are at 1% of the penetration of the TAM, at $275 billion. #3218. iOS 27.3 introduces new iPhone Duo feature for one-handed use

iOS 27.3 beta 1 launched today with a variety of new features, including a big upgrade for one-handed iPhone Duo use thanks to Reachability.

When iPhone Duo reviews first arrived last month, some complained that the extra-wide design of the outer display made it difficult to use one-handed.

At the time, Apple said that it would introduce Reachability via a future software update to help.

Today with iOS 27.3 beta 1, Reachability has officially arrived for iPhone Duo users.

Unlike Reachability on other iPhones, which shifts the screen down vertically, the iPhone Duo version works horizontally.

Once the feature is enabled (Settings ⇾ Accessibility ⇾ Reachability), a short swipe to the side of the screen will shift everything to the left or right, making it easier to reach.

If you’re struggling at all with one-handed iPhone Duo use, iOS 27.3 might make a big difference.

Currently iOS 27.3 is only available in developer beta, but a public beta is expected to launch in the coming days. However, if you’re concerned about bugs or performance issues, we recommend waiting for the launch version. Apple has said that iOS 27.3 will ship to all users next month, with mid-December the most likely window.

Have you tried Reachability on iPhone Duo yet? How is it working for you? Let us know in the comments.

#3217. Google’s latest Home updates just fixed my biggest annoyances with its speakers and cameras

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Google details 42 fixes to its Home app and the devices compatible with it.

Google’s latest release notes detail early access updates to Gemini for Home and software updates to the Google Home app, focused on bug fixes and general improvements to cameras, doorbells, Nest Wi-Fi, Google TV Streamers, and in-app controls and interfaces.

Also: Google Home Speaker vs. Amazon Echo Dot Max

There are 42 fixes Google addresses in its release notes, ranging from stability improvements to more pressing issues such as Gemini misunderstanding commands and devices connecting more quickly after a network timeout.

Google fixed a few issues that, if they had continued, would have made me consider using another manufacturer for my home’s cameras and doorbell.

Google’s release notes promise improvements in Gemini’s ability to transfer music between rooms. If you have several Google Home speakers around your house, you might want to use your voice to command one to transfer audio.

According to Google, Gemini’s understanding of these commands is now deeper and more aware of the rooms in your home. (It’s something that Sonos does really well.) Now, you can tell Gemini to “move the music here,” and it should work.

Also: I changed these Android Auto settings to limit what Gemini learns about me

In the same vein, Google says it fixed a volume issue where users would command Gemini to adjust the volume on a speaker in another room, but the speaker in closer proximity would respond instead.

Google’s release notes also cite fixes to timer and alarm volume issues, unprompted responses from speakers and displays, and more reliable YouTube TV commands on smart displays.

Google’s release addresses major bugs in the Google Home app when users are trying to access a camera’s live view. For iOS users, the issue with scrolling to the end of an event and receiving a “Video Not Available” error should be fixed. On foldable Androids, watching a live event while folding or unfolding the phone would prompt an error. Google says this issue is also fixed.

Additionally, software updates for Nest Cam (1st gen), Nest Cam Outdoor (1st gen), Nest Doorbell (wired, 1st gen / Nest Hello), Nest Cam IQ Indoor, and Nest Cam IQ Outdoor have all migrated to the Google Home app as Google continues to phase out the older Nest app.

I enjoy my home’s outdoor Nest cameras, but their connectivity issues are often frustrating, especially during inclement weather. The camera above my garage would often disconnect from Wi-Fi, so I purchased a cheap extender to help it maintain a connection.

If my power went out, even for a brief moment, the garage camera wouldn’t come back online for hours, an issue my backyard camera didn’t experience. According to Google, a software update has addressed the issue that caused cameras to stall or crash when reconnecting after brief interruptions.

Also: Amazon’s Echo Show 16 makes Apple’s 7-inch HomeView look puny

During the same brief power and Wi-Fi outage at my home, my Nest Thermostats also appeared as Offline, even though my furnace and air conditioner were working fine. My power momentarily disconnects often during hurricane season, so these issues were very frustrating. According to Google, devices that were inaccurately displaying as Offline were affected by an iOS-specific bug that has now been fixed.

If you have a wired 1st-gen Nest Doorbell, the software update also includes improvements to Familiar Face detection and audio/video synchronization.
