#3216. Jean-Luc in Blue Jeans: Picard Cosplay Taught Me How Much Patrick Stewart Is Loved

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

My husband was assimilated at an Emerald City Comic Con, and even the Borg adored him. Thank you, Patrick Stewart.

Star Trek fans never doubted the amount of love the community had for Patrick Stewart, who died Wednesday at age 86. But I experienced that love firsthand. Back in 2021, my husband, Rob, dressed as Captain Jean-Luc Picard for Emerald City Comic Con in Seattle, and the adoration he received, simply for cosplaying Stewart’s beloved character, was overwhelming.

Our planning wasn’t complicated. Looking for a costume that would go with his shaved head, and being a big fan of the show, it made sense for him to put on a red and black Star Trek uniform shirt, pin on a combadge and four pips to denote the Starfleet rank of captain, and step into some black shoes. Except for his glasses (and mask since this was 2021, the second year of the COVID-19 pandemic), it was an eerily accurate look.

Read more: Patrick Stewart, Who Gracefully Steered Star Trek Into Its Next Generation, Dies at 86

Once we walked into the Seattle Convention Center for the con, it was as if the real Patrick Stewart had shown up. The respect Stewart had built up for Picard transferred seamlessly to his lookalike. Just walking around with Rob made me feel like a celebrity escort. We couldn’t travel more than a few feet without someone noticing and calling out to him, always with glee, always with respect.

“Hey, Captain! Captain!”“Jean-Luc!”“Make it so, sir!”“Engage!”“Darmok and Jalad at Tanagra!”

Rob didn’t even wear costume-authentic black pants. In a hurry to get out the door and not expecting this level of attention, he had just pulled on his jeans. That led to a few of the funnier comments.

“Hey Captain! Was it casual day on the bridge?”

Comic Con attendees go all out. There were eerily realistic characters from Star Wars, Pokemon creatures, groups of friends dressed as The Incredibles, at least five Spider-Men, the Doctor from Doctor Who and exquisite, elaborate characters from anime. Many, many people had put more time, money and sweat equity into their costumes than we did, but few received such a universally awed reception.

Read more: Remember Patrick Stewart by Streaming Star Trek, X-Men and Other Genre-Defining Roles

Other Star Trek characters were also portrayed, for sure. Two separate Will Rikers, Picard’s trusted “Number One,” raced up to us at different times to take photos with their captain. One woman cosplaying as Kathryn Janeway, captain of the USS Voyager from Star Trek: Voyager, also posed with Rob for a two-captain photo.

And then, they saw us. A group of Comic Con attendees dressed as the Borg, the villainous cyborgs who take Picard hostage to assimilate him and temporarily turn him into Locutus of Borg.

These Borg did not throw their costumes together last-minute. They could have walked off a Hollywood set. They had working lights on their outfits, ocular and cranial “implants,” corpse-like face makeup, arms built into cybernetic tools. Of the Borgs, three were towering men and one was a woman. The woman played the Borg Queen, her bald head covered in white makeup, elegant and terrifying.

The minute the Borg saw Rob’s Picard in the convention center crowd, they came after him. Resistance, as they say in the show, was futile.

Thankfully, they were a jollier sort than the television Borg, and after one joke about his casual-day jeans, they whisked him away to stroll around as a group and snap photos.

These Borg were so realistic that I felt a bit unnerved the entire time he was gone — and relieved when they returned him unharmed, thanked us, waved and headed on their way. I’m sure there were other serendipitous meetups between cosplayers at the convention, but this one was amazing to see and even more so to be even a small part of.

We’ve been to Emerald City Comic Con other times. Our daughter has cosplayed a variety of characters, and Rob once went as Dr. Stone, a science prodigy with green-tipped white hair (which required a wig). People in the know enjoyed that cosplay, too, and he was similarly asked to pose for photos.

But the sheer love we experienced when he dressed as Captain Picard was like nothing I’ve ever felt. Since his death, I’ve seen Stewart called a generation’s space dad, and there’s truth in that. People at the convention were delighted to see their space dad, even if just a doppelganger. It buoyed us along on an unexpected high on that cold December day in 2021.

In the famous Star Trek: Next Generation episode Darmok, Picard is trapped on a planet with the Tamarian captain, Dathon. They can’t understand each other. The entire Tamarian language is constructed out of mythological and historical metaphors, none of which Picard knows

Slowly, Picard begins to comprehend. He figures out that one of the most frequent phrases, “Darmok and Jalad at Tanagra!” references Darmok and Jalad, warriors who united on the island of Tanagra and eventually became friends, just like he and Dathon.

But there’s another phrase I’ve been thinking of lately. “Kiazi’s children, their faces wet.” An online Tamarian dictionary translates it as “downplaying the severity of a perceived injury.”

There’s no downplaying this loss. We’re all Kiazi’s children today. Our faces wet.

You could see these shoes the same day Rockstar releases the long-awaited game.

Rockstar Games is releasing the long-awaited Grand Theft Auto 6 in just a few weeks, on Nov. 19, and rapper Travis Scott and Nike are reportedly getting in on the game’s hype. According to Sneaker News, Nike, Rockstar Games and Travis Scott are working together to release a set of Nike Air Force 1 ’07 sneakers themed around the upcoming game. Reports suggest the shoes will retail for $130 and be available on Nov. 19, the same day as the game’s release.

The shoes will reportedly be available in three colorways. Those palettes are supposedly “White/White/Fire Pink,” “Black/Black/Fire Pink” and “Multicolor/Pale Ivory/Black/Bold Berry/Fire Pink.” The sneaker account prm.stocks.01 shared images of what the black pair would look like if you want to take a peek.

The shoe will reportedly have the reverse swoosh logo traditionally seen on other Travis Scott sneakers, and the leather appears to feature a grid that looks like city blocks.

The shoes have six stars on the heels, the report says, a nod to the six-star wanted level, which makes its return to the Grand Theft Auto series in the upcoming game. Grand Theft Auto 5 replaced the six-star system with a five-star system.

The sneakers will also supposedly come with a $100 GTA-branded money band around the shoe’s toe box. Other Nike shoes, like the different colors of the Concepts x Nike SB Dunk Low Lobsters, have had removable rubber bands, too.

And the shoe’s midsole reportedly replaces the “AIR” lettering normally on all Air Force One models with the letters “GTA.” There are likely more details that reference the game hidden throughout the shoe.

Neither Nike nor Rockstar Games immediately responded to my request for comment.

While there will reportedly be three colors of this shoe available, I think Nike, Rockstar and Travis Scott could have stopped at the black pair. I’m sure the other two colorways are fine, but it’s a joke that black Air Force 1 sneakers are used in various criminal and illegal activities, making that pair a perfect representation of the Grand Theft Auto series.

I appreciate the six-star and money band details we see in the photos, and the pink gives the pairs a nice hint of Vice City-coded color without being too much. The black pair of these shoes reportedly comes with black and pink laces, and I’d lace up the pink ones if I ever got these shoes.

However, since these are a collab between Nike, Rockstar and Travis Scott, I’m not expecting to see them on my feet. Travis Scott and Nike collaborations usually release in limited quantities, so it’s difficult to get a pair. You could always buy the shoes on eBay, StockX or a similar marketplace, but some Travis Scott and Nike collabs sell on the aftermarket for more than $1,000, depending on your size. And I’m not spending that much on a single pair of shoes. I’ve got a mortgage to pay, thank you very much.

#3214. Your Netgear router may be vulnerable to a security exploit – how to check and patch it

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

A vulnerability in some Netgear routers could allow an attacker with access to your network to run malicious commands on the device.

Do you own a Netgear router? The bad news is that the device could be susceptible to a security flaw that would leave it vulnerable to an attacker. The good news: This exploit affects only a small number of Netgear routers, and the company has already issued patches to squash the bugs.

Also: Run this 10-step security check on your phone once a year

The vulnerabilities differ slightly among the various affected models, as described in Netgear’s security advisory. In general, these flaws could be exploited by an attacker who gains access to your network, allowing them to run unauthorized and potentially malicious commands on the router.

All the flaws are ranked as medium severity but clearly still pose a threat, prompting Netgear to roll out new firmware for each impacted model. You should be able to update your router to the latest firmware directly through its settings, but you can also grab each update from Netgear’s website.

Here are descriptions of the vulnerabilities, the names and models of the affected routers, and links to download the patches.

Described in CVE-2026-11732, the first vulnerability could allow an attacker who already has access to your network, most likely through your Wi-Fi credentials, to run unauthorized commands on the device. The flaw is exploitable only if you’ve enabled the Block Sites feature, which blocks access to specific web sites based on domain name or keywords.

Also: Firefox and Chrome patch 200+ security flaws combined

Affected products and the firmware download pages to patch the bug:

Among these, the RAX5 4-Stream AX1600 WiFi 6 Router has reached end of service (EoS), meaning no further updates will be available after this latest one. In this case, Netgear advises owners to upgrade to a newer router.

Defined in CVE-2026-11731, the second vulnerability could allow an unauthenticated attacker with access to your local network and your router’s management service view and modify certain device details and administrative settings.

Also: Chrome warns you about suspicious websites now

Affected products and the download pages to patch the bug:

Documented in CVE-2026-11730, the third vulnerability impacts two Netgear range extenders. Here, an attacker who already has local network access could hijack an authenticated administrator session on the device’s web management portal.

Affected products and their firmware download pages:

Among these two, the EX3700 AC750 WiFi Range Extender Essentials Edition has reached end of service, which means it’s time to move to a newer device.

The remaining routers impacted by security flaws have all reached end of service. Again, that means no further updates will be available, and Netgear advises owners to switch to a newer device.

Described in CVE-2026-9218, an attacker who’s connected to the router’s local network and has the administrator username and password could run unauthorized commands on the device.

Also: The best Wi-Fi routers: Expert tested and reviewed

Affected products and their firmware download pages:

With the CBR40 Orbi AC2200 Tri-band WiFi Cable Modem Router, the latest firmware will not fix the current security bug, so owners should move to a newer device to stay secure.

The remaining Netgear router impacted by security flaws is also at end-of-service, and the latest firmware won’t fix its security flaws. Again, Netgear advises owners to switch to a newer and more secure device.

#3213. iOS 27.3 expands Siri AI with many new capabilities across Apple apps

iOS 27.3 has just entered beta testing and includes major new features for Siri AI across iPhone, iPad and Mac. The company has unlocked many new capabilities across major Apple apps, like Music, Messages, Safari, Reminders and more.

We are still digging into the beta, but here’s a taste of what new things you can get Siri AI to do:

With the Music app, you can now create playlists and save them to your library, like you can ask it to make you “a playlist for songs for a day at the beach”, and then save it for later.

In Messages, you can now ask it to schedule iMessages to be sent later, edit and unsent messages, as well as respond with emoji reactions. You can compose new Notes with bold, italic, and rich text formatting, organize your Notes folders, and more.

Photos gets a big expansion with new Siri AI capabilities that let you favorite photos, rotate and edit images, and rename people and pets all with your voice.

You can now use Siri AI with the Calendar app to create events featuring invitees, location, video call links and more. And in Reminders, you can now create urgent reminders for the first time with Siri.

In Safari, you can now use Siri to create tap groups from a list of URLs, sort your tabs, clear your history, delete reading list items and more.

Journal support with Siri AI is new for the first time. You can create entries with text transcription, or record audio entries.

There’s also wide support for file and folder management with Siri AI Files integration. You can get file content, create files and folders, send files to the trash, organize by type, rename files, and more, using just your voice.

We are also seeing new Siri features for Weather, Maps, Preview and Shortcuts, and will keep testing to find new integrations. Apple is also opening up this support to third-party developers.

iOS 27.3 is currently in beta testing and will be released publicly later this year.

#3211. Rhythm Pharma (RYTM) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Japan launch and U.S. demand lifted sales sharply this quarter.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Rhythm Pharmaceuticals, Inc. (RYTM -7.49%) reported $92.1 million in global net product revenue for the third quarter, driven by the commercial launch of IMCIVREE for acquired hypothalamic obesity in the United States. Management indicated that patient demand remains consistent through the second full quarter of launch, supported by expanding payer coverage and a growing base of prescribers. The company initiated international expansion with a commercial launch in Japan and advanced plans for Phase III development of bivamelagon in both hypothalamic obesity and Prader-Willi syndrome. To support these initiatives, Rhythm secured a $750 million debt facility and amended its licensing agreement with LG Chem to reduce long-term royalty obligations across its MC4R portfolio.

Operator: Ladies and gentlemen, thank you for standing by. Welcome to Rhythm Pharmaceuticals Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. At this time, all participants are in a listen-only mode. After the speaker's presentation, there will be a question-and-answer session. To ask a question during the session, you would need to press star one on your telephone. You will then hear an automated message advising your hand is raised, and to withdraw your question, please press star one again. We ask that you please limit to one question. Please be advised that today's conference is being recorded. I would now like to turn the call over to Dave Connolly, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Dave Connolly: Thank you, Michelle. I am Dave Connolly here at Rhythm Pharmaceuticals. For those of you participating on the conference call, our slides can be accessed and controlled by going to the investor section of our website, ir.rhythmtx.com. Last night, we issued a press release announcing the amendment to our bivamelagon licensing agreement, and this morning, we issued our press release that provides our Q3 2026 financial results and a business update. Both press releases are available on our website. Our agenda is listed on slide 2.

On the call today are David Meeker, our Chairman, Chief Executive Officer, and President, Jennifer Lee, Executive Vice President, Head of North America, Hunter Smith, Chief Financial Officer, and Yann Mazabraud, Executive Vice President, Head of International, is on the line joining us from Europe. On slide 3, I will remind you this call contains remarks concerning future expectations, plans, and prospects, which constitute forward-looking statements. Actual results may differ materially from those indicated by these forward-looking statements as a result of various important factors, including those discussed in our most recent annual or quarterly reports on file with the SEC.

In addition, any forward-looking statements represent our views as of today and should not be relied upon as representing our views as of any subsequent dates. We specifically disclaim any obligation to update such statements. With that, I will turn the call over to David Meeker, who will begin on slide 5.

David Meeker: Thank you, Dave. Good morning, and thank you for joining today. Rhythm continues to execute on multiple fronts, and we are excited to update you on our progress. Let us start on slide 5. We are very pleased to announce a strong third quarter, driven by an excellent start to the U.S. launch. Start forms are growing as expected, with encouraging market access translating to strong revenue performance of $92 million for the quarter. Jennifer will provide more details. We are excited about launching in Japan, with the first commercial patients already on treatment. We have every expectation that Japan will become our second-largest market. Yann will provide more color there.

I will say more about our clinical development plans and the recently announced amendment to our LG Chem deal over the next couple slides. Slide 6 is a reminder of our three major strategic pillars. The first pillar is the genetic indications, where we have multiple approvals, and we will be looking to expand the list of genes we are investigating. More to come on that in 2027. Second is HO, where we have a growing conviction in the magnitude of this opportunity globally, as you will hear more about today. Third is Prader-Willi syndrome, a devastating genetic disease with only one approved therapy in the U.S. and a desperate need for more treatment options.

Let me spend a minute on why PWS is so strategically important to Rhythm and why we believe we can make a meaningful difference in this disease. I often draw the analogy to where the cystic fibrosis community was at the time the first disease-modifying treatments were being approved. Like CF, PWS patients are almost universally diagnosed at birth. The newborn is hypotonic, floppy, which leads to early genetic testing. Average survival is age 30, which speaks to the severe unmet medical need, and providing care for these patients is challenging for their families, the healthcare system, and society as a whole.

The PWS community is well-organized with a strong patient organization, specialized clinics staffed by experienced clinicians, providing these patients with greater access to the healthcare system than many patients with HO, for example, who still don't have a diagnosis. It is a complex genetic disease with multiple genes involved, but central to the disease is impaired signaling through the MC4R pathway. The six-month phase II data Dr. Miller presented at ENDO in June, showing a reduction in hyperphagia scores, anxiety scores, and BMI values, supports the potential role of an MC4R precision agonist in the management of this disease. Now, I will extend the CF analogy one step further.

Vertex recognized with their first approval in CF that they had a unique ability to make a major difference in this disease, so they literally doubled and tripled down on trying to optimize outcomes. Our strategy will be similar. We will run our first phase III trial with bivamelagon, but with the expectation, given the size and importance of this opportunity, we would develop both of our next-generation therapies in this disease. As previously indicated, the decision to start with bivamelagon has some practical aspects, most specifically related to CMC and availability of supply. We simply have an ability to start earlier than we would with RM-718.

Furthermore, as with CF, we expect a monotherapy to work and be approved, but given the complexity of the disease, optimal outcomes will be achieved by combination therapies. We are not prepared to discuss our portfolio at this time, we will do that in 2027, but the message today is simply that we are working to develop the best possible approach to MC4R diseases based on our understanding of the biology, and that will include proprietary combination approaches. Moving to slide 7, we're excited to initiate our phase III bivamelagon HO study. This is a 52-week comparably sized study to the original TRANSCEND study, with BMI as the primary endpoint.

We hope to begin screening patients at the first sites by the end of the year and expect to dose the first patients in January. With a decision to proceed with bivamelagon in PWS, we will now engage with regulators with the goal of initiating a six-month phase III study in PWS with hyperphagia, as measured by HQ-CT, as a primary endpoint in 2027. I want to provide a shout-out to the Rhythm teams who have not been idle on the development front.

In preparation for the biva phase III studies, we needed to complete the following: a bioequivalence study with a new formulation, a food effect study, a drug-drug interaction study, and a hepatic impairment study, all of which have been completed satisfactorily in the past year, further de-risking bivamelagon as a core asset as we move into phase III trials. Finally, a brief word about our recently announced amendment of the LG Chem deal. Our decision to amend was driven by two factors. First, our growing belief in the overall opportunity related to MC4R pathway diseases, giving us the confidence to buy down the existing royalty.

Secondly, the original structure, despite our best efforts to align the two companies' interests, left us with an economic disincentive to fully develop bivamelagon, as that would drive a disproportionate royalty burden relative to developing RM-718, for example. In the current structure, we are fully aligned and can simply, as we would want to do, follow the science and develop the best possible treatment for the indication. I remind you that the patent protection for both bivamelagon and RM-718 extends into the 2040s, providing sustainable long-term value for shareholders. Hunter will provide more details on the LG transaction. I'll now turn the call over to Jen.

Jennifer Lee: Thank you, David. I'll begin on slide 9. I'm pleased to report on the strong performance we're seeing in the U.S. launch of IMCIVREE for acquired hypothalamic obesity. In the third quarter, the second full quarter of launch, patient demand continues to be strong and consistent with what we experienced our first quarter of launch. We're seeing growth in a broadening base of prescribers. On the patient access side, reimbursement trends are highly encouraging, reflecting our ongoing payer engagement, leading to an increase in IMCIVREE policy adoption. On slide 10, I'll start with metrics related to patient demand.

Since launch on March 19 and through the first two quarters, we have received more than 700 patient start forms for acquired HO, including start forms for 71 clinical trial patients. Consistent with the first quarter, the patient age distribution remains evenly split amongst older and younger than 21, with 20% of patient start forms from patients between 4 and 12, pointing to the urgency that comes with caring for children. We are pleased with the distribution of time from hypothalamic injury among patients with prescriptions. Consistent with the prior quarter, approximately 15% of prescriptions have come from patients injured within the last two years. Hence, they were diagnosed and treated early in their disease journey.

More than a third of patient start forms have come in for those whose hypothalamic injury was 10 years ago or more. These early dynamics are encouraging and demonstrate meaningful demand across a broad range of patients and a long-term growth opportunity in both incident and prevalent patients. Slide 11 outlines how we are approaching the opportunity, balancing the institutional medical centers where patients begin their journey and then following the patients through their care. The first point of contact for patients with hypothalamic injury comes at a major medical center or large healthcare organization, where there is a concentration of new patients each year.

Upon launch, we identified 43 of these priority accounts, and as we've had more engagement in the field, we continue to see a growth in the number of these identified accounts. Approximately 30% of patients remain engaged with the care teams at these larger centers, while approximately 70% of patients transition beyond their original point of care. The total number of accounts and percentage of patients within these accounts will continue to evolve throughout the launch.

With that said, our HCP tiering provided to our sales teams are based off of where the volume of potential patients are, and our commercial approach balances physician engagement at these institutional accounts, as well as the physicians across other care settings, reflecting where patients enter care and where they are receiving ongoing follow-up care. We remain focused on driving earlier diagnosis and treatment of acquired HO patients within a year of onset of their acquired hypothalamic obesity symptoms, while working to ensure prevalent patients who have been living with acquired HO for several years also get to an accurate diagnosis and treatment. Onto slide 12. We continue to see strong growth and a broadening base of prescribers.

Launched to date, we have received start forms for more than 500 prescribers, including approximately 200 first-time acquired HO prescribers during the third quarter. Of the HO prescribers to date, approximately 25% of them have written two or more IMCIVREE prescriptions for acquired HO, an incremental increase from the 20% repeat prescriber metric at the end of the second quarter. This points to a positive experience with prescribing IMCIVREE, but also reflects the early stage of the launch and the opportunity that remains, as many of these HCPs have more than one potential acquired HO patient under their care.

Overall, 80% of prescribers are endocrinologists, evenly split between adult and pediatric endos, further supporting that acquired HO is a specialty opportunity. Slide 13. We've made significant progress with payers during the third quarter, and the early access trends and speed of approvals for reimbursement are highly encouraging. Payers are recognizing the differentiation and severity of acquired HO. Of approvals launched to date, 75% of them have come by the prior authorization stage, and over 80% of approvals have come within 60 days of receiving the start form. We are encouraged with the strong progress in securing positive payer policies.

As of the end of Q3, we have IMCIVREE policies in place for acquired HO that affect approximately 60% of Medicaid-covered lives and approximately 75% of commercial-covered lives. We expect that ongoing policies are going to be put into place throughout the end of the year. Importantly, these advances in payer coverage are resulting in positive access experiences for physicians and patients early in launch. Onto slide 14. Lastly for me, a brief update on BBS. We continue to grow the BBS business during the third quarter through the efforts of our dedicated team of territory managers now exclusively focused on BBS. BBS remains an important contributor to Rhythm's success. Now, let me hand it over to Yann.

Yann Mazabraud: Sorry. Thank you, Jennifer. I will begin on slide 16. We are very pleased to have launched IMCIVREE for acquired HO in Japan on October 14, following approval by the Ministry of Health, Labour, and Welfare, or MHLW, and inclusion on Japan's National Health Insurance Drug Price List. This launch represents an important milestone for patients and families in Japan. IMCIVREE is the very first approved therapy specifically for acquired HO, a serious disease for which there were previously no approved treatment options. It is also an important milestone for Rhythm and reflects several years of intense and focused work.

We made the decision to establish a presence in Japan because we saw significant unmet medical need, with an estimated patient population of 5,000-8,000 patients, and a specialist community that was highly engaged and focused on improving the diagnosis and treatment of acquired HO. Our first discussions with the Japanese regulatory authorities began in 2023. 12 Japanese patients participated in the TRANSCEND clinical trial, and through close collaboration across our global and Japanese teams, we were able to move efficiently from clinical development through regulatory review, pricing, and now commercial launch. The MHLW approval for IMCIVREE came less than six months after the approval in the U.S., five months and five days, to be more precise.

Our commitment to pursuing approval to benefit the lives of patients living with acquired HO in Japan is a point of pride for Rhythm and very much appreciated in Japan, especially by the healthcare authorities. We are excited to provide further details today, as this is a meaningful and durable long-term opportunity for Rhythm. Slide 17. A successful rare disease launch is focused on disease awareness, medical education, and scientific engagement. We believe this foundation is developing very well in Japan. In September, the Japan Endocrine Society and an MHLW-funded research group published official guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of acquired HO.

These guidelines are important because they describe the significant burden of acquired HO, recognize that conventional approaches to obesity are generally inadequate for these patients, and provide a more consistent clinical framework for disease recognition, diagnosis, and treatment. Also, in October, the Japan Endocrine Society, the Japanese Society for Pediatric Endocrinology, and the Japanese Society for Hypothalamic and Pituitary Tumors issued a joint statement on the safe and appropriate use of setmelanotide for acquired HO. The TRANSCEND publication in the New England Journal of Medicine, which included four Japanese authors, further supports awareness of both the disease and the clinical evidence among Japanese physicians.

These data were presented and very well received in June in Kyoto at the annual meeting of the Japan Endocrine Society. The approval and the launch, combined with these new treatment guidelines, support from leading medical societies, and growing clinical experience in Japan, provide a substantially stronger foundation for identifying and treating patients with acquired HO. Moving to slide 18. We began building our Japanese organization in April 2025 because we believed success in this market would require deep local capabilities and sustained engagement with physicians and patients. Today, we have more than 50 employees in Japan.

This includes 16 hospital affairs leads, a position similar to the territory managers in the U.S., and six scientific affairs managers supporting medical education and scientific community engagement. This is a very experienced team with deep rare disease background and a strong understanding of the Japanese healthcare system. Our targeting strategy reflects the way patients with acquired HO move through the healthcare system. We have identified and targeted 350 priority hospitals where a significant majority of patients with brain tumors are treated, and by extension, where patients with acquired HO are. This concentration allows us to take a disciplined, high-touch approach.

Our teams are focused on increasing disease awareness and helping institutions build the processes required to initiate and maintain treatment. At the same time, we are working to ensure physicians and institutions have the knowledge and support required to identify the appropriate patients and provide a high-quality treatment experience. Slide 19. Japan represents a large, accessible, and durable rare disease opportunity, and our significant pre-launch physician engagement and patient identification work give us a strong starting point. To date, our field teams have engaged with 300 of the 350 priority hospitals, and through this work, we have already identified more than 1,000 patients who may be eligible for IMCIVREE.

Rhythm is forging new ground in Japan, introducing a new disease to the market. With an integrated medical and commercial model initially focused on high-volume brain tumor centers, we have built a scalable approach to expand patient identification and treatment access across Japan. Our approach begins with intensive high-touch engagement in these priority centers, with the goal of replicating successful practices throughout Japan. While confident in the long-term opportunity, there are structural features of the Japanese market that we expect will influence the early launch trajectory. During the first year of a new drug launch, prescriptions are limited to a two-week supply.

This means patients must return to the hospital to consult with their physicians every two weeks to continue receiving treatment. This requirement applies during the first year of the product's launch in Japan. We expect the restriction to be lifted in November 2027, after which eligible patients may receive prescription supply for up to three months. We anticipate a greater commercial contribution from Japan in the second and third years of launch. The first year will be focused on building institutional experience, supporting patient identification, and establishing accessible treatment pathways. As physicians gain experience and the prescription supply restriction is lifted, we expect the launch to accelerate in years 2 and 3 and continue building over time.

Lastly, on slide 20, I will provide a brief update on Europe. We estimate that there are approximately 10,000 patients with acquired HO in Europe. With paid early access programs, physicians in France and Italy have treated well over 100 patients with HO, generating positive experience and real-world evidence. Following European Commission authorization earlier this year, we have continued to advance the country-level market access processes required for launch. In Germany, the G-BA process, which is our final step prior to launch, is nearing completion. We have also submitted reimbursement dossiers in France, Italy, the U.K., Spain, and the Netherlands. Our experience commercializing IMCIVREE for BBS and other rare MC4R pathway diseases provides a strong foundation for these discussions.

Payers and many national experts are already familiar with setmelanotide, the MC4R pathway, and Rhythm's rare disease approach. We continue to expect country-level launches for acquired HO in Europe during 2027, beginning with Germany, and with the timing in each of the additional markets dependent on the reimbursement process. With the launch now underway in Japan and market access activities advancing well in Europe, we are establishing the next phase of IMCIVREE's international growth and expanding our ability to bring this therapy to patients living with acquired HO around the world. With that, I will turn the call over to Hunter.

Hunter Smith: Thank you, Yann. Rhythm exited the third quarter in a strong financial position and encouraged by the early U.S. launch execution of acquired HO. The success of the launch is reflected in our quarterly revenue performance and underscores the quality of our business execution and increases our confidence in Rhythm's potential sustainable long-term value creation. I'll provide more details on our quarterly performance shortly, but I'll start with the details on the bivamelagon license amendment and our financing. On slide 22, our amended license agreement for biva represents a significant investment in Rhythm's MC4R agonist franchise. The original license with LG Chem completed in 2024 has been a tremendous success.

The data generated in the phase II trial in acquired HO deepened our conviction in bivamelagon's value potential and reinforced our belief that it can serve as a foundational asset in our MC4R agonism franchise. With this amendment, we are investing additional cash to increase our stake in bivamelagon, and hence our entire MC4R portfolio. We project that our cross-portfolio royalty obligations could have been 5%-7% under the previous agreement, pending future indication approvals for bivamelagon. We are buying down this royalty obligation to 1% flat, assuming U.S. approval for bivamelagon. In exchange for this reduced royalty, we will pay LG Chem $350 million in installments over the next four years.

Separately, in addition to the $205 million in development and commercial milestones due to LG Chem under the original agreement, under the amended agreement, those are now payable on MC4R portfolio sales, and LG Chem will receive an additional commercial milestone of $200 million if we achieve $3 billion in sales in a calendar year. When it comes time to pay that milestone, we would be happy to make that payment. Fixed payments totaling $350 million to LG Chem begin with the first payment of $70 million due 15 days from closing. Three additional payments will follow: $100 million in September 2027, $100 million in September 2028, and $80 million in September 2029.

While the payments will be made in the annual installments as I've described, the present value of the aggregate amount will be recognized in the fourth quarter as research and development expenses. Please note that for your models. Next year at this time, we anticipate two global pivotal trials evaluating bivamelagon, one in HO and one in PWS, will be well underway. This transaction represents a strategic investment in our core business and our growing confidence in its potential. On slide 23, to finance this investment and strengthen our balance sheet, we entered into a five-year term loan facility, providing Rhythm access to as much as $750 million.

We are pleased to continue and expand our partnership with HealthCare Royalty Partners, which dates back to the first half of 2022, when setmelanotide was approved for BBS, and before we read out positive data from the phase II trial of setmelanotide in HO. Also, we are now pleased to partner with Blackstone, a top-tier global investor whose insights and collaboration were critical to catalyzing this transaction. We believe the terms of this loan facility are competitive. The term loan commitment totals $500 million, with an additional $250 million available by mutual option.

The structure gives us access to capital without requiring us to draw the full amount, so we can match future borrowing decisions to funding requirements and continued development of the business. We will draw $250 million initially. Borrowings carry interest at SOFR plus 4.6%. The facility has a five-year term, no scheduled principal amortization before maturity, no equity component, and no exit fee. Funded amounts are subject to a 1% original issue discount and market standard non-call and prepayment penalty provisions. As part of this transaction, we also amended our existing revenue interest financing agreement with HealthCare Royalty.

These amendments remove certain debt-like covenants and default provisions, limit HCR's lien to backup security interests, and modify the agreement's material adverse event provisions. We are a far different company today than we were in 2022, and these changes reflect that improvement. Taken together, the amended license agreement and financing strengthen our ability to invest in bivamelagon, support our global commercial execution, and continue to advance the broader MC4R portfolio in our pipeline. This transaction represents a bullish investment in bivamelagon and in Rhythm's future. On slide 24, we continue to be well-capitalized with significant financial flexibility. We finished the quarter with approximately $321 million in cash equivalents, and short-term investments.

This quarter closed cash on hand does not include any of the proceeds from the term loan, nor the initial payment of $70 million to be paid to LG this quarter. As we've been saying for some time, we expect this cash amount to be sufficient to fund planned operations for at least 24 months. On slide 25, we saw continued strength in our global commercial business during Q3. Global net product sales of IMCIVREE totaled $92.1 million, which represents 29% sequential growth over the second quarter. Patient demand remained strong during the third quarter, with the global number of reimbursed patients on therapy globally increasing by 20%.

During the third quarter, $67.5 million, or 73% of product revenue, was generated in the U.S. The U.S. HO launch was the primary driver of sequentially quarterly revenue growth and accounted for the significant majority of the increase in reimbursed patients. On slide 26, I will walk you through the components of the sequential quarter-over-quarter revenue change. Global net revenue increased from $71.3 million in the second quarter to $92.1 million in the third quarter. We saw $15.1 million in revenue growth attributable to increased product demand in the U.S. More than 90% of that growth was attributable to the strong demand from patients with acquired HO.

The growing demand for IMCIVREE product shipments to Rhythm's specialty pharmacy outpaced patient dispenses by $4.5 million, resulting in a $1.3 million inventory effect on second-quarter revenue. Inventory on hand at the specialty pharmacy increased from 20 to 21 days. U.S. gross to net during the quarter was 86%, in line with Q2. International revenue increased $4.4 million sequentially to $24.7 million in the third quarter. Majority increase was attributable to the absence of $3.8 million retroactive charge associated with the French contribution mechanism recognized during the second quarter. Excluding this item, the underlying international business increased quarter-over-quarter, with growth from patient demand offset by the inherent variability of shipments to named patient sales markets.

Our international business remains strong, as evidenced by continued growth of almost 10% in patients on reimbursed therapy during the third quarter. On slide 27 is a financial snapshot of the third quarter compared to the third quarter of 2025. Cost of goods sold was 13.2% of product revenue, primarily driven by cost of materials and royalty payments. R&D expenses were $52.5 million for the third quarter compared to $46 million the same period last year. Sequentially, the increase was $9.1 million versus the second quarter. The increase was primarily driven by increased personnel costs, development costs for bivamelagon studies, and a development milestone associated with our CHI program. SG&A expenses were $66.8 million for the third quarter.

Sequentially, SG&A expenses decreased slightly by approximately 1% compared to the second quarter, largely reflecting timing around certain activities related to the U.S. and global HO launches. Weighted average common shares outstanding were approximately 69 million for the third quarter. GAAP EPS was a net loss per basic and diluted share of $0.61, including $0.01 per share from accrued dividends on convertible stock of $1.0 million. Cash used in operations was approximately $3 million during the quarter. We ended the third quarter with $320 million in cash equivalents, and short-term investments, as I mentioned previously. Looking ahead to slide 28, for the second final quarter of this year, we are updating our annual OpEx guidance.

We now anticipate approximately $360 million-$380 million in non-GAAP operating expenses for 2026, comprised of non-GAAP R&D of $165 million-$175 million and non-GAAP SG&A of $195 million-$205 million. SG&A guidance has changed very little. The midpoint of R&D has been reduced by $15 million due to research and formulation development activities planned to take place in late 2026, now likely occurring in early 2027. As a reminder, non-GAAP operating expenses exclude stock-based comp and milestone payments associated with licensing agreements. Therefore, our guidance will not be affected by the recognition of the upfront payments due to LG Chem. With that, I will turn the call back over to David.

David Meeker: Thank you, Hunter. Hopefully you have heard again this morning. Really excited about where we are. Confirming, I think, after two quarters of launch, the potential of aHO. I think we made great progress there and expect that to continue, and very much looking forward to accelerating development of our next-generation assets, and as I said in my comments, updating you about future developments in the pipeline in 2027. With that, we will open it up for questions.

Operator: Thank you. As a reminder, to ask a question, please press star one on your telephone and wait for your name to be announced. To withdraw your question, please press star one again. Again, as a reminder, please limit to one question. Our first question comes from Phil Nadeau with TD Cowen. Your line is now open.

Phil Nadeau: Good morning, and congrats on a really strong quarter. Thanks for taking our question. Our question, I think, is the obvious one on what you are expecting for patient dynamics over the next quarter or two. It does seem like you are adding about 100 PSFs per month. Is that sustainable? Where do you think you are in patient recruitment at this point in the launch? Thank you.

Jennifer Lee: Thanks for the question. I think overall, I would just say that we're still early in the launch, and there's so much opportunity that remains. I was happy to see that overall, in terms of what we reported out Q2 versus Q3, that volume in terms of RXs has not slowed down, and that remains the case even early into Q4. There's still, in terms of opportunities, I would say probably the lowest hanging fruit is physicians who have a diagnosed patient. This is the quickest to convert, especially if they already have experience treating this patient with other therapies and they realize that they need something more, just in terms of IMCIVREE treatment.

We have educated a lot of physicians along the way who have identified a potential aHO patient that they suspected, and so they need to go through that validation process as that patient comes in for the next visit, and then ultimately have that discussion around IMCIVREE treatment. We also have physicians who are used to and already have patients who are on another therapy, and this was probably because IMCIVREE wasn't available at that time, and they want to wait and see how the patient does before they think about Rxing for IMCIVREE specifically, as well as a lot of other physicians that are still on our list that we need to educate.

All of this is going to take time to unlock, with some opportunities quicker than others. But I feel very confident in terms of our ability to continue on with that disease as well as product education moving forward.

Phil Nadeau: That's very helpful. Thank you.

Operator: Thank you. The next question is going to come from Derek Archila with Wells Fargo. Your line's open.

Derek Archila: Hey, good morning, and congrats on the progress here. Beyond the reimbursed patients, it seems like they increased 20% quarter-over-quarter. It does seem access has improved materially with two-thirds of patients essentially getting reimbursed or paid for by 60 days. I guess, how does that continue to trend from start form to paid patient conversion, and ultimately, how should we be thinking about that in 2027? Thanks.

Jennifer Lee: Sure. From an access perspective, we are very happy. I think, once again, all of that groundwork done to educate the payers to differentiate our patient population, that just flowed through in terms of what we're seeing on the access side for aHO, and potentially for any future approvals as well. I would say that the speed in terms of the approvals from Rx to actually getting payer approval has been quicker than what we saw during the BBS launch for that reason.

However, I will say that where we are, even though the percentage of covered lives is still a work in progress throughout the rest of this year as P&T meetings happen, we're already at a similar pace of approval times that we are with BBS. I don't expect that timeline in terms of approvals to dramatically increase as we increase the number of aHO-specific policies that we have in place. We've had the ability to get approvals even without a policy in place specific for aHO because of all that, once again, background work. I would say that the pace would stay the same just in terms of Rx to approvals moving forward.

Operator: The next question comes from Tazeen Ahmad with Bank of America. Your line's open.

Tazeen Ahmad: Hi, guys. Good morning. Thanks for taking my question. How should we be thinking about the, I guess, the slope of the launch, given all the dynamics that you've mentioned? You've been careful to say that we should expect to see steady uptake, but once it becomes easier to get insurance payments, once those turnaround times normalize to where you expect it to be, and once more physicians are educated on the drug itself, should we expect to see any acceleration from the rate that we're seeing right now? Thanks.

Jennifer Lee: Yeah. I think that the reality is just what it looks like just in terms of a lot of different rare diseases and the different states in terms of where those physicians are. It just takes time to go from even suspecting, and then diagnosing, and ultimately, especially in a realm where they may have been used to prescribing another drug because IMCIVREE wasn't available, making that turn in terms of their actual experience with our drug and that process changing. The other reality is that these physicians are extremely busy.

Their practices are so busy, and just in terms of that ability to go through those steps, through the busy practice of that patient coming in iteratively, will also take some time. That's why we outline just in terms of that steady pace. But once again, confidence just in terms of what this launch will look like, as we're just very early.

David Meeker: Yeah, and just to build a little bit on what Jennifer said, the steadiness, and I think the key part of her answer is, there's elements of a rare disease launch in this, which is patient by patient. There's individual factors which may impact how quickly an individual patient is able to get to a diagnosis, get seen by their physician, and get on treatment. What is strikingly different and why the opportunity here is so much different than BBS is that the epi is fundamentally different, and the concentration of patients is fundamentally different. So steady as it goes, but with a very different potential, longer-term potentially. Next question.

Operator: The next question comes from Mike Ulz with Morgan Stanley. Your line's open.

Mike Ulz: Good morning. Thanks for taking the question, and congrats on the strong quarter as well. Maybe just another follow-up on the HO launch. Can you talk about the level of awareness you're seeing among the endocrinologists, since the launch, you're a little bit, two quarters over into the launch, and just want to get a sense of where that is and how that could evolve going forward. Thanks.

Jennifer Lee: I will say that when we started our education, our disease education efforts, which started even before our approval, there was a strikingly large opportunity to actually educate the physicians on what acquired HO actually was. That still remains the case, just in terms of that ability to differentiate and outline that the weight gain in this patient population is not attributable just due to things around other hormones being administered to these patients, differences in lifestyle just because of a surgical procedure, et cetera, et cetera.

I think we have made progress for sure in terms of our efforts across our teams through different forums, in addition to the 101s, but there's a lot more physicians for us to educate to, once again, make them understand that, similar to other hormone deficiencies, the cause of HO is based off of the injury that is caused through that procedure and management of the tumor. More opportunity to continue on, though very happy at least with the progress that we've made today.

David Meeker: And Mike, I would contrast this again with Prader-Willi, where it is a genetic diagnosis. There is no challenge in a sense of getting to a diagnosis in almost all patients, whereas this is a clinical diagnosis. And as Jennifer said, some of these features can be seen in other settings, other diseases, and so getting to a diagnosis is different. And that is the work that is done, and that is the rare disease effort. And so, tremendous opportunity to continue to increase awareness, as she said.

Operator: Thank you. And the next question is going to come from Paul Matteis with Stifel. Your line is open.

Matthew: Hi there. This is Matthew on for Paul. Thank you so much for taking our question. I guess I wanted to dig into, for the acquired HO population, what has the retention rate on drug been, and how does that compare relative to your early BBS launch? Thank you.

Jennifer Lee: Yeah. So, the retention of our HO patients, it is early in the launch. We expect that the patients that are probably the most motivated may start early on. The retention has been strong to date, and the vast majority have remained on drug. I will say that our confidence in this particular patient population is a bit different in terms of that retention piece of what we expect compared to BBS, primarily because, one, this perceived lack of efficacy is a bit different because of the strength in terms of that BMI reduction that we saw in our clinical study in this particular patient population, for example.

Other factors may include the fear or the burden of injections, and this patient population is more used to having injectable therapies due to their other hormone deficiencies. So, there are differences, I would say, holistically in terms of this particular population, where we feel that their retention may be a bit different than BBS. But it's early, and it's something that we're going to continue to monitor as we move forward.

Operator: Our next question will come from Priyanka Grover with J.P. Morgan. Your line's open.

Priyanka Grover: Hi, guys. Congrats on the quarter. One thing you mentioned in the beginning of the call is, Japan may be the second-largest market for you guys. Yann Mazabraud: Yes, for sure. First, as you just said, the prevalence is meaningful. Two, we have in Japan a very well-organized healthcare system. Three, we have a national coverage with a good price. Those are extremely positive aspects, especially for a rare disease where patients sometimes are difficult to find. I think that the 1,000 patients that we have already identified tells our efforts are paying and how many patients are there.

David Meeker: Priyanka, Europe obviously, to Yann's point about a single country, that 10,000 in Europe is spread across countries with very different dynamics. The accessibility of a slightly smaller epi, 5,000 to 8,000, as opposed to the accessibility of the full 10,000 in Europe is just fundamentally different. All those reasons would say, yeah, Japan's a tremendous opportunity for us.

Priyanka Grover: Thanks for answering my question.

Operator: Thank you. The next question is going to come from Whitney Ijem with Canaccord. Your line is open.

Whitney Ijem: Hey, guys. Mike, and congrats on the quarter. Another one on Japan, and sorry if I missed this, but can you talk about where you landed on price, and I guess the trajectory, or how we should be thinking about the trajectory of price over time in Japan? Is it more similar to U.S. or Europe as we think about annual price changes? Then just the second part of that question, do you plan to provide any patient start form or any other of those types of metrics as we watch the Japanese launch? Thanks.

Yann Mazabraud: Yes, thank you. First of all, we are pleased with the price we achieved. One, it is consistent with the rare disease prices, and also it is consistent with what we were expecting and what we have forecasted. The price is public, and it is $2,200 per vials, which is 60% to the U.S. WAC, which is also very good compared to the U.S. rare disease drugs. The second questions, or the related questions in terms of long-term price, it is a price which is set for the next 10 years.

Of course, there are some capping processes, as you can imagine, but we are also here very comfortable with where we are with MHLW estimated peak and how this price should be maintained in the upcoming years.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question will come from Samantha Semenkow with Citi. Your line is open.

Samantha Semenkow: Hi, good morning. Congratulations on the quarter, and thanks for taking the question. I have one on Prader-Willi. I am wondering if you could just talk a bit about the decision to run a six-month hyperphagia-focused study. Will you include BMI changes in this initial study, or will that be a separate BMI-focused study? I am wondering what you think you need from both an FDA approval perspective, but also a payer utilization perspective in terms of hyperphagia versus BMI, or both for utilization. Thank you.

David Meeker: Yeah. Thanks, Samantha. Let me try to fill in a little bit on the Prader-Willi here. We will run a six-month hyperphagia study, as I said in my initial comments. That is based on, one, we see that change. It is a very important part of this disease. It fits with the mechanism of our drug. We do satiety signal patients get reduced hyperphagia, and that translates into changes in the HQ-CT, as we have seen in the six-month data we presented, number one. Two, when Soleno, now Neurocrine, when their drug, VYKAT, was approved by the FDA, as is often the case with first approvals, they set a bit of a precedent and a template for others to follow.

I think we have heard indirectly that probably is a reasonable assumption to make, that a six-month hyperphagia study is acceptable and, if positive, is approvable. BMI changes, weight, we know from our other development efforts in the MC4R pathway diseases, those are 12 months. The regulators want to see sustainability of that BMI change over 12 months. If that was the primary, the expectation is that would have been at 12 months. From a very practical standpoint, this is a shorter and more direct route for approval. Your second question was, will we collect BMI in this? Absolutely. Will BMI change in six months? Yes.

We have seen that already in the six month, and so we would expect those positive results to be reflected in the label. Now, it will not be in a primary indication, but it will, like I said, we do expect that to be in the label. And from a payer standpoint, again, I think VYKAT's a good example, in rare diseases, payers tend to be very They stick to the label, right? They do not tend to interpret. You do not tend to get step edits for unapproved therapies and the like.

And so if you get an approved drug in Prader-Willi, again, we can expect that it will be used, and they would not differentiate on whether hyperphagia was our primary endpoint or BMI, is my opinion.

Seamus Fernandez: Oh, great. So, David, on the PWS side of things, it does seem like your conviction is quite a bit higher for the overall portfolio opportunity, but interested to just better understand, maybe from you and Hunter, the buy-down opportunity that you saw with the royalty, and what the drivers of your expectations are for what looks like a very robust assumption for peak sales potential. How much did PWS weigh into that, or was this kind of primarily your views of the global aHO market opportunity, and sort of the switch opportunity that you see moving from setmelanotide over to the new portfolio of assets? Thanks.

David Meeker: Yeah. Thanks, Seamus. It was really, as I said in my comments, the two major drivers here were, number 1, as you know, we are running the phase III biva in HO. It will be the first next-generation product approved in HO. It does not have hyperpigmentation. It is an oral, lots of advantages. We think it will drive an incremental opportunity in the HO space, which we already think is large. And so, that just economically said, if we can lower our royalty burden overall in that context, that made sense.

But the second factor, back to your question of strategy and how do we think about developing it, the original agreement did have a part of it which said if we develop bivamelagon in new indications, there is an incremental royalty associated with that decision. For example, Prader-Willi, if we were to develop it in Prader-Willi, then yes, that would have carried a higher burden, and we didn't want to be constrained by that. We're starting with biva because it's available, and as I said, supply issues are driving that near-term decision.

But we very much like having both next-generation assets available, particularly for our two major options, but in general, to be able to make decisions around the portfolio totally driven by the science. So, turn it over to Hunter for thoughts on that.

Hunter Smith: Yeah, I'll just add one thing, Seamus, which is we did multiple scenarios to analyze the economics of this deal and the opportunity here, and we based our analysis on essentially the potential reduction in royalties against the risk-adjusted sell-side consensus. So, we were comfortable doing the transaction on that basis. If we were to outperform that consensus, either because probability of success goes up or the top line unadjusted revenue goes up, that represents greater upside to the transaction. We think we're shaving about 5%. You have to make a couple of assumptions on what was going to be approved, but 5% against sell-side consumptions yields to a pretty good payback relatively quickly.

Seamus Fernandez: Great. If you don't mind my just a quick follow-up on that, was this initiated by Rhythm, or was this kind of a competitive buy-down situation just because we know there are other royalty players out there?

Hunter Smith: It was initiated by Rhythm.

Seamus Fernandez: Perfect. Thanks so much.

Basma Radwan: Good morning, and thank you for taking our question, and congrats on the quarter. One question on aHO. Were you able to identify more patients with suspected aHO diagnosis than the 2,000 identified earlier in the launch? How does Rhythm help with this process and the conversion from suspected to confirmed diagnosis? Do you guys provide help with the brain scans, like the way you did with genetic testing for kids for BBS and the monogenic indication? That is it. Thank you for this. Thank you.

Jennifer Lee: Yeah. We continue to The more we are out there, the more physicians we educate, the more physicians are suspecting and getting patients to an aHO diagnosis. That number has continued to rise since we released that back in September, over a year ago. We are using more different metrics now post-launch relating to Rx volume and such, just to be more holistic in terms of patients identified and ultimately getting to an Rx, and that will be the metric that we use moving forward. In terms of our help, I would say that it is just education.

It is not necessarily These patients do not have a genetic testing that can be supported through our URO program, but it is the combination of do they have an injury? Once again, we were really happy that our label is broader than just tumors. So, do they have an injury that resulted in hypothalamic dysfunctions, which can be measured by the need for different hormonal treatments? Do they have weight gain because of this and associated with that timing? There are just a couple of different pieces of education to make that physician put those pieces together for that particular patient to get to that diagnosis.

David Meeker: And it's fundamentally very different, obviously, from BBS. I think when Jennifer's teams are out there talking to physicians who might potentially see a BBS patient, just given the epidemiology and the nature of that rare disease opportunity, the odds are each individual patient, the probability they may see a BBS patient is low. When we're talking to endocrinologists, the teams that are out there, the probability, A, is high, and B, the clinical diagnosis, the clinical phenotype that drives that diagnosis, as Jennifer just described, is highly recognizable. This isn't one where they have to stretch to try to remember or do a special test to figure out if that disease is present.

These are very obvious parts of the presentation. So, the diagnosis is readily made once you know what you're looking for. Next question.

Operator: Thank you. The next question is going to come from Lisa Walter with RBC Capital. Your line's open.

Lisa Walter: Oh, good morning. Thanks for taking our question. Given that this is the second full quarter of the HO launch, just curious if you can share which payer group most patients are coming from, whether that be Medicare or the commercial population. Could we also expect any seasonality in the first quarter, as some patients may change insurers or care providers in the new year? Any color here would be helpful. Thanks so much.

Jennifer Lee: Sure. Just in terms of the payer background, I would say that where we are right now in terms of percentage of Rxs that come from commercial and Medicaid payers is very much similar to the BBS, with the majority of those being commercial and Medicaid. I think what is interesting, and a positive, is that there are a bit more commercial payers on the HO side versus Medicaid payers. But we expect that there are going to be a lot of things that evolve over time, perhaps potentially the age mix of patients, which also may impact the payer mix and such, and it's one thing that we will continue to monitor moving forward.

From an insurance perspective, this is a dynamic that happens every single year, just in terms of for any drug out there, they may be impacted as patients are going through an insurance change. We have experienced in the beginning of the first quarter or in the first quarter, a bit of a bump up in terms of our patients on our bridge or free drug program, as we may have to temporarily bridge them onto this free drug therapy until we're able to get reimbursement on their new insurance plan. So, that's a dynamic that has happened year over year, and I imagine is the same for any drug as well.

Operator: Thank you. The next question's going to come from John Wolleben with Citizens. Your line's open.

Catherine: Hi, this is Catherine on for John. I just want to follow up on PWS. Can you just discuss a little bit about differentiation on hyperphagia of bivamelagon versus other programs, and any learnings from earlier programs as far as what we can expect as far as the placebo rate, and what is clinically meaningful as far as benefit over placebo? Thank you.

David Meeker: Sure. Prader-Willi, again, I do not need to remind all of you, it is just an incredibly challenging disease, and there is a reason almost all therapies, with the exception of VYKAT, and there have been many multiple attempts, have failed to date. We are very respectful of that, number 1.

Number 2, the placebo rate, there is a placebo rate for hyperphagia, absolutely, and part of the reason we will be running a six-month trial, although a shorter trial might be acceptable from a regulatory standpoint, is to make sure that we move well beyond that period of time, which might be, I would say, once you get out beyond 3-4 months, that placebo effect should absolutely have worn off. I think a six-month trial, we feel confident that will show that. The magnitude of the difference, that threshold has been set, again, by the VYKAT approval. That was on the order of 5 points or less. Obviously, we have not engaged with regulators yet, and that could evolve.

I expect them to more or less follow precedent there, and that would be our threshold of what we would be looking to achieve.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question comes from Kalpit Patel with Wolfe Research. Your line's open.

Kalpit Patel: Yeah. Hey, good morning, and thanks for taking the questions. For the launch, can you break down the new aHO start forms by month for the third quarter and sort of characterize how that pace has been heading into October and November? #3210. Developers can now create advanced ‘app skills’ for Siri AI

Apple today announced a major new Siri AI initiative for third-party developers, allowing any app to create Siri AI integrations for the first time. The first versions of Siri AI were limited to a much smaller set of supported schemas.

The new ‘app skills’ also let apps teach Siri how to coordinate complicated multi-step actions. These features will become available as part of iOS 27.3, macOS 27.3, and aligned releases.

The app skills sound very similar to what other LLM-driven AI models offer, enabling richer understanding of complicated tasks.

For example, a flight tracking app skill will be able to cleanly map what app intents Siri should use to service a particular kind of user request; something that the first version of Siri AI was simply incapable of doing.

Of course, Apple itself has also taken advantage of the new Siri AI foundational features, with a significant rollout of new capabilities across Apple’s apps.

Here’s an example of what Siri will be able to do, from the developer documentation:

Siri can find custom content from one app, transfer it to a specified app, and perform an action. For example, somebody might request “Hey Siri, send my favorite sneakers to my partner in name of a messaging app.” Siri finds sneakers that the person added to their favorites, understands who the partner is, finds them in Contacts, then sends the sneaker information to them using the messaging app.

It’s also going to be a lot easier to initiate Siri actions for third-party apps. With the 27.3 update, users don’t have to explicitly mention the app’s name in many circumstances. For instance, if a Live Activity for a ride-sharing app is active, Siri will automatically understand that a request to “change the ride address” corresponds to the app driving the Live activity.

This gives you a sense of the kinds of things Siri will be able to do with the 27.3 release, coordinating more complicated actions across Apple and third-party apps. The new OS releases are in developer beta right now.

#3209. I’m finally ready for a smart calendar – why the Echo Show 16 stands out

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

I'm finally ready to upgrade to a smart calendar - and Amazon's newest Echo device looks like an organizational solution for my family and I.

I’ve never claimed to be the most organized person, and I’m fully aware I need to take steps to be more on top of appointments, schedules, to-do lists, and everything that comes with family life. I’ve been tempted by smart display calendars like the Skylight, but they seemed a little gimmicky and expensive for what’s essentially a large tablet. (ZDNET’s Maria Diaz argues against that gimmick notion, by the way.)

The Echo Show 16, though, might just be the device that gets me to take the leap.

Also: Echo Show 16 makes Apple’s 7-inch HomeView look puny

When I first saw this device, I admit, it wasn’t the first thing to catch my eye. But then I started learning more about what it can do — and now I’m ready to boot my Echo Show 5 for an upgrade. It won’t be a cheap upgrade (I’ll address that later), but if it does what Amazon is promising, it’ll be more than worth it to me.

The first thing I noticed was how sleek the device looks. Amazon says it has 10% more viewing area than the Echo Show 15, but a frame that’s almost 40% thinner. Since I’ll be opting for a wall mount, I wanted something that wouldn’t be too obtrusive. Since my current device is an Echo Show 5 — the small counter-top version — it’s not exactly comparable. Still, it’ll be a huge upgrade to go from an Alexa device that shows pictures to something much more capable.

The biggest appeal for me is the organization. Amazon says the new Show offers a family hub with color-coded schedules, to-do lists, meal planning, and more. My Google Calendar holds all of that now, but it’s easy to miss a notification. And if I don’t make it a priority to check my app every day (something I need to get better about), it’s easy to miss something.

Also: The 4 biggest Amazon smart home announcements from this week

My current Show can display lists and events, but it doesn’t have a permanently present display.

Another significant upgrade is the camera. My current Show has a camera, but it’s not the greatest, especially at night or in low-light conditions, since it’s 2 MP.  The Echo Show 16 features a wide-angle 13-megapixel lens, the widest field of view on any Echo Show device to date. According to Amazon, this doubles the range of Visual ID from 8 feet to 17 feet (from the previous generation). The Show 16 also adds night vision, making it much easier to keep an eye on your home when it’s dark.

I check in on my dogs several times a day, and my current Show does an OK job, but it’s pretty much useless at night. The improved camera on the Show 16 offers a whole new level of functionality.

My biggest concern? The price. The Echo Show 16 starts at $500. If you add any accessories or upgrade to the anti-glare Nanomatte display, you’re closer to $600. That’s double the price of the similarly sized 15-inch Skylight calendar. At the time I’m writing this, a $100 coupon is available, bringing the price down to $400.

I’m already heavily invested in the Amazon ecosystem, so it makes sense that I’d bring a display into the fold as my new smart home centerpiece. A purchase like this is hardly a necessity, but if it can wrangle just a little of my life’s chaos, it’ll be a worthy investment.

#3208. Over 370,000 Dreo Space Heaters Recalled After 17 Catch Fire

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

The $100 unit was available from outlets including Best Buy and Costco.

Keeping cozy this season comes with an important caveat. Dreo has recalled its DR-HSH015 space heater due to the risk of the unit catching fire.

The recall covers Dreo’s $100 model DR-HSH015, a 13-inch-tall, black ceramic electric heater that came bundled with a remote control. Regulators noted the issue is limited to units manufactured between April 2025 and January 2026, which consumers can verify by checking the date stamped on the bottom of the device.

DREO said it received 17 reports of space heaters igniting, three resulting in property damage and one in a burn injury to the hand.

The company sold over 370,000 units in the US and Canada. The space heater was available from outlets including Home Depot, Best Buy, Kohl’s and Costco, as late as October 2026.

Owners should stop using the recalled space heaters immediately, disconnect them from power, destroy them by cutting off the power cable and contact the company for a free replacement.

Space heaters are a popular way to heat cold rooms, and CNET’s own tests found that properly functioning units can help owners reduce their energy bills over winter.

#3205. Samsung adds better sleep tracking to Galaxy Watches – here’s what to expect

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The FDA-approved sleep apnea tracking feature will first come to the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2, Watch 9, and Ring.

Samsung’s sleep-tracking feature has been around on the Samsung Galaxy Watch for a few years now, but it recently got an upgrade: A new AI algorithm, that can deliver more detailed sleep reports than Samsung’s previous sleep apnea detection technology.

Users can see the insights behind their breathing disorders each hour. Prior to this update, the smartwatch would simply detect whether or not a user had sleep apnea but would not provide details on the condition’s specifics or timing.

Users wear a Galaxy Watch to sleep for a few nights, and the sleep apnea results are divided into three stages: mild, occasional, and frequent. Samsung says this classification allows for greater specificity in condition management.

Many smartwatch and health tracker companies have implemented some sleep apnea detection features on their devices. The often underdiagnosed condition impacts around 30 million Americans, according to the American Medical Association (AMA). It’s a condition with gateway effects: if it goes untreated, it can lead to high blood pressure, heart disease, and impaired focus, according to the AMA. Despite sleep apnea’s prevalence, it’s highly treatable — and a great example of wearables passively detecting conditions at home.

Of course, the Galaxy Watch can’t aid in the treatment plan of a sleep apnea diagnosis.

The feature will be available in Korea first, starting in November, with no confirmed date for when it will arrive on US Samsung watches and smart rings. The FDA-cleared feature will first come to the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2, Watch 9, and Ring. Samsung says an update will bring the advanced sleep apnea detection to Galaxy Watch 7 and 8 through future software updates.

To use the feature, a Galaxy user will need to record two nights of sleep within a 10-day period to learn details about their condition.
