On a year to date basis, adjusted EBITDA margins were up 8 basis points Interest expense for the third quarter was $34 million, a $5 million improvement versus the prior year period driven by our repricing actions and last year's $75 million term loan pay down. Adjusted EPS increased to $0.29 per diluted share an improvement of 12% versus the prior year. Now let's review our segment performance. Sterigenics delivered revenue growth of 8.5% to $209 million or 8.2% on a constant currency basis, driven by favorable pricing of 4.8% increased volume and mix of 3.4% and a foreign currency benefit of 30-basis points. Segment income increased 9.6% $117 million or 9.2% on a constant currency basis.

Reflecting continued operating leverage and strong execution. Segment income margin improved 57-basis points year over year to 56.1%. In Nelson Labs, revenue grew 8.8% to $61 million or 9.2% on a constant currency basis. Growth was driven by strong volume mix of 6.6% and favorable pricing of 2.6%, partially offset by a 40-basis point foreign currency headwind. Revenue growth exceeded expectations as we saw an increase in Expert Advisory Services at activity in the quarter. Nelson Labs segment income rose 2.5% to $19 million or 3% on a constant currency basis. Segment income margin declined 199-basis points. to 32.1% driven primarily by business mix. Favorable pricing of 2.2% was offset by a volume mix decline of 13.7% and a foreign currency headwind of 90-basis points. I would also like to mention that although Nordion's revenue was down for the quarter, it did come in ahead of our expectations driven by earlier than anticipated timing of certain shipments. Nordion's segment income decreased 11.4% to approximately $34 million or 10.4% on a constant currency basis. Margin performance remained strong with segment income margin improving 71-basis points versus Q3 25, to 61.3% driven by operational productivity and favorable pricing. Turning to the balance sheet, cash generation and capital deployment. Year to date, we have generated $228 million in operating cash flow. Including $111 million in Q3.

Demonstrating solid generation during the period. Capital expenditures totaled $105 million during the first 9 months of the year, including $53 million in the third quarter. With adjusted EBITDA in the range of $632 million to $641 million These reported ranges incorporate an estimated 70-basis point foreign currency benefit for the full year, with foreign exchange anticipated to be a headwind of more than 100-basis points in the fourth quarter. We expect full year consolidated adjusted EBITDA margins to be approximately flat versus last year, with anticipated margin expansion at Sterigenics and Nordion offsetting a reduction in Nelson Labs.

Our outlook continues to assume total company pricing for 2026 to be within our long term range of 3% to 4%. As we look to the fourth quarter, we expect growth to moderate from third quarter levels while continuing to benefit from the previously mentioned Expert Advisory services activity. Based on market rates, we are narrowing our 2026 interest expense outlook to a range of $137 million to $140 million Our effective tax rate applicable to adjusted net income remains unchanged at 27% to 28%. On a weighted average basis, we continue to expect a fully diluted share count in the range of 289 million to 291 million Taking these factors into account, we expect to remain on track to deliver adjusted EPS of $0.95 to $1.01 per diluted share in 2026. #3201. Android 17 adoption hits a staggering 1% – why you really should update now

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Mobile OS > Android

Only a quarter of Android phones have even made it to Android 16.

Android 17 adoption hasn’t been speedy. According to the most recent data from heise.de via Android Studio, as reported by Android Authority, Android 17 has reached just 1% of active devices since its release in June 2026.

While Android 16 is finally the most used Google OS for Android devices, at 25.4% of active Android devices, these distribution figures indicate that getting users to upgrade to even newer software is an uphill battle.

It’s true that Android 17 has had less time to reach devices than Android 16 did when the previous distribution snapshot was published, but the minuscule adoption rate underscores how slowly the latest release is infiltrating the Android ecosystem.

Also: How Android 17 stops network snoops and SMS blasters now

Plus, the data show that more Android users than not are running versions that are many years old. I’m all for not fixing what’s not broken, but when Android 14 is the second most widely used version (15.% of devices are still running it), while Android 15 trails not far behind at 14.7%, there’s a pretty large chunk of individuals who may be putting themselves (and their data) at risk.

And it doesn’t end there. Android 13 and Android 11 are still on the table for 11.8% and 10.1% of users, with almost another 10% still using Android 12. That’s about another 30% of users still running Android 13 or older.

Though the numbers indicate that almost 60% of active Android devices are running Android 14 or newer, about 40% of users haven’t even upgraded to Android 14 or later.

Also: This Android 17 setting logs suspicious activity on your phone for troubleshooting

While the numbers are staggering, they’re not surprising. Android updates typically lag behind iOS updates. While the iPhone and its software are both designed, controlled, and distributed by Apple, Android updates must roll out from a single starting point to a wider array of mobile devices and systems to reach users. While Google is responsible for the core of the Android system, those updates must then be curated, reviewed, and pushed to every device that uses Android. This includes phones from Google, Samsung, Nothing, and more, which usually requires adaptations from each manufacturer. Apple’s updates are often adopted faster because there’s no middle entity between iOS and the user, while Android’s process is rather fragmented.

Keep in mind that Google no longer publishes a regularly updated public distribution chart, so this data isn’t from a real-time survey of every Android device. There’s only cumulative adoption data through Android Studio, and these estimates are derived from those figures and cover devices that contacted the Google Play Store during a seven-day period.

It’s always good practice to keep your device updated to the latest available software that your system allows. There are a few great reasons why those eligible for Android 17 should upgrade, including improved features — like the ability to “bubble” apps and stop network snoops and SMS blasters.

#3200. Anthropic Addresses Video Game Cloning With Minor Claude Update

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

There's a fine line between AI creations inspired by video games and those that are infringing copyright.

One of AI’s biggest selling points is its ability to build things quickly. AI models can help users sort through mountains of files, generate videos that have Hollywood studios worried, and create everything from websites and businesses to custom video games. With what’s called vibe coding, ordinary people can build playable video games in minutes using simple text prompts in popular AI tools like OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Google’s Gemini.

But the AI company Anthropic appears to be drawing a line in the sand about what kinds of games its AI model Claude can make. If a Claude user is trying to recreate someone else’s intellectual property, the AI tool will decline to build it.

That’s according to Addy Osmani, an engineering leader at Anthropic who posted on X. He was responding to concerns that Anthropic had changed Claude Opus 5.5 to prevent it from generating copies of existing games, which could violate copyright rules and the company’s usage policy.

“Original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets are meant to keep working,” Osmani said. “We’ll continue to iterate to ensure we’re striking the right balance.”

We added two sentences to Claude Code's prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else's specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy. Original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets are meant to…

He offered to review cases where amateur game developers believe Claude wrongly refused their requests.

A representative for Anthropic didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Anthropic’s stance, as expressed by Osmani, acknowledges that using AI to try to clone a video game, even a simple one, could constitute intellectual property infringement, an issue that predates the rise of AI tools like Claude.

Even with the change, Claude will still generate video games that resemble popular hits from the past few decades. A CNET request to build a game “that resembled Breakout but with the word Claude on each brick” yielded a playable web version of the arcade classic, but not one that any video game fan would mistake for the original.

The same thing happened after Flappy Bird became a hit in 2014, spawning a wave of copycat games in app stores. Copyright infringement of games is complicated, said David Kocan, an intellectual property lawyer at Nixon Peabody who co-leads the firm’s esports and gaming team.

“This is something courts have wrestled with long before AI came along,” Kocan said. “The basic distinction has always been that copyright protects a game’s original creative expression, but generally not its underlying ideas, rules, or gameplay mechanics. Copyright protects the game you created, not the genre you helped popularize.”

You can’t copyright the concept of, say, a battle royal game or a side-scrolling platformer, which is why when a new type of game emerges as a hit, you’ll see many similar games.

“That distinction may sound straightforward in theory, but in practice, the line between borrowing an idea and copying someone’s creative expression can be blurry,” Kocan said. “That’s particularly true in gaming, where so much of the experience combines functional mechanics with creative expression.”

RTB Ruhan, founder and CEO of Null Station, an animation and video game art studio, said that AI has made it”fast and cheap” to cross the line into infringement, allowing people with no art or design skills to clone a popular game. But that doesn’t mean someone can publish or sell a cloned game without running into trouble.

“‘(Claiming) AI made it’ won’t protect them,” Ruhan said.

“Remove the title and logo and ask whether a player could still tell the two games apart,” Ruhan said. “If they can’t, you’ve crossed the line.”

Legal experts CNET spoke with said there are no laws requiring AI companies to outlaw game clones on their tools. But adding those guardrails could prevent trouble down the road, said Eric Blatt, a corporate, securities and intellectual property lawyer at Scale and a former examiner at the US Patent and Trademark Office.

“Anthropic is prudent to tap the brakes here,” Blatt said. “If Claude — Anthropic-owned software operating on Anthropic servers — receives an instruction to copy a game, and if Claude then copies the game, there is a facially plausible argument that Anthropic performed the copying. The chat logs would be a gold mine for the plaintiff’s counsel.”

Blatt said that litigation hasn’t kept pace with AI’s growth, but he thinks lawsuits could quickly follow if a rebuilt game made with AI directly threatens a company’s business model.

But some of those attempts could be stopped before they start if AI models refuse to make exact copies.

“Ultimately, copyright law draws the legal boundaries,” Kocan said. “But AI companies have to decide where they’re comfortable drawing their own. And those aren’t necessarily going to be the same thing.”

Via HomeKit Security Camera, only users registered to the home can view HomeView’s video streams and recordings. Additionally, a green status light will appear, and a chime will sound to alert house dwellers that HomeView is recording or someone is starting a camera stream.

#3197. Starbucks Drive-Thru AI Could Know What You Want Before You Do

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

The company will begin testing AI for some orders, including using a form of customer recognition.

Could an AI barista know you’re craving an iced caramel macchiato? Starbucks says it will begin testing artificial intelligence for drive-up ordering — including recognizing customers as they approach — as the company focuses on integrating more automated tech, CEO Brian Niccol said on last week’s fourth-quarter 2026 earnings call.

The idea is to make ordering “faster, more convenient and more personal” for drive-up customers, which account for roughly half of all Starbucks patrons, according to Niccol. The company would begin testing background AI models for drive-thrus sometime during fiscal year 2027, which ends Sept. 28, 2027. There were no specifics as to where the testing would take place or how it would affect food and drink prices.

Niccol said AI would help input orders “more accurately and efficiently” while the baristas talk to drive-up customers to increase personal connection and speed up service.

The AI could also know what you want, or might want, before you even engage with the human barista. Niccol said the company is exploring ways for automated systems to recognize repeat customers as they drive up and offer “personalized digital menus,” possibly including suggested purchases.

While the exact kind of systems that would be tested to recognize customers weren’t specified, possible methods could include facial recognition, license plate reading or perhaps mobile app detection. It also remains to be seen which methods would require explicit customer consent or offer an opt-out mechanism. In an email to CNET, a Starbucks representative did not confirm which specific technology would be employed.

The representative said that Starbucks is already using AI in its operations through Green Dot Assist, which helps workers look up drink recipes, troubleshoot equipment issues and coordinate staffing. The company also uses Smart Queue to figure out sequencing of orders that come in via in-store, drive-thru, mobile app or delivery.

Several major fast-food chains are using or testing AI to process drive-thru orders, including McDonald’s, Taco Bell, KFC, White Castle and Wendy’s. Customer reviews have been mixed so far, with the main problems being botched orders, lengthy processing and the inability of bots to answer questions, according to customer research from restaurant tech website Canopy.

Burger King, meanwhile, decided to pull back on using AI for drive-thru because some customers drove off rather than place their orders with a bot. The company is still testing AI but said it wants to give people the option of ordering from a human.

It’s unclear what Starbucks’ goal is or what customers the company is trying to appeal to, said Uttara M. Ananthakrishnan, AI researcher and associate professor at the University of Washington. But there’s plenty to be skeptical about.

“AI in face-to-face customer service will fail in many edge cases and has many potential PR problems with no clear benefits,” Ananthakrishnan told CNET. “It is better to defer until there is a broader general acceptance among the public.”

Ananthakrishnan said one flaw of using bots is voice recognition — many AI models are trained on general US accents and don’t perform well with non-native speakers or international accents. Surrounding noise from vehicles and weather can also affect how well the bot understands the customer through a kiosk microphone. That could pose health risks, Ananthakrishnan said, if, for example, someone is allergic to nuts and the AI misinterprets the request as “no nuts.”

McDonald’s ended its AI drive-thru experiment with IBM in 2024, when bots were unable to understand various accents and dialects. The fast-food giant recently launched a new experiment with AI bot Archy as part of an $8.5 billion modernization plan. There was also a fake order that went viral when someone ordered 18,000 waters at a Taco Bell, and the AI processed it.

Most of Ananthakrishnan’s students have said they don’t want to talk to AI during their customer service interactions. However, more people might accept drive-thru AI if they know that mistakes will be rectified quickly, Ananthakrishnan said.

Starbucks has said it doesn’t use surveillance pricing, a discriminatory method that’s been increasingly used by hotels, airlines and retailers. Still, a 2025 report in The Washington Post indicated that loyal customers using the Starbucks app more often might be getting fewer promotional deals.

In a 2026 statement on the use of AI, the company says: “Our business is rooted in human connection — and our technology is designed to strengthen it, not replace it.” But Starbucks’ human connection with its workers has been problematic, and AI isn’t known for improving labor relations.

Since initiating a major organizing blitz starting in late 2021, Starbucks employees have formed unions at nearly 700 stores in the US, demanding higher pay and more robust staffing levels. Workers say they are not given enough hours so the company can avoid providing benefits, and are often given very short notice about shift changes. Last year, the NLRB said Starbucks “engaged in a scorched earth campaign and pattern of misconduct in response to union organizing.”

Since taking over as CEO in September 2024, Niccol has cut more than 2,000 employees as part of his Back to Starbucks strategy, which has resulted in simplified menus, reduced wait times and the closure of some shops.

In August, Starbucks Workers United, which represents 12,000 baristas, announced an open-ended national consumer boycott against corporate-owned Starbucks locations. The call accused the company of violating US labor law and attempting to break up the union, while also criticizing the corporate push for AI. “Starbucks has repeatedly demonstrated a lack of care for the workers who fuel the company’s profits by wasting millions of dollars on AI and technology that doesn’t work, launching countless gimmicky drinks designed to distract from real problems, and inventing pointless policies that do nothing but make workers’ jobs harder,” the call read.

In a 2025 interview with Current Affairs, union organizer Jason Woods said the company was trying to use AI to place orders but couldn’t handle staffing when an employee calls out. “They want to use algorithms to deploy our plays,” he said. “It’s inhumane. It’s anti-worker, anti-labor.”

Starbucks Workers United didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Management fees on that capital turned on at that first close and that is reflected in this quarter's management fees.

As a reminder, fees on subsequent closes are retroactive to the date of the first close, so the catch up fees associated with future closes will be recognized when those closes occur. The fund is off to an encouraging start. We have already been able to deploy capital into interesting opportunities that fit squarely within our playbook. Diversified relationship source deals where we believe our market position and existing knowledge give us an edge in underwriting, pricing, and conviction. We look forward to providing additional updates as we continue to progress. Turning to Venture. As we mentioned on our prior call, we held the first close for our latest venture fund last quarter on more than $370 million of commitments.

For context, our first venture fund raised $615 million in total, which means this initial close already represents more than 60% of the size of the first fund. Another strong proof point that our flagship venture platform continues to build real momentum in market. Management fees have already turned on for this latest close. And just as a reminder, this product charges management fees on a committed capital basis and thus every subsequent close will generate retro fees from here until the final close. Alongside these established flagships, we are also advancing a healthy pipeline of newer strategies that we are excited to bring to market in the coming quarters. Which we touched on during our prior call.

So we have launched our inaugural GP led secondary fund, an important step in the continued growth of our secondaries platform. We view this new strategy as a natural complement to our core secondaries platform and a representation of the next phase of growth for our broader secondaries efforts. Building on the platform we have established, we believe GP led secondaries allow us to address an increasingly significant segment of the market and to partner even more closely with GPs as a trusted capital provider.

In credit, our newest credit strategy reflects the next step in reshaping our direct credit platform and is expected to pursue a strategy that spans both diversified lending, which provides financing across the capital structure of mid market businesses, to capture both credit downside protection and equity like upside as well as specialty finance, which targets differentiated less correlated opportunities such as credit secondaries, and asset backed and niche lending transactions. We are encouraged by the progress across both of these efforts. Beyond our larger flagship funds currently in, we have also built a long track record of success with a number of smaller niche closed end platforms that round out our broader specialized fund offerings.

Our third impact fund is a good example. It has now raised nearly $340 million of investor commitments continuing the growth we have seen across each successive vintage of that platform. We have seen similar success over the years scaling several white label and regionally specific vehicles. And in aggregate, these smaller platforms have contributed over $4 billion to our specialized fund business. While each may be modest in size on its own, together they reflect our consistent ability to identify, launch, and scale differentiated products well beyond our flagship offerings. They also show what it means to be a true solutions provider. Having the investment ability to aid clients across all facets of their private market needs.

Taken together, we view this as 1 of the more active and encouraging stretches for our closed end platform. Several of our flagship products are either already in market or will be shortly with a healthy slate of newer launches sitting right behind them. that is been the playbook since our IPO. Grow and scale the existing lineup and tactically layer in new products where we already have the team the deal flow, and the relationships to execute and to do that well. The work continues, and we certainly are not done. Real estate, expanded credit, additional secondary offerings, and co investment offerings are all areas where we expect to keep building. Let me move now to customize separate accounts.

At quarter end, customized separate account fee earning AUM stood at $41 billion and grew $663 million or 2% over the last 12 months, and was up $362 million quarter-over-quarter over quarter. Gross contributions came from a mix of new client wins, plus re up activity from existing clients, plus contributions for investment activity and then being offset by fee based step downs which is largely a timing related impact as well as capital distributions stemming from exit activity. We also added to our separate account dry powder as we executed and closed on $1.7 billion of new total contract mandate value.

This stems primarily from our existing clients in the form of both re ups and the expansion of service lines with existing relationships. Our pipeline of mandates still yet to close also remains healthy. Measured in the multiple of billions in total future contracted mandate value. As we have said before, these mandates do not always convert immediately into fee earning AUM, particularly where the underlying portfolio construction is more heavily oriented towards primary investing, or where there are commitments being made to our transaction products either drawdown or evergreen. There is often a natural pacing element to deployment for the primary element and that timing should be expected.

But what matters most to us is that the capital has been awarded client relationships have been established, and the foundation for future fee earning growth is in place. Again, the total mandate value may not all end up being captured in the customized separate account line, And let me take a step back here because I think it is worth emphasizing the why and not just the what? Our clients understand that optimal portfolio construction requires a mix of strategies, not simply investing in primary funds. You can see that directly in our flows whereby meaningful SMA capital immediately migrates over to specialized funds. And it is not just the mandates already on our books.

It is showing up in the newer mandates and processes we are working through right now. When a client or prospect comes to us to build their private market program, they are explicitly asking us to blend primaries with secondaries and co investment access from day 1. That tells you where the client mindset has shifted. And it tells you that this is not a 1 off trend. It is becoming the default expectation. Which brings me back to something I mentioned earlier on this call. We are expanding our specialized fund lineup and that is not a side project that runs parallel to our separate account business, It is directly additive to it.

Every time we add a vehicle, secondaries fund, a venture strategy, or infrastructure fund, our separate account clients benefit from that same growth because we are able to dial their customized portfolios into the same access points the same deal flow, and the same general partner relations that power our commingled products. That is the flywheel. Our specialized funds get stronger, and our separate account clients ride alongside that strength inside portfolios built specifically for them. Turning now to the technology and data side. Yesterday, we announced a new strategic partnership with FactSet. A leading global financial data analytics and AI solutions provider. The relationship is set to deliver an integrated private market analytics solution for institutional investors.

Institutional investors have long managed public private portfolios in isolation. On separate systems with separate tools. As allocators increasingly think about their portfolios as 1 unified whole, that gap becomes a constraint. Bridging it is key, and we and FactSet recognize that. Through this partnership, our institutional grade private markets data covering more than 70 thousand funds 240 thousand private companies, and our proprietary fund and deal level benchmarks become natively accessible within FactSet's portfolio analytics platform. That is designed to give limited partners institutions, financial advisors, and researchers the ability to performance, identify trends, and build portfolios with real transparency across strategies, vintage years and geographies. The integrated solution breaks down into 3 pieces.

First, proprietary benchmarking, our end, built on decades of high quality private market data become natively accessible inside FactSet's performance measurement environment. Giving clients a differentiated transparent alternative to public index proxies, along with the ability to build and apply custom benchmarks directly into their existing workflows. Second, enhanced risk and commitment pacing models. We are embedding our data directly into FactSet's analytics infrastructure giving allocators better inputs and better engines to act with conviction across their entire portfolio. Third, whole portfolio construction and monitoring. Clients can track public and private exposures in 1 place with performance attribution, and risk analytics that span asset classes. there is a commercial arrangement attached to this as well.

We have secured multiyear annual recurring revenues with an agreed upon floor that is structured to scale with the success of the partnership and reflective of the strategic importance of both the data we are providing and FactSet's ability to deliver best in class public private analytic solutions. The revenue will show up in our reporting, monitoring, and data analytics segment of our management advisory fees going forward. And with that, I will now pass the call to Jeffrey.

Jeffrey Armbrister: Thank you, Erik, and good morning, everyone. For this first half of fiscal 27, we continue to generate solid growth in our business. Management and advisory fees were up 18% from the prior year period while total fee related revenue was up 29% driven by strong growth in our fee related performance revenues. Specialized fund management fees increased by $46 million or 27% compared to the prior year period. This was driven primarily by a $6 billion increase to fee earning AUM in our Evergreen platform. An approximately $1 billion increase from our latest direct equity fund over the last 12 months and the first close of our latest secondary fund.

Moving on to customized separate accounts, revenue decreased slightly compared with the prior year period. This was due to 1-time true-ups for separate accounts committing to specialized fund products. Revenue from our reporting, monitoring, data, and analytics offerings increased by nearly $3 million or 15% compared to the prior year period as we continue to produce strong growth in our technology solutions offering. Lastly, the final component of our revenue is incentive fees, which totaled $154 million for the period. Amount includes fee related performance revenues, stemming from the quarterly crystallization of performance fees from certain of our evergreen funds. Let's turn now to our unrealized carry balance.

The balance is up 11% from the prior year period even while having recognized $107 million of incentive fees excluding fee related performance revenues, during the last 12 months. The unrealized carry balance now stands at approximately $1.6 billion. Moving on to expenses. Fiscal year to date total expenses increased $57 million or 27% compared with the prior year period. Total compensation and benefits increased $39 million or 26% due primarily to increases in operating performance headcount. G&A increased by $18 million primarily driven by revenue related expenses consolidated funds, technology expenses and 1 time benefits in the prior year period.

Revenue related expenses include the third party commissions related to our US Evergreen funds along with other Evergreen Fund platform fees, closed-end fund placement agent fees, and fund reimbursement expenses, which are expected to lead to corresponding revenue over time. Increasing these expenses is a good thing and can be an indicator of growth to come. We continue to successfully offset this with cost savings expense discipline in other parts of the business where we have discretion. Moving to FRE. Fiscal year to date FRE came in at $250 million and was up 34% relative to the prior year period while FRE margin year to date came in at 52% compared to 50% for the prior year period.

Both FRE and FRE margin benefited from strong year to date fee related performance revenues. Let me turn to the balance sheet. The largest piece of it remains our GP commitments alongside clients in our customized separate accounts and specialized funds. We do not think of these commitments as simply a line item. We view them as a genuine long term growth driver, and we intend to keep deploying our own capital alongside our clients' capital. When this part of the balance sheet grows, it indicates something important. We are growing with our existing clients, winning new ones, raising larger and more numerous vehicles and making sound investment decisions along the way.

We see that growth as a clear signal that the business is flourishing we expect it to remain that way. Another important part of our balance sheet investments are the commitments we have made to technology and strategic partnerships. Last quarter, we mentioned events on 3 investments, Securitize, Canoe, and Russell, and I wanted to provide an update on each of these. First on Securitize, the business combination closed in the reporting period, which resulted in a $15.6 million gain included in the non operating gain net line of our income statement.

We now hold approximately 1.5 million shares of securitized, which trades under the ticker SECZ, will be marked to the publicly traded share price at the end of each quarter going forward. Our shares remain subject to a 180-day lockup period after which we will continue to evaluate the position. Respect to CANU, their acquisition by Bloomberg was closed in October, which resulted in a $17 million gain in the third quarter of fiscal 27. Lastly, the announced acquisition of Russell by a consortium led by B Capital and CalPERS is expected to close in the first quarter of calendar year 27. Subject to regulatory approvals and other customary closing conditions.

Assuming the transaction closes as expected, we would anticipate recording a gain of approximately $18 million at that time. Let me close with 1 further point on this. We expect to continue to use our balance sheet tactically to help products get off the ground. In practice, that is generally meant providing seed capital and for a period of time consolidating those vehicles onto our balance sheet during the ramp up and scaling phases. That consolidation can introduce some noise into our financials, but we view it as a short term phenomenon. Objective is always to deconsolidate once initial stake is diluted down as the product scales and brings in outside capital. More importantly, want to underscore the broader point.

We have meaningful capacity on our balance sheet and the ability to deploy it tactically in support of continued growth. We believe this is an important part of how we run the business and we will continue to evaluate these opportunities going forward. On the liability side, our leverage profile remains modest and consistent with where we have managed leverage historically. With that, thank you all for joining us. we will turn it over for Q&A.

#3193. Take Care of That New iPhone Duo, Because Repairs Could Cost Up to $1,500 Without AppleCare

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Apple's pricey and intricate folding phone could lead to a costly repair if something happens to it.

The first iPhone Duos are now in customers’ hands, and we’re seeing in real time what happens when years of confidential Apple design meets the real world for the first time. Although reports still seem limited, several just-unboxed units are suffering from dramatic cracks on the inner screen. CNET is doing our own testing of the phone’s hinge by continuously opening and closing an iPhone Duo — which is now up to more than 200,000 times.

Apple has already promised to replace cracked units, a repair that also falls under the phone’s one-year warranty, but what if a crack or some other defect appears outside that window of time? Should owners and potential buyers add AppleCare Plus for their new Duo? (Or at the very least, an iPhone Duo case?) Based on Apple’s repair prices, it might not be a bad investment — unless you’re JerryRigEverything, whose warranty is most definitely voided.

After all, the iPhone Duo starts at expensive and goes up to exorbitant for its higher-capacity configurations. If something happens and you need a repair, the costs could be substantial without AppleCare coverage.

The base 256GB storage option is priced at $1,999, but if you want to max out Apple’s new foldable phone with 2TB of space, it’ll cost $3,199. That’s pricey by iPhone standards, compared to the iPhone 18 Pro that begins at $1,199, though in line with the retail prices of Android folding phones like the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra and Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold.

Adding AppleCare coverage on top of the iPhone Duo’s price is an ongoing cost in addition to the price of the phone, but in terms of potential repairs, it does make sense. Because if you don’t fork out for a plan, and the inner display of your iPhone Duo gets crunched, expect to pay $999 to get it replaced, according to Apple’s support documentation. These are prices for repairs made directly by Apple, not third-party services.

The range of repairs starts at a modest $49 for “cover layer damage” and jumps all the way up to $1,499 for “other damage,” though it’s not clear what the latter entails. Here’s the breakdown:

AppleCare Plus with Theft and Loss is priced at $20 per month or $200 per year until canceled and includes “unlimited repairs for accidents like drops and spills” and theft and loss coverage for up to two claims every 12 months. It also features Express Replacement Service, which gets you a new iPhone Duo instead of waiting for a repair.

Alternatively, the AppleCare One service costs $20 a month until canceled and applies AppleCare Plus to up to three devices. It also adds a third theft-and-loss coverage event in the 12-month span.

If something happens to your iPhone Duo under AppleCare, the repair pricing ranges from zero for battery service to $149 for theft or loss. The list of repair services doesn’t match up exactly to the ones noted without coverage. Here’s what Apple details as estimated costs:

Keep in mind these are the amounts provided by Apple’s services. If you’re purchasing the iPhone Duo through a wireless carrier, it might have different warranty options.

We’re looking forward to testing not just how well the iPhone Duo works, but how resilient Apple’s most complex iPhone will be. In the meantime, be sure to check out our review of Apple’s first foldable and ask yourself if the iPhone Duo is really for you.

#3192. Firefox’s new Mini Window is every multitasker’s dream – Chrome can’t do this

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The open-source browser's newest feature lets you pop out a page - or part of a page - into its own mini window. See why this is incredibly cool.

The developers at Mozilla are always hard at work to make Firefox the most useful browser on the market. To that end, they’ve added a new feature (still in beta), called Mini Window. I started using Mini Window as soon as it appeared in Firefox Nightly, and I’ve been very happy with how it performs.

Also: Why I’m sticking with Firefox as my browser

The idea behind the Firefox Mini Window feature is simple: allow users to move a currently open tab (or a section of a tab) into a separate mini window. Think of it as moving a tab from one window to what appears like a web app. Essentially, I can move a page (or section) into what looks like a browser window, minus the browser bits. At first blush, there’s no address bar, controls, scroll bar, or anything else that would normally be associated with Firefox. The Mini Window appears to be a web app, without having to actually create it.

However, when I hover my cursor inside the Mini Window, I do see the address bar, the back/foward/reload buttons, and the window close button– and that’s it. The browser gets out of your way, so the only thing I see is the content.

Also: Firefox and Chrome patch 200+ security flaws combined

On top of that (pun intended), the Mini Window stays on top of other Firefox windows, so I can have that popped-out content always in focus while I work on other things. This feature comes in handy when I’m working with limited display space (say, on a laptop) and need to reference a page while working on another. For multitasking, it comes in very handy.

Using the Firefox Mini Window feature is quite simple, but until the feature comes out of beta, it can only be found in Firefox Nightly. I’ve been using Nightly as my default browser on both Linux and MacOS for some time now and have yet to run into a problem (YMMV).

For those who don’t want to risk using a potentially less-than-stable alpha version of Firefox, know that the Mini Window feature is slated to move to stable on November 10. Update Firefox on that day and can start enjoying the feature without upgrading to Nightly.

Until then, you can test Mini Window by installing Firefox Nightly, which can run alongside the stable Firefox release.

Also: Firefox just fixed my biggest annoyance with web browsers

Once I installed Nightly, there was nothing more to do. I didn’t have to enable Mini Window, as it’s already there. I simply had to right-click on an open tab and select Move Tab > Move to Mini Window.

Once I did that, the mini window popped out and hovered over Firefox. If I hovered my cursor over the mini window, the address bar and title bar for the window appeared, so I could drag the pop-up to wherever I needed.

I could also open a specific section of a tab in a Mini Window. To do that, I highlighted the section in question, right-clicked the section, and then clicked Move Section to Mini Window.

Let’s say I’m writing a paper on Linux and need to read a particular article for background information. I could have my document open in the main window, and then open the article in question in a Mini Window. I could then reference the article without having to click back and forth between them — even when working on a smaller display.

Here’s another use case I’ve found: When using MacOS’s Stage Manager feature, I only have one window available at a time. The Mini Window bypasses that limitation, so I can have my main browser window focused as well as the page open in the Mini Window.

Another handy way I like to use Mini Window is to open a favorite search engine, move it to a Mini Window, and then I have an always-ready search tool at my fingertips. I could also open my favorite AI service and use it in the same way.

The closest thing Chrome has to Mini Window is Picture-in-Picture mode and the Mini Player. The caveat to Chrome’s feature is that those two options are only used for video and media playback. The next closest thing Chrome has is the ability to save a website as a web app, which you could then open alongside the main Chrome window. That feature, however, isn’t nearly as flexible as Firefox’s Mini Window option, and it’s not guaranteed to always hover over the main window.
